Note to Accredited Entities on the use of the funding proposal template
• Accredited Entities should provide summary information in the proposal with cross-
reference to annexes such as feasibility studies, gender action plan, term sheet, etc.
• Accredited Entities should ensure that annexes provided are consistent with the details
provided in the funding proposal. Updates to the funding proposal and/or annexes must be
reflected in all relevant documents.
• The total number of pages for the funding proposal (excluding annexes) should not
exceed 60. Proposals exceeding the prescribed length will not be assessed within the usual
service standard time.
• The recommended font is Arial, size 11.
• Under the GCF Information Disclosure Policy, project and programme funding proposals
will be disclosed on the GCF website, simultaneous with the submission to the Board,
subject to the redaction of any information that may not be disclosed pursuant to the IDP.
Accredited Entities are asked to fill out information on disclosure in section G.4.
Please submit the completed proposal to:
fundingproposal@gcfund.org
Please use the following name convention for the file name:
“FP-[Accredited Entity Short Name]-[Country/Region]-[YYYY/MM/DD]”

A
The two main Executing Entities (EE) are FAO and the Government of Malawi acting
through (i) the Ministry of Agriculture (MoA), (ii) the Ministry of Finance and Economic
Affairs, and (iii) the National Local Government Finance Committee (NLGFC). Short
profiles can be found below. More details are provided in Section B.4 and in the
Feasibility Study.
The Government of Malawi acting through;
(i) The Ministry of Agriculture (MoA). MoA – more particularly the Department of Land
Resources Conservation (DLCRC) - originated the Project idea. MoA is strongly engaged
since the beginning of the project design process. Through its network of decentralized
staff, MoA is in a very good position to implement technical activities at local level with
the districts and all the stakeholders of the decentralized local government system i.e.
District Executive Committees (DEC), District Environment Sub-Committee (DESC),
District Director of Agriculture and Natural Resources, Traditional Authorities (TAs),
Group of Village Heads (GVH), Village Natural Resources Management Committee
(VNRMCs).
(ii) The Ministry of Finance and Economic Affairs (MoF). MoF is implementing the IFAD-
funded Financial Access for Rural Markets, Smallholders and Enterprise (FARMSE).
MoF/FARMSE’s development objective is to increase access to, and use of, a range of
sustainable financial services by rural households and micro, small, and medium
enterprises (MSMEs). It has a national coverage and has a strong comparative
advantage to support EbAM in enhancing the financial inclusion of smallholder farmers.
A.20. Executing Entity
information (iii) The National Local Government Finance Committee (NLGFC). NLGFC is the public
constitutional body with the mandate to facilitate fiscal decentralization, financial
management and local development in local governments. As this is the case for the
FAO/GEF-7 funded Sustainable Forest Management, Dryland Sustainable Landscape
Impact Programme - DSL IP, NLGFC will provide procurement services to the EbAM
project, being in charge of investigating sources of supply, obtaining price quotations,
negotiating with suppliers on price and delivery and monitoring the transfer of procured
inputs to the project beneficiaries. Through this partnership, the Project will support
implementation of the Decentralization Act (1998), which devolves powers and funding
from the central government to districts, hence ensure project sustainability, and support
a paradigm shift towards an increased ownership by districts.
FAO will act as an Executing Entity (EE) and will ensure strong country-driven execution
of project activities and will be in charge of the execution of selected activities funded by
GCF proceeds based on its comparative advantages. It will also coordinate the work of
the co-EE supporting EbAM (MoA, MoF and NLGFC – see below). This will allow Malawi
to benefit from the technical and operations experience of a specialized development
assistance agency from the United Nations (UN), while providing opportunities for the
government to increase their capacity through technical assistance and development
and implementation of activities under the three components. FAO will also execute the
activities co-financed by the FAO managed GEF7 project and Technical Cooperatoin
Programme.
Details of activities implemented by each executing entity is provided in section B.4 and
in the Feasibility Study (Annex 2).

GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 4
A
a) Malawi is listed as a Least Developed Country (LDC) by the United Nations (UN), and one of the low
development countries according to the UNDP Human Development Index, and ranks among the 20 most vulnerable
countries in the World by the Notre Dame Global Adaptation Initiative Index 2021, which measures vulnerability to
climate change. For the proposed project, climate vulnerability is defined as a function of climate exposure, climate
sensitivity and climate adaptive capacity. Each of the three aspects is examined in section B.1, which provides the
rationale for the project’s scope and selection of targeted areas. Malawi’s high exposure to climate change can be
characterized by the rise of temperatures, intensification of aridity, rainfalls becoming more erratic, and increased
frequency of climate-changed induced disasters, including droughts and floods. At the same time, the country is very
sensitive to climate change because of its high population density and growth, seriously degraded landscapes and
ecosystems, large rural population in deepening poverty, high food insecurity and precarious health situation. Adaptive
capacity is constrained by the limited literacy rate and low human development. The 11 targeted districts (Dedza in the
Centre; Zomba, Mangochi, Thyolo, Neno, Mwanza, Nsanje in the South ; Nkhata Bay, Rumphi, Karonga and Chitipa in
the North) have all been selected in relation with their high climate vulnerability, with the South being extremely exposed
to climate change, while Northern districts landscapes and ecosystem conditions are characterized by a severe climate
sensitivity, in relation with extreme soil loss and degradation. In all targeted districts, the main climate effects will alter
the onset of the rainy season, translate into limited and modified water availability, increased water stress, with negative
impacts on both cash and subsistence crops, resulting in adverse effects on the overall rural socio-economy and
livelihoods.
b) The proposed Project will address the negative impact pathways from increased temperatures and rainfall
variability leading to climate-induced disasters, all resulting in heightened ecosystem degradation and reduced
agricultural production and productivity. The project’s objective is to increase climate-change resilience of rural
communities at watershed level in Malawi. The project aims to be a catalyst for a broad shift for ecosystem, livelihoods
and agriculture in the country, from their baseline state of very high vulnerability to an alternative paradigm in which
watershed ecosystems are conserved, restored, and sustainably managed, thus granting their adaptation to climate
change and their supply of services to communities, people and their farming systems. To achieve this, EbAM will
promote the locally-led Ecosystems-based adaptation (EbA) approach combined with Integrated Landscape
Management (ILM) to repair degraded ecosystems, and low-carbon climate resilient agricultural practices to allow
agriculture and other livelihoods to become resilient to climate change. The EbA approach – which is the core
transformational driver of the project, involving use of biodiversity and ecosystem services to assist people to adapt to
climate change (see B.3 and Annex 2) - is fully aligned with Malawi’s Updated Nationally Determined Contributions
(NDC), 2021. EbAM will also follow a food system approach – that will aim to create linkages between farmers benefiting
from EbA and national and regional/international value chains. Thus combined, ILM, EbA and food systems
interventions would yield social sustainability, together with environmental sustainability and resilience – hence
delivering on GCF impacts ARA1, ARA2, ARA4 and MR4.
c) EbAM’s scalability, replicability and sustainability will be enabled by different factors, including: (i) the
integration of EbA in village- and catchment-level planning processes, farmer field school (FFS) programs and national
policies, contributing to the creation of an enabling environment around EbA, which will benefit other projects and
programs, (ii) incentives to the private sector to partner with EbA producers through the public-private-producers
partnerships approach, (iii) innovative financing mechanisms, such as support to local financing institutions to develop
new products for financing EbA, with assistance from the MoF/Financial Access for Rural Markets, Smallholders and
Enterprise (FARMSE) Project, (iv) technical assistance to Malawi’s National Climate Change Fund (NCCF) and national
conservation trust funds, which can facilitate further mobilization of catalytic climate finance, in order to sustain, replicate
and expand the scale of EbA investments in other districts/watersheds of the country.
d) The project objective is to increase the climate-change resilience of the most vulnerable rural communities at
watershed level in Malawi. The Project will benefit a total of 574,855 people, target 267,500 hectares under EbA
planning. Within these 267,500 ha, the project will support about 83,240 hectares over 6 years with direct restoration/
EbA management interventions and generate mitigation benefits of -2,750,323 tCO2eq, hence contributing to MR4
(emission reduction). The project will directly contribute to the following targeted results in alignment with the GCF’s
Updated Strategic Plan (USP-2); T1 (by supporting the Country’s adaptation and mitigation goals), T4 Food (270,820
beneficiaries adopting low-emission climate-resilient agricultural practices) and T5 Ecosystems (267,500iii hectares to
be conserved, restored and sustainably managed) through T9 locally-led adaptation approach. The Project will also
support dissemination of climate information to communities through SMS and community radios, directly contributing
to T3 CIEWS. The Project also aligns with T10 (by supporting resilient market chains) and T11 (by supporting the
National Climate Change Fund and local conservation trusts). These impacts will be achieved through the
implementation of three interlinked components (described in section B.2): (i) Integrated landscape management, (ii)
Resilient livelihoods and food systems, and (iii) Enabling institutional and financial environment.

=== PAGE 9 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 5
A
e) Component 1. The objectives of this component are to increase the climate resilience of watershed ecosystems
(Outcome 1.2) and reduce GHG emissions from improved watershed ecosystems (Outcome 1.1). This component will
aim at enhancing ecosystems’ functions at a landscape (watershed) level large enough to facilitate climate change
adaptation at scale. It will use EbA as the main tool to build climate resilience, which will be firmly integrated in local
planning through integrated landscape management, at watershed and village levels. The component will improve
communities’ technical capacity, understanding and know-how, as well as increase stakeholders’ engagement,
including women and other vulnerable groups’, to plan the respective landscape restoration and climate-change
adaptation interventions based on EbA (sub-component 1.1). Through the implementation of integrated management
plans (sub-component 1.2), the project will contribute to generating public goods, most importantly thanks to well-
functioning ecosystems, that are more adapted to extreme climate, and hence increase resilience of landscapes and
livelihoods.
f) Component 2: The objective (Outcome 2) of this component is to stabilize productivity and farmers’ incomes
thanks to more resilient livelihoods and food systems. By enhancing extension services through farmers field schools
- FFS (sub-component 2.1), the Project will increase farmers’ understanding of technical responses to adapt to
changing climatic conditions and enhance their capacity to integrate EbA into their farming systems. The component
activities will support small and medium enterprises (SMEs), producers organisations (POs) and farmers’ groups within
the local food system to access markets (sub-component 2.2) and finance – such as village savings and loans
associations, micro-finance institutions and banks (sub-component 2.3), which are some of the key barriers to EbA
adoption. The component’s interventions, by boosting nature-positive food production and building resilience to
vulnerabilities shocks and stresses, will contribute to build more resilient food systems at local level.
g) Component 3: The objective (Outcome 3) of this component is to enhance the enabling environment (finance
and policies) to sustain, replicate and scale-up climate resilient watershed ecosystems and agriculture practices. It will
contribute to ensure the sustainability of interventions promoted under components 1 and 2. This component will
address the financial and policy barriers of low and volatile investments in integrated landscape management, as well
as the need to propose innovative solutions (support to the National Climate Change Fund, NCCF and local national
conservation trusts; leveraging private sector experience on carbon credits with Climate Asset Management – CAM
and the Restore Africa Program) to attract more climate finance (sub-component 3.1). The integration of EbA in national
plans will allow replication and scale-up of EbA through other projects and programmes. In addition, interventions
mainstreaming and deep-rooting EbA in national policies and investment plans (sub-component 3.2) will bring the EbA
agenda at sectoral policies level – for massive-scale impact and sustainability.
h) The project will be executed by FAO, together with the Government of Malawi, through: (i) the Ministry of
Agriculture – MoA (through the Department of Land Resources Conservation - DLRC), (ii) the National Local
Government Finance Committee (NLGFC) and, (iii) the Ministry of Finance and Economic Affairs (through the FARMSE
Programme), in a co-execution modality to deliver the project activities. With FAO’s technical support, MoA will
implement technical activities at districts level, together with all the actors of the decentralized local government system.
NLGFC, constitutional body with the mandate to support local governments, will provide the procurement services to
the Project, for an increased sustainability and ownership by districts. MoF will execute component 2.3 on access to
finance through FARMSE. During implementation, in addition to the above executing entities (EE), the project will also
engage relevant government counterparts from MoA, Ministry of Climate Change and Natural Resources (MoCCNR),
non-governmental organisations (NGOs), knowledge institutions and training centers, local non-profit conservation
trusts, finance service providers and the private sector.
i) Total Project costs are 53.22 million USD, including: (i) 24.60 million USD for component 1, (ii) 22.50 million
USD for component 2, (iii) 1.18 million for component 3, (v) 2.32 million for M&E and (vi) 2.62 million for project
management. In addition to the 42.81 million USD grant requested, the Ministry of Finance and Economic Affairs (MoF),
the Ministry of Agriculture (MoA), and FAO will provide co-financing for a total amount of USD 10.42 million.
j) The articulation between assumptions, barriers, risks, project activities, outputs, outcomes and goal is
highlighted in the Theory of Change (section B.2b). The Project Monitoring and Evaluation (M&E) system, based on
the Results Framework (section E) will monitor progress towards these results. The project is fully in line with GCF
Investment Criteria (section D). It has built a Gender Strategy, based on a comprehensive gender Assessment (see
Annex 8), is aligned with GCF environmental and social (E&S) policy and gender guidelines (section G).

GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 6
B
PROJECT/PROGRAMME INFORMATION
B.1. Climate context (max. 1000 words, approximately 2 pages)
See also Annex 2 (Feasibility Study) for more detail on the climate context. A list of Acronyms is provided at the end of
the document.
DEVELOPMENT PROBLEM OF MALAWI: AGRICULTURE, WATERSHED ECOSYSTEMS AND FOOD INSECURITY
1. Malawi is a predominantly agricultural country with inadequate watershed management practices, and
consequently, low productivity in agriculture. Malawi is a country defined by smallholder farmers, who constitute 75-85% of
the total population,4 reside in the rural areas5 and produce over 80% of the food consumed in the country.6 The proportion
of GDP attributable to agriculture, forestry and fishing was over 20% in 2021, which was above the average of-sub-Saharan
Africa.7 Agriculture is estimated responsible for over 40% of export earnings in 2024.8 While agriculture is the linchpin of
the economy, the sector has been plagued by environmental/ecosystem degradation and erratic weather, in addition to
inadequate agricultural planning and practices.9 Around 85% of the population are estimated to depend on rainfed
agriculture,10 for which effective management of water and soil is particularly important. The availability of water has
become unreliable despite the country’s rich freshwater resources, both surface and ground water,11 and soil has turned
into one of the most degraded in sub-Saharan Africa. The need for more fertile farmlands – created by population growth
(2.6%/year in 2022)12 and soil fertility loss – has pushed the farmers to cultivate fragile areas, including steep slopes. The
practice has resulted in a cycle of decline and degradation of the environment,13 leading to low and stagnant agricultural
productivity and vice versa.14 As forests are important components of watersheds, the cycle is accelerated by deforestation
caused by increases in demand for fuelwood and charcoal, which originate in the increasing population.15 Given that
farmlands are part of larger watershed ecosystems, what is indispensable in improving productivity in agriculture, and
hence the overall economy, is adoption of sustainable management of watersheds with a focus on farming.
2. A handful of crops on a small plot define most of Malawian agriculture. Unsustainable agricultural methods
contribute to the cycle of environmental/ecosystem degradation and low productivity. The smallholders grow staple crops
(maize, rice, cassava, sweet potato, potato cowpeas) and cash crops (mainly tobacco, as well as tea, coffee, groundnuts
and soybeans) on land which averaged 0.61 ha per household in 2016 (female-headed smallholder households held 0.53
ha).16 Both farmers and policy makers focus on maize as the main crop;17 the common mindset says “maize is food and
food is maize,”18 and at least 75% of agricultural budget is allocated to subsidies of inputs used for maize production.19
Tobacco – the country’s main cash crop and dominant export commodity for which smallholder farmers account for 95%
of the total production – has had negative impacts on ecosystems through deforestation,20 land degradation21 and
biodiversity loss.22 The degree of diversification had decreased between the cropping seasons in 2004/05 and 2010/11,23
and less than a third of farmers grew three or more categories of crops as of 2019.24 The weak diversification of crops has
led to land degradation, low productivity 25 and insufficient adaptation to climate change, further leading to more fertility
loss.
3. The most vulnerable will be the most affected by climate change, pronouncedly so in a society marked by high
income inequality. Malawi is listed as a Least Developed Country (LDC) by the UN and ranked as the seventh poorest in
the world in 2024.26 Its Gini Index has been historically high;27 roughly 70% of Malawi’s population lived below the international
poverty line of 2.15 USD/day in 2023 with close to half of its national income held by the top 20%of the population.28 In other words,
nearly all smallholder farmers are likely under the poverty line. The COVID-19 pandemic is estimated to have pushed an
additional 1.6 million people into poverty, mostly in rural areas.29 As the real GDP of the country falls due to the price
increases in fertilizer and fuel caused by the conflict between Ukraine and Russia,30 national household consumption is
expected to shrink, with larger impacts on poorer and rural households and leading to an increase in inequality.31
4. The national dialogue on food systems in 2021 underscored the importance of protecting watersheds for agriculture
and food security. A high proportion of the population is chronically food insecure, and its causes are considered structural.
A national dialogue on food systems in Malawi was held in 2021 to contribute to the United Nations Food Systems Summit
in the same year.32 It emphasized the importance of protecting ecosystems, especially watersheds and their soil functions,
for sustainable food production.33 The degradation of watersheds has also affected nature’s capacity to attenuate droughts
and floods, which are more frequent and intense due to climate change. The government sees landscape restoration as
essential in climate resilience, agricultural productivity and food security.34 According to the IPC (Integrated Food Security
Phase Classification), Malawi’s situation for 2022-2026 is characterized by one-third of the population experiencing
moderate or severe chronic food insecurity,35 which reflects the low food self-sufficiency of farmer households in the
country.36

DEVELOPMENT PROBLEM OF MALAWI: AGRICULTURE, WATERSHED ECOSYSTEMS AND FOOD INSECURITY
1. Malawi is a predominantly agricultural country with inadequate watershed management practices, and
consequently, low productivity in agriculture. Malawi is a country defined by smallholder farmers, who constitute 75-85% of
the total population,4 reside in the rural areas5 and produce over 80% of the food consumed in the country.6 The proportion
of GDP attributable to agriculture, forestry and fishing was over 20% in 2021, which was above the average of-sub-Saharan
Africa.7 Agriculture is estimated responsible for over 40% of export earnings in 2024.8 While agriculture is the linchpin of
the economy, the sector has been plagued by environmental/ecosystem degradation and erratic weather, in addition to
inadequate agricultural planning and practices.9 Around 85% of the population are estimated to depend on rainfed
agriculture,10 for which effective management of water and soil is particularly important. The availability of water has
become unreliable despite the country’s rich freshwater resources, both surface and ground water,11 and soil has turned
into one of the most degraded in sub-Saharan Africa. The need for more fertile farmlands – created by population growth
(2.6%/year in 2022)12 and soil fertility loss – has pushed the farmers to cultivate fragile areas, including steep slopes. The
practice has resulted in a cycle of decline and degradation of the environment,13 leading to low and stagnant agricultural
productivity and vice versa.14 As forests are important components of watersheds, the cycle is accelerated by deforestation
caused by increases in demand for fuelwood and charcoal, which originate in the increasing population.15 Given that
farmlands are part of larger watershed ecosystems, what is indispensable in improving productivity in agriculture, and
hence the overall economy, is adoption of sustainable management of watersheds with a focus on farming.
2. A handful of crops on a small plot define most of Malawian agriculture. Unsustainable agricultural methods
contribute to the cycle of environmental/ecosystem degradation and low productivity. The smallholders grow staple crops
(maize, rice, cassava, sweet potato, potato cowpeas) and cash crops (mainly tobacco, as well as tea, coffee, groundnuts
and soybeans) on land which averaged 0.61 ha per household in 2016 (female-headed smallholder households held 0.53
ha).16 Both farmers and policy makers focus on maize as the main crop;17 the common mindset says “maize is food and
food is maize,”18 and at least 75% of agricultural budget is allocated to subsidies of inputs used for maize production.19
Tobacco – the country’s main cash crop and dominant export commodity for which smallholder farmers account for 95%
of the total production – has had negative impacts on ecosystems through deforestation,20 land degradation21 and
biodiversity loss.22 The degree of diversification had decreased between the cropping seasons in 2004/05 and 2010/11,23
and less than a third of farmers grew three or more categories of crops as of 2019.24 The weak diversification of crops has
led to land degradation, low productivity 25 and insufficient adaptation to climate change, further leading to more fertility
loss.
3. The most vulnerable will be the most affected by climate change, pronouncedly so in a society marked by high
income inequality. Malawi is listed as a Least Developed Country (LDC) by the UN and ranked as the seventh poorest in
the world in 2024.26 Its Gini Index has been historically high;27 roughly 70% of Malawi’s population lived below the international
poverty line of 2.15 USD/day in 2023 with close to half of its national income held by the top 20%of the population.28 In other words,
nearly all smallholder farmers are likely under the poverty line. The COVID-19 pandemic is estimated to have pushed an
additional 1.6 million people into poverty, mostly in rural areas.29 As the real GDP of the country falls due to the price
increases in fertilizer and fuel caused by the conflict between Ukraine and Russia,30 national household consumption is
expected to shrink, with larger impacts on poorer and rural households and leading to an increase in inequality.31
4. The national dialogue on food systems in 2021 underscored the importance of protecting watersheds for agriculture
and food security. A high proportion of the population is chronically food insecure, and its causes are considered structural.
A national dialogue on food systems in Malawi was held in 2021 to contribute to the United Nations Food Systems Summit
in the same year.32 It emphasized the importance of protecting ecosystems, especially watersheds and their soil functions,
for sustainable food production.33 The degradation of watersheds has also affected nature’s capacity to attenuate droughts
and floods, which are more frequent and intense due to climate change. The government sees landscape restoration as
essential in climate resilience, agricultural productivity and food security.34 According to the IPC (Integrated Food Security
Phase Classification), Malawi’s situation for 2022-2026 is characterized by one-third of the population experiencing
moderate or severe chronic food insecurity,35 which reflects the low food self-sufficiency of farmer households in the
country.36

CLIMATE-DEVELOPMENT NEXUS, CLIMATE DRIVERS AND CLIMATE CHANGE IMPACTS
5. Climate change is feeding the cycle of watershed degradation and poor agricultural productivity. Climate change
is intensifying the potency of climate drivers – El-Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO)37 and Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD)38 –
to make cyclones more destructive39 and rapidly increasing the number of disasters.40 Heavy rains have contributed to soil
loss41 (and consequently, soil fertility decline) and are expected to inflict greater damage under climate change according
to the Soil Loss Estimation for South Africa (SLEMSA).42 The temperature is expected to rise; a study43 conducted by the
Department of Climate Change and Meteorological Services (DCCMS) of Malawi concluded that the annual mean
temperature is clearly destined to shoot up near-, mid- and end-century44 under Representative Concentration Pathways
4.5 and 8.5 45 (more information generated by DCCMS on historical and projected temperature and rainfall is contained in
Annex 2, Part 1). Droughts will continue to be more frequent and aridity to increase.46 Not only floods, but also droughts,
are known to erode soil organic matter47 and fertility. In a warmer climate – which is expected under climate change –
rainfall variability is likely larger even without accompanying changes in the sea-surface temperature,48 and highly uncertain
rainfall is likely to raise variability in crop yields.49 ENSO is one of the important determinants of crop yield in East and
Southern Africa,50 whose effects are expected to become more dipolar with the changing climate.51 Soil moisture eases
the drought effects on crops,52 but has become increasingly unreliable with degradation of watershed in addition to
intensification of aridity caused by climate change. Hydrological droughts have been less frequent than meteorological
droughts thanks to mitigation effects of Lake Malawi, but watershed degradation is threatening this function through
siltation53. Well-managed watersheds can mitigate extreme weather (e.g., minimize fluctuations of soil moisture and
ambient temperature and minimize soil erosion), but their degradation allows unchecked destruction of the ecosystems by
climate change, and hence on agriculture and the economy.
6. The impacts of droughts and floods on crop yields have been heavily damaging, especially when the intervals
between extreme weather events are short. Erratic rains and prolonged dry spells in 2015-2016 delayed the start of the
agricultural season by two to four weeks.54 Consequently, the crop production in the southern and central regions was
estimated 13.4% lower than the previous season 2014-2015, which was already 30% less than the season before due to
the severe flooding in 2015.55 Earlier major droughts (seven during 1980-2012) affected Districts across the country; the
major crops impacted were maize, potato, groundnut and beans.56 Floods caused by cyclones and tropical storms provoked
a proliferation of weeds,57 aphids’ attack of kidney beans58 and outbreak of fall armyworm.59
7. Both cash and subsistence crops will be affected throughout the country to location-specific extents. Damage
caused by crop pests and diseases is set to increase. The studies on crop yield projections (FAO study based on water
balance60 and IFAD study using EcoCrop suitability model61) suggest that the impact of the changing climate will differ by
crop (maize, rice, sorghum, cassava, beans, pigeon pea, soybean, cowpea, groundnut) and locality, possibly at a scale
smaller than each Agricultural Development District (ADD),62 and with variations among them.63 These studies and
historical records indicate that maize, beans and cassava could be the most affected by climate change, while cowpea,
sorghum and soybean could be the least affected (see Annex 2, Part I). The climate impacts on crops have differed on
small scales64 and will continue to be so. As climate models project varying ranges of rainfall, so do crop yield models (as
they are dependent on the projections). Incidence of pests and diseases accompanies extreme weather events;65 its
increase is hence expected in the future.
8. Climate impacts on ecosystems and agriculture are best described as combinations of climate hazards. Climate
hazards identified (i.e. higher frequency and intensity of: extreme heat; droughts/aridity; floods; strong winds; and
disruptions in the water cycle) are experienced by ecosystems as higher frequency and intensity of: plant/animal stress;
increased soil erosion; decline in soil fertility; further deforestation and degradation of watersheds; intensified incidence of
pests, diseases and weeds; and inconsistent water supply (see Appendix 1 of Annex 2, Table 3). In other words, a
combination of parameters – rather than a single climate parameter- determines yields.66 For example, beyond the amount
of rainfall, the onset of the rainy season can have significant impacts.67 Climate-change also exposes the water sector to
increasing risks of droughts/aridity and floods, in addition to changes in the timing of water flow.68
9. The effects of climate change are likely to trigger a downward spiral in agriculture, food, nutrition and of the rural
socio-economy. Reduced agricultural productivity will spill over to food and nutritional security, human health and social
fabric, all of which are presently in inadequate states. Already one third of the population is expected to remain in moderate
or severe chronic food insecurity for two-three years as of 2024.69 In 2023, acute food insecurity reported in the country
was attributed to significant production decrease of maize – the main staple food – from floods and other destructive
weather conditions brought about by tropical cyclones, coupled with the existing soil degradation.70 Maize accounts for
more than 54% of national caloric intake,71 which implies lack of crop and nutritional diversification. Malawi has been
suffering from very high levels of micronutrient deficiencies caused by insufficient dietary diversity; Vitamin A supply is

=== PAGE 12 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 8
B
reported 13% below the WHO recommendation.72 Climate change is expected to worsen the micronutrient deficiency. For
example, Vitamin A supply will be 32% below WHO recommendation under RCP 4.573 by 2050. Under RCP 8.5, Vitamin
A supply will be 64% below, Iron 53% below and Zinc 40% below their respective WHO recommendations by 2050.74 The
Global Health Security Index ranked the country among the worst quartile in the world in 2021,75 and its life expectancy
had been reduced by one year from 64 years in 2019 to 63 years in 2021.76 Climate change will negatively affect the health
of the population,77 which will in turn limit climate change adaptation: the smallholder households in Malawi with no
chronically sick person were 3.2 times more likely to adopt both short-term and long-term sustainable land management
practices compared to those with chronically sick persons.78 These developments will affect agricultural productivity, and
hence security in food and nutrition, as well as livelihoods.
10. Climate change is compounding other socioeconomic shocks that are driving the wedge between the haves and
have-nots. As is the case for any socioeconomic shock, the most vulnerable rural communities, female-headed households,
women and children, persons with HIV/AIDS, displaced people and the elderly will be the hardest hit by the changing
climate and plunged into more severe poverty to widen the social inequality gaps.79 The drying of Lake Chilwa is already
associated with more cases of early marriages for girls and transactional sex is expected to increase.80 The vast majority
of the population in the Crisis phase of IPC Acute Food Insecurity 2023-2024 were in rural areas which experienced
decrease in crop production from climate change.81 The political and governance shocks that weaken the country are now
aggravated by climate shocks.82
CAPACITY TO ANTICIPATE AND RESPOND TO CLIMATE CHANGE
11. Literacy rate and human development are low, both of which limit access to written information.83 The widespread
agricultural practices are neither suited for adaptation to nor mitigation of climate change. Access to formal information is
limited by the literacy rates, which were 65.9% for women and 71.6% for men in 2018. The lowest rates were found in:
Lilongwe, excluding the capital; Salima; Dezda; Mangochi; Machinga; Chikwawa; and Nsaje Districts. The UNDP Human
Development Index confirms this point by consistently categorizing Malawi among the low human de8v4elopment countries,
a group that consists of some 30 states.85 The current practice of low crop diversification not only degrades land, but also
severely limits the capacity to adapt to climate change. Neither is low diversification conducive to climate change mitigation,
as it discourages soil biodiversity and hence limits soil organic matter. Both farmers and policy makers focus on maize as
the main crop, although it is not as drought tolerant as the root crops under cultivation, such as sweet potato and cassava.86
Rainfed agriculture without adaptation to the evolving climate reality is said to have contributed to low productivity, among
other factors indicated above.87
12. Forests need sustainable management, not only for their roles in watershed ecosystems, but also for mitigating
socioeconomic or environmental/ecological shocks, including agricultural failure. Trees anchor the soil, enhance soil
biological activity and provide ecosystem services and products beneficial to nearby organisms. Non-timber forest products
(NTFP) are of significant importance in achieving food and nutritional security and also for generating income.88 Their
importance increases for vulnerable households during agricultural and economic stress; the demand for NTFP is expected
to increase under climate change. For example, fruits, vegetables, medicinal products, mushrooms and honey from the
forests are consumed in southern Malawi.89 Up to 75% of the population in southern Malawi used NTFP in 2014, some as
food and others for various household needs, and nearly 40% of the households were involved in trading of one or more
NTFPs with high return per labor input.90 Forest degradation thus affects the rural livelihoods not only indirectly through
water scarcity, soil degradation, decreased microclimate regulation and poor pollination, but also directly by reducing the
sources of alternative food, livelihoods and additional income.
13. Watershed management and other adaptation measures have been scarce so far.91 The adaptation strategies
promoted or adopted are often inefficient and can be counterproductive, i.e., potentially maladaptative92. Farmers have
adopted various strategies in the face of climate change, most of which are limited in nature, scope or both.93 The ridge
and furrow cultivation94 and conservation agriculture95 have been introduced to curtail soil erosion but applied to 1-2% of
cultivated land despite its promotion at a national scale.96 Climate change has encouraged the prevalence of existing pests,
diseases and weeds, as well as the emergence of new ones.97 The most common methods to control pests and weeds in
Malawi are pesticides98 and herbicides,99 without which sufficient yields are unattainable under the conventional agricultural
regimes. As is the case with synthetic fertilizers, they are detrimental to soil fertility as well as to adaptation and mitigation
capacities, but their use is expected to increase in response to climate change.100.Regarding forests, management methods
such as agroforestry, farmer-managed natural regeneration, community management of natural forest lands have been
promoted mainly by NGOs, but the areas of intervention have been limited.101 Forest dependent communities in Malawi
have been observed to cope with climate change with means available to them, often in line with ecosystem-based
adaptation (EbA).102 Their strategies have not achieved full potential, because of: lack of access to funds; insufficient
knowledge and skills for higher effectiveness; unsatisfactory availability of planting materials; among others.

14. Malawi has a youthful population, and local knowledge of ecosystems exists among its farmers. These advantages
are insufficiently leveraged for climate change adaptation and mitigation. A potential for dynamic climate adaptation exists,
as the median age of the total population is 17 years,103 and the youth are as a rule forward-looking and quite receptive to
social changes. The distribution of youth population showed a pattern very similar to those of population density and
markets access.104 Increasing emigration105 is indicative of limited adaptation to evolving socioeconomic and climatic
conditions. Emigration and remittances from the diaspora are thought to be increasing rapidly.106 The emigration rate has
been the highest in: Nkhata Bay; Mzimba; and Mangochi districts.107 Detailed information of local ecosystems is necessary
for successful adaptation, especially for ecosystem-based adaptation and agroecology. Such information, including
weather forecasting,108 exists as local knowledge109 and its utility for adaptation is acknowledged by the government.
However, it has not been fully integrated into interventions110 or supplemented by western science for maximum efficacy in
adaptation.111
GREENHOUSE GAS EMISSION PROFILE
15. According to the Nationally Appropriate Mitigation Actions (NAMA) 2015, the category of Agriculture, Forestry and
Other Land Use (AFOLU) was responsible for over 95% of total greenhouse gas emissions. 112 The AFOLU emissions
easily surpassed Energy (2.9%), Waste (1.7%) and Industrial Products and Other Products Use (0.3%).113 The Business
As Usual (BAU) scenario as of 2015 indicated that the dominance of AFOLU will be eclipsed somewhat by the two coal
power plants to become operational in 2020, but still accounting for as much as 83% in 2030.114 The NAMA acknowledged
the gravity of deforestation and proposed as a solution forest regeneration and reforestation as mitigation actions based
on existing governmental programmes; the efficacy of the programmes against continuing timber harvesting and forest
conversion into agricultural land is unknown. The NAMA does not mention decaying biomass from land flooded by hydro
reservoirs,115 which is likely much more potent as an emission source in humid tropical climate.116 Land use, other than
agriculture, had turned from carbon sink to carbon source around 2014, emitting 1.96 million tCO2e in 2017.117 In sum, the
BAU amount of emissions in 2030 is likely considerably higher than the latest available estimate from 2015 of 35 million
tCO2e.118
16. The two major sources of emissions in FOLU are expansion of agriculture and settlements and unsustainable
fuelwood extraction. 119 The potential of crop agriculture in mitigation is likely larger than currently estimated. The Updated
Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC)120 from 2021 did not include forestry and other land uses (FOLU) in its baseline
and instead provided an indicative reduction contribution in 2040 through afforestation (18.44 million tCO2e), agroforestry
(9.14 million tCO2e), sustainable forest management (31.38 million tCO2e) and riparian restoration (0.55 million tCO2e), a
total of 34.61 million tCO2e, covering an area of up to 2 million hectares. Nearly 80% of the funds needed for mitigation in
FOLU is conditional on international support: 5% of BAU scenario in 2040 with unconditional funds and 51% with conditional
funds. The NDC 2021 separated agriculture and FOLU and identified agriculture as the largest emitting sector with 5.07
million tCO2e/year, 54% of total when FOLU is excluded: 39% of total from livestock and 15% from crop management.
Under crop management, practices such as efficient use of fertilizer (including crop residue and manure), crop rotation and
improved tilling were proposed for reducing 9.9 million tCO2e BAU in 2040 to 1.6 million tCO2e. The 2021 IPCC report121
emphasized the necessity to direct greater attention to non-CO2 greenhouse gases with shorter-lives but higher warming
effects for swift and efficient mitigation of climate change; such as methane, nitrous oxide and sulphur dioxide. As the target
temperature set by the Paris Agreement approaches, the importance of gases with these characteristics has increased and
will continue to do so, but the100-year Global Warming Potential (GWP100), which is widely used by UNFCCC and national
governments, underestimates the climate change potential of such gases.122 Considering that nitrous oxide dominates the
crop agriculture emissions, the potential of crop agriculture in mitigation is likely much larger than estimated in the NDC.
PROPOSED CLIMATE SOLUTION: ECOSYSTEM-BASED ADAPTATION
17. The proposed climate solutions based on Ecosystem-based Adaptation (EbA) approach strengthen the capacity of
ecosystems to provide services and to prevent and heal damages to themselves; the solutions increase the resilience of
ecosystems to climate chage, while being holistic to avoid maladaptation. As described above, Malawi’s watershed
ecosystems and communities are experiencing compound climate impacts. Measures to halt the vicious cycle of ecosystem
degradation and low agricultural productivity – which is accelerated by multiple climate drivers and hazards – call for a
solution which restores ecosystems and accommodates the climate uncertainties.123 Since farmlands are part of larger
watershed ecosystems, sustainable management of watersheds improves food security and the overall economy. This
points to ecosystems-based adaptation (EbA), which restores and strengthens ecosystems, reduces climate risks, and
establishes climate resilience, as an important adaptation solution to climate hazards for Malawi.
18. The updated Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) 2021 places its people, ecosystems and economy at the
center of adaptation and mitigation efforts. EbA is featured as one of the strategic adaptation actions. The NDC includes in
its priorities the development of adaptation planning tools, EbA, community-based adaptation options, integrated watershed

=== PAGE 14 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 10
B
management, crop diversification and soil and water management, afforestation, agroforestry, sustainable forest
management and riparian restoration. However, adoption of EbA solutions is not yet widespread in Malawi. Transformative
interventions are necessary as highlighted by the NDC; funds from GCF and the expertise of FAO are essential for the
purpose. The effectiveness of funds is ensured by FAO’s strong know-how and experience in agriculture, forestry,
food/nutritional security and rural development.
19. EbA is superior to other climate-change adaptation strategies in many aspects. EbA boosts ecological resilience124
through restoring, strengthening and sustainably managing ecosystems.125 EbA (or agroecology, which is the application
of EbA on food production) applied to farms and surrounding ecosystems brings improvements in soil structure and fertility,
which leads to temporally and spatially balanced water cycle and consistent soil moisture, in addition to reduced ambient
temperature fluctuations and risks of climate hazards, such as droughts and floods. Farms strengthened as ecosystems –
including their biodiversity – reduce the incidence of pests, diseases and weeds and achieve a higher total crop yield from
a given parcel of land to improve food and nutrition security. In Malawi, farmers who adopted EbA/agroecology experienced
agricultural, environmental, livelihood, and food and nutrition security benefits in comparison to farmers who solely relied
on conventional agriculture.126 Resilient ecosystems are equipped with self-healing and adapting capabilities, which render
EbA measures effective in a wider range of climate situations than other adaptation strategies. EbA generates short- and
long-term term benefits127 and is applicable at regional, national and local levels.128 It is considered more cost effective in
climate change adaptation than grey infrastructure when economic, social and environmental benefits are included. The
body of evidence is growing in favor of EbA/agroecology for climate change adaptation and other co-benefits, but precise
benefits and trade-offs vary by social and environmental contexts.129 Productive farms support farmers to safeguard the
natural resource base and open the possibility to free themselves from the vicious cycle of environmental/ecosystem
degradation and low agricultural productivity, which is connected to food/nutrition insecurity and poverty. When
local/traditional knowledge (holistic socio-ecological knowledge, practices and beliefs)130 is integrated, EbA has good
chances of avoiding maladaptation.131 EbA is also a paradigm-shifting pathway listed by the GCF Sectoral Guide on
Ecosystems and Ecosystem Services.132
20. EbA involves use of biodiversity and ecosystem services to assist people and agriculture to adapt to climate
change.133 Agriculture constitutes major uses of watershed lands, which may negatively affect the surrounding ecosystems
that provide services indispensable to humans and agriculture itself – clean water in a regulated manner, organisms that
control pest insects, habitats for crop pollinators, soil fertility and so on.134 EbA in agriculture, thus, aims at creating an
assemblage of crops and livestock to resemble ecosystems in functions and biodiversity as well as minimizing disturbances
that are damaging to the nearby ecosystems (Components 1 and 2). Agroecology has been widely accepted as a means
of climate change adaptation based on ecosystems in agriculture135 and is the first paradigm-shifting pathway of the GCF
Sectorial Guide on Agriculture and Food Security.136
21. The Project addresses the main barriers to successful adoption of EbA practices by smallholders:
• Planning barriers: EbA, more particularly climate-resilient landscape management for watersheds, is not well
integrated into local planning, such as Village-Level Action Plans (VLAPs). Long-term planning for climate-change
adaptation is rare at the community level due to poverty and lack of information; and this is aggravated by weak
long-term management/coordination and limited knowledge on climate change adaptation solutions among the
stakeholders. These issues have led to disaster relief rather than prevention137 and unsatisfactory results.138 In order
to strengthen the ownership and effectiveness of the Project, the Integrated Landscape Management (ILM) is
applied (see Annex 2, 5.2 Detailed description of components and activities, Component 1: Integrated Landscape
Management).
• Technical / Knowledge: technical capacity to adapt to the changing climate is limited among farmers and extension
workers. Insufficient extension capacity 139 has been correlated with stagnating productivity and national
development140. The various strategies adopted by farmers to cope with climate change have not been
satisfactory141; they are limited in nature, scope or both. Limited outreach coverage is also to blame.142 Detailed
information of local ecosystems which is necessary for successful adaptation, including weather forecasting,143
exists as local knowledge144 and its utility for adaptation is acknowledged by the government. However, it has not
been fully integrated into interventions 145 or supplemented by western science for maximum efficacy in
adaptation.146
• Social: community adaptation capacity is unsatisfactory due to low access to information, markets, services and
technology required for climate resilient livelihoods, combined with the disempowerment of vulnerable groups, such
as women (which has led to lack of integration at various levels of their knowledge and needs, hindering an
ecosystem use that is collectively sustainable). Men are the default target group for information, services and
innovations;147 information relevant to women is scarce in a society where tasks are often assigned by gender.
Women’s access to credit and natural resources is also limited. These constraints are borne and compounded by
unequal distribution of decision making power within the household and society.148

=== PAGE 15 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 11
B
• Financial: Farmers’ sustainable access to finance, while recognized as a crucial factor in the adoption of climate
resilient agriculture, remains limited. Malawians have low access to financial institutions compared to neighboring
countries149, and experience a less mature finance market with limited scope and offerings150. High transaction
costs, financial products ill-suited for EbA, limited income, insufficient collateral, inadequate repayment schedules
and low financial literacy prevent smallholder farmers from accessing financial services, particularly women. Another
significant barrier to agricultural lending is the internal capacity of financial institutions (FIs). For example, FIs lack
information about their clients (more particularly farmers’ ability to produce crops to repay loans), they do not
integrate climate risks into credit risks assessments and lack capacities to develop digital credit scores151.
• Institutional capacity is limited for climate mainstreaming, mobilizing innovative finance and integrating EbA into
national policies. Over 75% of the country’s financial needs for climate adaptation and mitigation are dependent on
external sources152. The roles and responsibilities of climate-related institutions are unclear and inter- and intra-
institutional coordination is unsatisfactory.153 Funding to these institutions is limited.154 The Nationally Determined
Contributions and some strategies155 include EbA, but some other policies do not clearly recognize it as the most
sustainable solution. Climate related policies do not see marginalized groups separately, although they are different
from one another in their needs and strengths.
22. The Project sustainably lowers the vulnerability and strengthens the adaptive capacity of both watershed
ecosystems and farmers, the stewards of the ecosystems. The Project is based on beneficiary-driven approaches:
Integrated Landscape Management (ILM); and Farmer Field School (FFS). In Malawi, it was found that participatory
extension methodologies, such as FFS, increases the participation of vulnerable people and promote the uptake of
improved practices against climate change156. Recognizing the importance of holistic solutions, the project includes
capacity building on both ecological/technical and socioeconomic issues. The beneficiaries, whose capacities are widened
and strengthened, will be the final decision makers for the future of their villages, with the assistance of external experts,
the government and FAO. For example, it will be the farmer beneficiaries who choose the plants (tress, grasses, crops,
etc.) to be adopted under the intervention. Their blueprints in the forms of Village Level Action Plans and Sub-Catchment
Management Plans will be based on EbA, including ecosystem restoration. The project is expected to directly benefit around
270,820 individuals (about 1.47% of total Malawian population) vulnerable to climate-change in 11 pre-identified districts
and 30 main sub-catchments. By mid-term of the project, more than 287,000 beneficiaries will enjoy improved health, well-
being, food and water security (ARA2) and by the end of project the number of the beneficiaries of the same is to be over
574,000 persons. The details on the expected performance against investment criteria are in Section D.1 and those on the
expected impacts are in Section E. Logical Framework. The proposed interventions are tightly linked to the projected
climate; their summary is given in Table B.1.1 below. The EbA techniques in the field associated with future climatic events
are given in Annex 2, Part 1, together with other related information.

determined by three indicators: historical trends of standardized precipitation; February dry spell trends; and historical
annual max temperature trends. Climate sensitivity was measured by: historical average Revised Universal Soil Loss
(RUSLE) which is based on precipitation, Vegetation Index (NDVI), soil types and slopes; population density; and poverty
rate. Climate adaptive capacity was approximated by: youth population rate; access to markets; literacy rate; and emigration
rate. Low percentage of youth in the population and literacy rates as well as high emigration rates were interpreted as low
adaptive capacity. Good access to markets was taken as existing adaptation opportunities that the proposed project could
leverage.
24. Eleven districts characterized by high climate vulnerability were chosen: six in the south (Zomba, Mangochi, Thyolo,
Neno, Mwanza, Nsanje); one in the central (Dedza); and four in the north (Nkhata Bay, Rmphi, Karonga and Chitipa). Site
selection will be based on further analyses of watershed degradation (as part of sub-activity 1.1.1.1.). The 11 targeted
districts have all been selected in relation with their high climate vulnerability, with the South being extremely exposed to
climate change, while Northern districts landscapes and ecosystem conditions are characterized by a severe climate
sensitivity, in relation with extreme soil loss and degradation157.

COUNTRY OWNERSHIP (see Annex 2 for details)
25. Malawi has ratified the UNFCCC, the Kyoto Protocol, the Paris Agreement and most recently the Glasgow Leaders’
Declaration on Forests and Land Use. The Malawi Growth and Development Strategy 2017-2020, the National Agricultural
Policy 2016 and the National Agricultural Investment Plan 2017-2023 put agriculture and climate change at the center.
Climate change is one of the imminent issues to be tackled, according to the National Forest and Landscape Restoration
Strategy 2017 and the National Forest Policy 2016 (which emphasizes the importance of forests for soil and water and
prioritizes payments for ecosystem management, among others). In 2016, Malawi joined the AFR100 (African Forest
Landscape Restoration Initiative, which aims to restore 100 million hectares of degraded land in Africa by 2030).
26. The National Climate Change Policy 2016 and the National Adaptation Plan 2020 see climate change as a major
impediment to development. According to the Third National Communication to the Conference of the Parties of the
UNFCCC, climate change is one of the largest threats to this agriculture dependent country and climate resilient agriculture
and strong engagement of local communities are recommended. The National Forest and Landscape Restoration Strategy
2017 considers gender equity and equality essential, and the preparatory exercise for NAP identified inclusion of
marginalized groups as important.159 According to the National Gender Policy 2015, climate change management is
important in the lives of women, and gender inequality aggravates deforestation impacts.
27. The Updated Nationally Determined Contribution 2021 includes in its priorities the development of adaptation
planning tools, EbA, integrated watershed management, crop diversification and soil and water management. In particular,
the 2021 NDC includes the following priorities (amounts in parenthesis indicate conditional funds required for the entire
country in 2020-2040): farmer-managed natural regeneration of catchments (USD 30 million); water, soil and catchment
conservation for drought resilience (USD 20 million); soil/water conservation and soil fertility improvement (USD 10 million);
crop/diet diversification and use of drought tolerant crops (USD 12 million); integrated pest management (USD 30 million);
cultivation of legumes for soil health/diet (USD 30 million); climate resilient agronomic practices (USD 20 million); integrated
crop-livestock-aquaculture-forest production systems (USD 30 million); drought tolerant or early maturing crops (USD 10
million); and integrated land use management policies (USD 25 million). EbAM will directly contribute to these priorities. As
for mitigation priorities from the 2021 NDC, EbAM aligns with identified agroforestry measures (for which the NDC proposes
USD 6 million in conditional financing).
SYNERGY WITH OTHER PROJECTS (see Annex 4 for details)
28. The proposed EbAM project scales up the efforts of the World Bank on watershed management (Watershed
Services Improvement Project – MWASIP). It will collaborate with other GCF funded activities in Malawi (Scaling up the
use of Modernized Climate information and Early Warning Systems in Malawi - GCF FP002) for mutual learning and
adaptive management, and liaise with the Restore Africa Program, funded by Climate Asset Management (CAM) and
implemented by the Global Evergreening Alliance (GEA). The project will work within the institutional framework established
by a European Union/FAO project (KULIMA) and enhance the capacity of extension workers. It will build on the experience
of the GEF/FAO project (under the Sustainable Forest Management, Dryland Sustainable Landscape Impact Programme
– GEF7 DSLP) with respect to payment for ecosystems and water services, and will work with an IFAD-funded Programme
under the Ministry of Finance and Economic Affairs (Financial Access for Rural Markets, Smallholders and Enterprise
Programme – FARMSE160) on financial services to improve financial access of rural farmers for climate change adaptation
purposes. EbAM will in turn support MoF/FARMSE in mainstreaming climate into rural financing.

World Bank. Watershed Services Improvement Project – MWASIP (2020-2026, USD 78.5 million). See linkages with component 1.
B.2 (a). Theory of change narrative and diagram (max. 1500 words, approximately 3 pages plus diagram)
29. The theory of change is based on the present and future scenarios described in the climate analysis. The latter
evidenced: (i) the impacts of current (observed) and projected climate change (increased temperatures and aridity,
changing temporal distribution of precipitation, increased frequency and intensity of extreme weather events) on agriculture
production and livelihoods, and (ii) the degrading impacts of climate change on landscapes and watershed ecosystems,
which further reduce the supply of ecosystem goods and services for livelihoods, and consequently increase communities’
vulnerability. The main climate effects will alter the onset of the rainy season, translate into limited and modified water
availability, increasing water stress, with negative impacts on both cash and subsistence crops, resulting in adverse impacts
on livelihoods and the overall rural socio-economy. As a consequence, climate-change puts smallholders and their
communities under increased pressure to resort to a vicious cycle of maladaptation, unsustainable ecosystem use and
management, further constraining ecosystems’ capacity to deliver services.
30. The push factor to transform this baseline trend, and promote a more virtuous dynamic of climate-resilient socio-
ecological systems, will be driven by mutually connected investments under each of the 3 components presented below
(and further described in section B.3). Overall goal, outcomes, outputs and activities are presented in the theory of change
diagram (see figure B.2.1).
31. Component 1. The objectives of this component are to reduce GHG emissions from improved watershed
ecosystems (outcome 1.1) and to increase climate resilience of watershed ecosystems (outcome 1.2). These
outcomes will be attained by enhancing ecosystem functions at a landscape (watershed) level large enough to facilitate
climate change adaptation and mitigation at scale: under EbAM, farmers will positively adapt, by safeguarding the natural
resource base, and providing better services to ecosystems (reciprocal relationship between farmers and nature), a
paradigm shift brought by EbA & ILM. The component will indeed use the EbA approach which involves use of biodiversity
and ecosystem services to assist catchment and village communities to adapt and become more resilient to climate change.
EbA – as described in section B.1 - will be firmly integrated in local planning through integrated landscape management
(ILM), at sub-catchment and micro-catchment levels. The EbA approach integrated in ILM is the core transformational
driver and innovation of the component. The approach will improve communities’ technical capacities as well as increase
stakeholders’ engagement, including women and other vulnerable groups, to plan landscape restoration and climate-
change adaptation interventions based on EbA (output 1.1). With the implementation of integrated management plans
(output 1.2), the project will strengthen communities’ capacity to protect and restore public goods, such as well-functioning
ecosystems, which are more adapted to extreme climate and continue to provide goods and services (e.g., carbon
sequestration and storage, water infilteration and retention and soil fertility) under the changing climate. This will mitigate,
in turn, the impact of projected increased temperature, erratic rainfalls and increased occurrence of extreme weather events
impacting the top soil which is the major contributing layer to soil fertility. These benefits will directly support sustainable
agricultural production and local livelihoods.
32. Component 2: The objective (outcome 2) of this component is “more climate resilient livelihoods and food
systems are leading to stable productivity and incomes”. The project will boost the efficacy of EbA in food systems
through the adoption of EbA at all scales, including production systems, and an enhanced and sustainable access to
markets, business opportunities, as well as finance. This shift will support farmers to stabilize and increase their income,
hence making their livelihoods more resilient in the context of climate change. By combining the promotion of EbA through
Farmers’ Field Schools (FFS) with an enhanced access to biodiversified, native and/or well-adapted seeds and seedlings
(output 2.1), the Project will increase farmers’ understanding of technical responses, and improve their capacity to adapt
to changing climatic conditions. Through a Food System approach, the Project will support farmer groups, producers
organisations (POs) and small and medium enterprises (SMEs) to access (i) markets through public-private producers
partnerships (output 2.2) and (ii) finance – such as village savings and loans associations, micro-finance institutions and
banks (output 2.3), which are two of the key barriers to climate-change adaptation. The component’s interventions, by
boosting nature-positive food production and building farmers’ resilience to shocks and stresses, will in turn contribute the
increased resilience of food systems at local level.
33. Component 3: The objective (outcome 3) of this component is to enhance the enabling environment (in terms
of finance and policies) with the purpose to sustain, replicate and scale-up climate resilient watershed ecosystems
and agriculture practices, ultimately facilitating mobilization, blending, and disbursing of catalytic climate finance, and
contribute to expanding the scale of the Project climate-resilient investments, while EbA will be mainstreamed and deep-
rooted in national policies and investment plans. Strengthened capacities of national institutions (National Climate Change
Fund - NCCF, and local national conservation trusts) to mobilize innovative public and private finance, together with
leveraging private sector experience on carbon credits as part of the exit strategy (output 3.1), complemented by improved

investment flows towards climate resilient watershed ecosystems and agricultural practices, for massive-scale impact and
sustainability.
34. The below diagram illustrates the relationship and complementarity between the three components, as described
in the paragraph below:
35. Component 1 protects and restores public goods, such as ecosystem services, hence improving i.a. water
infiltration, the soil water holding capacity and fertility. Well-functioning ecosystems are more adapted to extreme climate
and will also make farming systems resilient. Farmers, having access to knowledge, climate-resilient inputs, markets,
technologies and financial services (component 2), will positively adapt, safeguard the natural resource base, and provide
better services to ecosystems (reciprocal relationship between farmers and nature) and thus contributing to component 1
objectives. Component 3 will enhance component 1 and 2 by developing the enabling environment, and by increasing
investment flows towards climate resilient watershed ecosystems, and resilient livelihoods and food systems. Component
1 and 2 will inform policy, decision making and investment strategies. EbAM will be a catalyst for a broad shift and new
sustainable equilibrium for ecosystem, livelihoods and agriculture across Malawi, from their baseline state of very high
vulnerability, to an alternative paradigm in which watershed ecosystems are conserved, restored, and more sustainably
managed, thus granting their adaptation to climate change, and their supply of services to climate-resilient farming systems,
people and communities. Together, the 3 components will generate co-benefits that will directly contribute to
Sustainable Development Goals such as No Poverty (SDG1), Good Health and Well being (SDG3), Gender Equality
(SDG5) and Life on Land (SDG15) (see B.2b).
36. The Goal Statement is “if 1) landscapes and watershed ecosystems are sustainably managed with the
involvement of vulnerable groups, 2) farmers’ capacity to implement climate-resilient agriculture and to access markets is
increased, and 3) policies conducive of climate change adaptation and sustainable climate finance is in place,
then a new sustainable equilibrium for ecosystem, livelihoods and agriculture across Malawi will be attained,
because vulnerable rural communities will have more climate resilient livelihoods, with reduced GHG emissions.
37. These results and goal are subject to the following assumptions: (i) catchment and village committees embrace
integrated landscape management; (ii) farmers (including women and youth) adopt ecosystem based adaptation (EbA)
measures; (iii) socio-cultural barriers do not prevent women and youth from participating in “climate-responsive” FFS and
practicing new techniques; (iv) extension workers effectively lead FFS (iv) financial service providers willingly serve clients
with characteristics different from conventional ones; (v) the private sector is interested in 4Ps and is ready to act upon it;
(vi) no major socio-political shocks occur; and (vii) recovery from COVID-19 is confirmed. Results are also conditional to
risks – which are described in section F.1 of the Funding Proposal, and highlighted in the ToC diagram below.
38. The project interventions respond to the multifaceted barriers (see B.1.) to climate change adaptation in Malawi.
These include:
• Planning barriers: climate-resilient landscape management for watersheds is not well integrated into Village-
Level Action Plans (VLAPs).161 This barrier will be addressed by supporting/ training Catchment Management
Committees (CMCs) and Village Natural Resources Management Committees (VNRMCs) to prepare EbA-
based Catchment Management Plans (CMPs) and Village Level Action Plans (VLAPs) through ILM (activity
set 1 in the ToC).

=== PAGE 21 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 17
B
• Technical / Knowledge: technical capacity to adapt to the changing climate is limited among farmers and
extension workers. This barrier will be addressed under activity sets 1.2 and 2.1, through the implementation
of VLAPs and EbA agriculture extension support through FFS.
• Social: Community adaptation capacity is unsatisfactory due to low access to information, markets, services
and technology required for climate resilient livelihoods, especially among women162 and other vulnerable
groups. This barrier will be addressed under activity sets 1.1, 2.1, 2.2 and 2.3, through the implementation of
ILM and VLAPs, FFS and 4Ps, and through the improvement of financial inclusion with community-based
financial organisations (Community-based financing organisations – CBFOs/ village savings and loans
association/ VSLAs).
• Financial: Farmers have poor access to financial resources and their managerial capacity in finance is limited
for uptake of EbA. Farmers’ access to finance, while recognized as a crucial factor in the adoption of climate
resilient agriculture, remains unsatisfactory.163 This barrier will be addressed under activity set 2.3, that will
result in financial service providers being incentivized to invest in climate-resilient agriculture; hence enhancing
farmers’ financial inclusion.
• Institutional: Institutional capacity is limited for climate mainstreaming, mobilizing innovative finance and
integrating EbA into national policies. This barrier will be addressed under activity sets 3.1 and 3.2, that will
result in (i) more sustainable and innovative public and private climate financing through NCCF and local trusts
being in place, and (ii) EbA and ILM integrated in national policies and investment plans.

42. Component 1: Integrated Landscape Management. The objectives of this component are (i) to reduce GHG
emissions from improved watershed ecosystems (outcome 1.1) and, (ii) to increase the climate resilience of watershed
ecosystems (outcome 1.2). This component will contribute to GCF ARA2 “Health, well-being, food and water security”,
GCF ARA4 “Ecosystems and Ecosystem Services” and GCF MRA4 “Forestry and Land Use”. This component will address
the negative climate impact pathways from increased temperatures and rainfall variability leading to droughts and floods,164
all contributing to accelerated ecosystem degradation. It will use ecosystem-based adaptation (EbA) as the main tool to
build climate resilience, which will be firmly integrated in local planning through integrated landscape management, at
watershed and village levels. The component will improve the technical capacity of watershed management committees
and the local residents, and increase stakeholders’ engagement, including women , youth and other vulnerable groups, to
plan watershed restoration and climate-change adaptation interventions based on EbA and landscape approach (sub-

=== PAGE 24 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 20
B
component 1.1). Through the implementation of integrated management plans (sub-component 1.2), the project will
contribute to restoring and strengthening the functionality of public goods, in particular well-functioning watershed
ecosystems, so that they are more adapted to extreme climate, and hence with increased resilience.
43. The Component addresses the planning, knowledge, social and institutional barriers: the planning barrier
by assisting watershed management planning, the knowledge barrier by capacity building necessary for planning, formation
of watershed management committees and implementation of management plans, the social barrier by developing capacity
on technical and social issues, including gender and social inclusion, as well as increasing social capital through
participatory approaches and the institutional barrier by way of bolstering watershed management committees at WRU
sub-catchment and WRU micro-catchment levels. Integrated landscape management is holistic, participatory and
integrated in local planning, and deals with both private and communal lands; it promotes equitable and inclusive land
tenure in local communities.
44. Activities under the component are innovative in that they accompany local communities through
establishment of integrated landscape management (ILM) as an EbA strategy. The Project employs an ILM approach
(holistic, participatory and integrated in local planning) to watershed management with EbA as a technical guide. The
landscape approach was chosen among other strategies based on the past experiences in the discipline, which have led
to widespread dissatisfaction with top-down development paradigms. 165 The definition of integrated landscape
management for EbAM is: watershed management to achieve climate-change adaptation objectives through processes
that recognize, reconcile and synergize interests, attitudes and actions of relevant stakeholders, and that are driven by
local stakeholders.166
45. Activities under the component build on the legacy of past projects for more sustainability. They bolster
the watershed management structures and processes defined by the government (i.e. Forestry Act 1997, Water Resources
Act 2013, Malawi National Guidelines: Integrated Catchment Management and Rural Infrastructure 2015) at Water
Resource Unit (WRU), sub- and micro-catchment levels by strengthening existing watershed management committees at
these levels: Sub-Catchment Management Committee (SCMC) and Village Natural Resources Management Committee
(VNRMC), respectively (see Table B.3.1.1). The project will establish them where they do not yet exist and strengthen
those that are already in place. The watershed communities at the two levels will be assisted in formulating watershed
management plans (Sub-Catchment Management Plan – SCMP, and Village Level Action Plan – VLAP, respectively) as
ILM plans for EbA. VNRMCs were supported under the World Bank-funded “Shire Valley Transformation Program” (SVTP-
I). VNRMCs and SCMCs are leveraged under “Watershed Services Improvement Project” (MWASIP), which is also
promoting VLAPs for watershed management. EbAM will engage VNRMC and SCMCs in discussions geared towards the
co-designing of watershed management solutions and participatory processes for sustainable landscapes. EbAM
differentiates itself from other projects by focusing on climate change adaptation and creation of an enabling environment
at all levels for holistic and systemic transformation. EbAM also promotes a holistic, inclusive and local nature of ILM that
works towards long term sustainable actions, which is reinforced by building on local/traditional knowledge. It is hence
replicable in other WRUs in the country, which share many common challenges. EbAM envisages strong involvement of
beneficiaries on the ground by implementing ILM in an unencumbered form; it is based on the pioneering work of the World
Bank projects mentioned above, while ensuring deeper involvement of landscape stakeholders in the EbA planning and
subsequent processes.
46. The component will be based on the engagement of ILM Facilitators. A total of 60 ILM Facilitators (a team of
two persons for each targeted sub-catchment; one ILM Facilitator who is a national expert on community development and
one ILM Co-Facilitator who is another community development expert knowledgeable about the relevant sub-catchment
area) will be engaged through contracts with NGOs to accompany ILM stakeholders through sub-component 1.1, leading
to strengthening/establishment of committee and ILM plans at micro-catchment (see Sub-Activity 1.1.3) and sub-catchment
levels (see Sub-Activity 1.1.4): VNRMC and Village Level Action Plans (VLAP; ILM plan of micro-catchments); and SCMC
and Sub-Catchment Management Plan (SCMP; ILM plan of sub-catchments). ILM facilitators will also lead the
implementation of gender and social inclusion activities (see sub-activity 1.1.2.2) – and support implementation of the
VLAPs (see sub-component 1.2).
