47. Identification and selection of catchments within selected districts will follow a rigorous process (see
Feasibility Study for more details). The six stages of the targeting are: (i) identification of target Districts based on climate
vulnerability (as described in section B.1); (ii) identification of target Water Resources Units (WRUs) within target Districts
based on climate vulnerability and complementarity with other Projects (e.g. FAO-funded KULIMA); (iii) delineation of
selected WRU catchments into WRU sub-catchments based on hydrology and in line with the sub-catchment delineation
of other partners in Malawi (e.g. World Bank-funded MWASIP); (iv) selection and validation of WRU sub-catchments based
on climate vulnerability, hydrological, ecological and social considerations; (v) delineation of WRU sub-catchments into
WRU micro-catchments based on hydrology and number of villages contained; and (vi) selection and validation of target
WRU micro-catchments based on climate vulnerability, hydrological, ecological and social considerations. The last three
stages of the targeting will be carried out during project implementation, under sub-component 1.1, for ensuring participation
of local stakeholders, interest and consent. Figure B.3.3 shows the locations of the selected WRUs, and figure B.3.4 shows
an example of delineation process in WRU 8 in Nhakata Bay and Rumphi districts.

48. Sub-Component 1.1 Support to Village Natural Resources Management Committees (VNRMCs) and Sub-
Catchment Management Committees (SCMCs) on EbA Planning. (Output 1.1 Integrated landscape management plans
that include watershed ecosystems and founded on EbA are developed). The sub-component will support the development
of integrated landscape management plans for watersheds with ecosystems-based adaptation principles: Village Level
Action Plans - VLAPs (which are plans for micro-catchments contained in targeted sub-catchments) and Sub-Catchment
Management Plans - SCMP (see Table B.3.1). VNRMCs - which are committees for micro-catchments - and SCMCs will
be established in climate-vulnerable areas where they do not yet exist and strengthened, if needed, where they are already

=== PAGE 27 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 23
B
in place. This sub-component will be implemented through MoA/DLRC (i.e. decentralized staff within each of the 8 ADD
offices) and FAO as Executing Entities.
49. Activity 1.1.1. Targeting and Phasing of Sub-Catchments and Micro-Catchments. This activity will support the
selection of 30 target WRU sub-catchments (see Figure B.3.3.) for phased intervention. The activity will also support the
selection of 111 micro-catchments contained in the targeted WRU sub-catchments for village-level intervention. The
detailed targeting process led by MoA/DLRC is described in the Feasibility Study. The phased implementation of the
activities will create opportunities to benefit from lessons learned under the project. The Activity will comprise of the following
three sub-activities:
- Sub-activity 1.1.1.1: Identification and assessment of 30 sub-catchments and 111 micro-catchments
(financed by GCF, executed by MoA/DLRC). The sub- and micro-catchments where EbAM will intervene will be
chosen based on climate vulnerability, taking into account hydrological, ecological/environmental and
socioeconomic factors under the leadership of MoA/Department of Land Resources Conservation (DLRC), with
support of FAO (Project Implementation Unit – PIU staff), local government (districts), and relevant Traditional
Authorities. ILM Facilitators will be engaged as observers. A rapid GIS hotspot assessment using GPS/GIS data
and ground-truthing will be conducted for all delineated sub-catchments and micro-catchments of targeted WRUs
by an international GIS and water-resources-management expert (consultant), with the support of MoA/DLRC
officers167, and the assistance of MoA/DAES officials (Department of Agriculture Extension Services) trained under
the FAO-funded KULIMA Project. An average micro-catchment will contain about 10 villages.
- Sub-activity 1.1.1.2: Free, prior informed consent (FPIC) and environmental and social assessment for 30
sub-catchments and 111 micro-catchments (financed by FAO, implemented by FAO). This sub-activity will
finance FPIC implementation for all potential beneficiary communities168 to ensure their strong engagement and
adequate participation of youth, women and other vulnerable groups when targeting sub-catchment and micro-
catchments. FPIC facilitators will be trained and engaged for this purpose. An assessment of environmental and
social baseline and potential impacts will be also prepared. Based on institutional capacity development gaps
identified in the assessment, the project will provide trainings on environmental and social risk assessment and
monitoring to relevant government staff (e.g. MoA/DLRC officers, Environmental District Officers).
- Sub-activity 1.1.1.3: Validation and phasing of 30 targeted sub-catchments and 111 micro-catchments
(financed by GCF, executed by MoA/DLRC). Target sub- and micro-catchments will be validated under the
leadership of MoA/DLRC, together with FAO, local governments and relevant Traditional Authorities. Phasing of
project implementation in micro-catchments will be as follows: 11 will start in year 2, 70 in year 3 and 30 in year 4.
50. Activity 1.1.2 Capacity Development of ILM Stakeholders on Ecosystem-based Adaptation (financed by
GCF, executed by FAO). This activity will support awareness raising and capacity building of landscape stakeholders on
technical and social matters for effective ILM founded on EbA. For the same purpose, it will support capacity development
of ILM facilitators, Traditional Authorities (TAs) and local government officials. ILM Facilitators will be assigned to each
targeted sub-catchment to guide the landscape stakeholders of micro-catchment through planning, and plan
implementation. Facilitators will ensure good understanding of ILM process among stakeholders and guide communities
through various trainings and planning. They will also ensure active participation of women and youths. The Activity will
consist of the following Sub-activities:
- Sub-activity 1.1.2.1: Capacity Development for EbA Implementation. ILM Facilitators’ training as trainers will
be provided by national experts in each of the following fields: (i) ILM – including landscape demarcation, resources
inventorying and stakeholders identification, (ii) climate change – including climate vulnerability and impacts, as
well as climatic trends; (iii) water resources management; (iv) ecosystem services and ecosystem-based
adaptation (detailed information on EbA and its techniques are given in Appendix 1 of the Feasibility Study); (v)
payment for ecosystem services (PES); and; (vi) adaptive management. Specific trainings on Climate Change will
be delived by experts from the Department of Climate Change and Meteorological Services (DCCMS) – who has
been supported by the GCF-funded “Scaling Up The Used of Modernized Climate Information and Early Warning
Systems in Malawi” - GCF FP002, and by FAO on the Modelling System for Agricultural Impacts of Climate Change
(MOSAICC). Gender and Social Inclusion will also be mainstreamed throughout the training with the support of the
CPIU Gender and Social Inclusion Specialist. The climate change expert from DCCMS will join for two days in total
to make the link between climate change and EbA. After being trained as trainers, ILM Facilitators will build local
residents’ capacity at each micro-watershed on the same topics as their training as trainers. The detailed topics
are indicated in the Feasibility Study (Annex 2).

=== PAGE 28 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 24
B
- Sub-activity 1.1.2.2: Gender and Social Inclusion. Vulnerability to climate change originates from social
exclusion, which engenders lack of access to resources and lack of assets and economic opportunities: the very
factors that constitute vulnerability to various shocks and stresses. Therefore, gender empowerment will be tackled
at the root in order to create strong ownership of the Project, and promote meaningful participation of stakeholders
to facilitate awareness improvements and behavioral change on EbA for climate change adaptation. To this end,
the sub-activity will establish a social organization structure at village level for facilitating collective actions, called
the Dimitra Clubs, which are local groups for female and community empowerment.169 ILM is founded on
meaningful participation, which requires examination of decision-making power parity. Therefore, the sub-activity
employs a household methodology (participatory methodology for family members to work together to improve their
relations, decision-making and share of workloads related to household) to examine decision-making power parity
at the household level, which will be scaled up to the village level by Dimitra Clubs. 30 of the 60 ILM facilitators will
act as facilitators of Dimitra Club and household methodology. ILM Facilitators’ training as trainers will be provided
by international experts in each of the main following fields: (i) Dimitra Club facilitation; (ii) household methodology;
and (iii) gender and social inclusion A particular focus will be put on: gender and sex; advantages and
disadvantages of gender-specific roles and tasks; gender-based violence (GBV) and Sexual exploitation, abuse
and harassment (SEAH), including masculinities and patriarchy; Free Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC) process;
examples, motives and results of gender discrimination and social exclusion; and gender and social inclusion in
community development and welfare, including food and nutrition security. Some religious, traditional leaders and
other key figures will also participate in the trainings. Further to the training received, the 30 ILM Facilitators
focusing on Gender and Social Inclusion will promote Dimitra Clubs in all their villages of intervention, with the
target of 1,100 Dimitra Clubs created. See Annex 2 for mode details.
51. Activity 1.1.3 Strengthening/Formation of Village Natural Resources Management Committees (VNRMCs)
and formulation of EbA-based Village Level Action Plans (VLAPs) (financed by GCF; executed by FAO). In line with
the Forestry Act 1997, and building on previous projects sponsored by the World Bank, the Activity will establish Village
Natural Resources Management Committees (VNRMCs), or strengthen their functions where VNRMCs already exist, in
order to establish an operational watershed management structure at micro-catchment level. The Activity – implemented
in collaboration with MoA/DLRC and participation from the Department of Forestry (DoF) - will support mapping of existing
VNRMCs, and VNRMC charter establishment or its review and revision where it already exists. The Activity will also support
formulation of EbA-based VLAPs and obtaining their approval from the local authorities, i.e. Village Development
Committee (VDC). The EbA-based Plans will then be submitted to the District Council for inclusion in the Local Development
Plans, and to higher administrative levels: the Area Development Committee (ADC) at TA level; and finally to the District
Executive Committee (DEC). In some cases, about 10 villages are geographically close enough that they collectively
manage the common natural resources. For such groups of villages, one VNRMC will govern one group. VLAP elaboration
will be carried out in phases, i.e. 11 for year 1, 70 for year 2 and 30 in year 3. The Activity will consist of following Sub-
activities:
- Sub-activity 1.1.3.1: VNRMC charter revision and member selection. Under this sub-activity, that will start with
a mapping of existing VNRMCs (carried out by ILM facilitators), ILM Facilitators will oversee and guide landscape
stakeholders through VNRMC establishment (charter elaboration and member selection – average about 18
members per committee). Where a VNRMC has already been established, ILM facilitators will guide landscape
stakeholders through charter review/revision and additional member selection. ILM Facilitators will oversee
elaboration/review/revision and selection processes for transparency and fairness; awareness raising on gender
and social inclusion, including SEAH and GBV, will be integrated in this process. Discussions among VNRMC
members and other micro-catchment/landscape stakeholders on the matters of charter and member selection will
take place five hours per week for four consecutive weeks at each landscape or micro-catchment. ILM Facilitators
will ensure that about 60% of stakeholders participate in the discussions and that the VNRMC Charter in effect is
documented. ILM Facilitators will ensure that: discussions on inclusive and meaningful membership take place;
and 60% of participants in discussions are female and 30% are youths. The direct beneficiaries are approximately
60% or more of the inhabitants, or 168,000 residents, if the same persons participate in review and member
selection.
- Sub-activity 1.1.3.2: VNRMC Capacity Development for EbA Implementation. Training for VNRMC members
will be provided by national experts (DCCMS staff for climate change, and consultants for the rest of thematic
areas) in each of the following fields from a strategic point of view (hence, different in content from Sub-activity
1.1.2.1): (i) integrated landscape management; (ii) climate change risks; (iii) water resources management; (iv)
ecosystems and ecosystem-based adaptation (detailed information on EbA and its techniques are given in
Appendix 1 of the Feasibility Study); (v) payment for ecosystem services (PES); and (vi) adaptive management.
Gender and Social Inclusion (including FPIC and a special focus on SEAH and GBV) considerations will be
mainstreamed into the trainings with the support of the Gender and Social Inclusion specialist, and ILM facilitators

=== PAGE 29 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 25
B
focusing on Gender and Social Inclusion. The trainings are conducted at each micro-catchment/landscape. The
beneficiaries are about 2,000 VNRMC members. See more details in Annex 2.
- Sub-activity 1.1.3.3: Drafting and Finalizing EbA-based VLAP. Under this Activity, ILM Facilitators and a
national NRM expert (consultant) will guide the discussions to draft and finalize a Village Level Action Plan (VLAP)
under the leadership of VNRMC members, to identify investment opportunities for watershed restoration, based on
the climate vulnerability assessment (activity 1.1.1), landscape demarcation and resources inventorying, supported
by knowledge on EbA and local socioeconomic and cultural conditions. The VLAP preparation process will bring
together VNRMC members and ILM facilitators (see detailed steps for EbA based VLAPs in the Feasibility Study),
as follows: (i) discussion on Pillars (i.e. vision, goal and objectives) and Elements of VLAP as EbA Strategy; (ii)
discussion on detailed actions; (iii) formulation of practical arrangements for VLAP implementation; (iv) discussion
and consolidation of VLAPs; and (v) endorsement of VLAP by local government. In-between focused discussions,
wider exchanges involving representatives of all the villages in the micro-catchments will be engaged by VNRMC
members and ILM facilitators to share the conclusions of meetings, validate them and agree on the way forward.
The final VLAP will cover roughly 3 years and will be reviewed yearly for adaptive management by the VNRMC
members and other landscape stakeholders. The direct beneficiaries are about 8,800 local stakeholders.
52. Activity 1.1.4 Strengthening/Formation of Sub-Catchment Management Committees (SCMCs) and
Formulation of EbA-based Sub-Catchments Management Plans (SCMPs) (financed by GCF, executed by FAO).
This Activity will establish operational watershed management structures (SCMCs) at sub-catchment level, in line with the
government’s watershed management strategies/ policies. It will support the formulation of strategic plans with interventions
in line with climate change adaptation and biodiversity/ecosystem strategies (NDC 2021, National Adaptation Plan 2020,
National Forest and Landscape Restoration Strategy 2017, National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan 2015-2025 and
others – see Part 2.1 of this Feasibility Study). SCMP will propose strategic interventions for effective management of large
common lands, such as forests, grasslands/rangelands, floodplains, riparian buffer zones, and wetlands that VLAPs and
village communities cannot fully cover and address at lower level. It will also address upstream-downstream linkages of
micro-catchments contained in the sub-catchment. By strategically integrating climate-change adaptation interventions at
a higher catchment planning level, SCMPs will improve the enabling environment, and allow scaling-up/ replication of EbA
through other projects and programmes, for impact at a larger scale. The total number of SCMPs will be 30 to cover an
area of about 267,500 hectares. SCMP elaboration will be in phases, in accordance with the phases of project
implementation at micro-catchment level: roughly 16 in Project Year 4 and 14 in Project Year 5.
- Sub-activity 1.1.4.1: SCMC charter revision and member Selection. Under this sub-activity, that will start with
a mapping of existing SCMCs (carried out by ILM facilitators), ILM Facilitators will oversee and guide landscape
stakeholders through SCMC establishment (charter elaboration and member selection – average about eight
members per committee). Where a SCMC has already been established, ILM facilitators will guide landscape
stakeholders through charter review/revision and additional member selection. ILM Facilitators will oversee the
elaboration/review/revision and selection processes for transparency and fairness; awareness raising on gender
and social inclusion, including SEAH and GBV, will be integrated in this process. At sub-catchment level, ILM
Facilitators will coordinate SCMC members and consolidate inputs on Charter and selected SCMC members from
micro-catchments. The direct beneficiaries are approximately 3-4 inhabitants per village, or 3,330-4,440 residents.
- Sub-activity 1.1.4.2: SCMC Capacity Development for EbA Implementation. Ten-days training for SCMC
members will be provided by national experts (DCCMS staff for climate change, and consultants for the rest of
thematic areas) in each of the following fields from a strategic point of view: (i) integrated landscape management;
(ii) climate change; (iii) water resources management; (iv) ecosystems and ecosystem-based adaptation (detailed
information on EbA and tis techniques are given in Appendix 1 of the Feasibility Study); (v) payment for ecosystem
services (PES); and (vi) adaptive management. Gender and Social Inclusion considerations (including FPIC and a
special focus on SEAH and GBV) will be mainstreamed into the trainings with the support of the Gender and Social
Inclusion specialist, and ILM facilitators focusing on Gender and Social Inclusion. The location will be each targeted
sub-catchment (two SCMC will be trained together in one sub-catchment). The beneficiaries are about 240 SCMC
members.
- Sub-activity 1.1.4.3: Drafting and Finalizing EbA-based SCMP. Under this Activity, ILM Facilitators and a
national senior NRM expert (consultant) will guide the discussions among SCMC members to identify strategic
investment opportunities for watershed restoration and business development based on climate vulnerability,
landscape resources and supported by knowledge on EbA and local socioeconomic and cultural conditions, as
well as lessons from the VLAP development and implementation process. Investment opportunities will also be
informed by strategic national documents as refered above. Relevant stakeholders of the landscapes contained in
the sub-catchment in question (SCMC members, VNRMC members, TAs and district officials) will engage in

=== PAGE 30 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 26
B
exchange of ILM experiences and discuss the best way forward for SCMPs. MoA/DLRC will also actively
participate, together with the Department of Forestry (DoF). The emphasis will be on strategic planning based on
upstream-downstream linkages of micro-catchments. Steps for EbA-based SCMPs will include: (i) Discussion on
Pillars and Elements of SCMP as EbA Strategy, (ii) Formulation and Finalization of Draft SCMP and Approval and
Communication of Final SCMP, (iii) Discussion, Finalization, Approval and Communication of SCMP, and (iv)
Restitution workshop at central level. The final SCMP will cover roughly six years, and may be revised at mid-term
for adaptive management. See Annex 2 for more details.
53. Sub-component 1.2: Implementation of VLAPs based on EbA (output 1.2: Integrated landscape management
plans that include watershed ecosystems and founded on EbA are implemented). EbA interventions funded under this sub-
component will be the result of the identified investment priorities in the VLAPs. An estimated total area of 83,240 hectares
(communal and on-farm) will be targeted within the micro-catchments covered by the 111 VLAPs in the 30 WRU sub-
catchments, in the main 8 WRUs. EbA interventions financed under this sub-component will be public investments that are
of collective interest, generate public goods (such as services for and from ecosystems) and are proven applicable for the
Malawi context. Feasibility and scalability of EbA interventions is highlighted in the Government’s Malawi National
Guidelines: Integrated Catchment Management and Rural Infrastructure 2015 and in the National Forest Landscape
Restoration Assessment (NFLRA) 2016170 that identified the needs and opportunities for the restoration of the productivity
and ecosystem functions of degraded and deforested landscapes in Malawi at district level. Details on EbA interventions
are also described in the Feasibility Study (Annex 2).
54. Activity 1.2.1 Preparation of VLAP implementation. Under this activity, relevant expertise necessary to support
the implementation of VLAPs will be mobilized, looking at ensuring continuity with the support provided under sub-
component 1.1. Necessary coordination and preparatory arrangements will also be rolled-out to ensure a smooth
implementation of VLAPs at local level. This step will also be critical to ensure the necessary inputs for VLAP
implementation and to be procured by NLGFC each year (under sub-activity 1.2.2.1.) are identified in an exhaustive and
timely manner. The Activity will consist of the following Sub-activities:
- Sub-activity 1.2.1.1: Planning process to initiate VLAP implementation (financed by GCF, executed by
MoA/DLRC). VLAP implementation will entail a continuous planning process. Following the completion of VLAP
preparation, MoA/DLRC will accompany the preparation of the planning process, with support from facilitators and
the CPIU and prepare a 12 months VLAP procurement plan. Based on the agreed procurement plan, a detailed
list of required inputs will be compiled for submission to the National Local Government Finance Committee
(NLGFC – see below) – through the District Council. The precise organization will be discussed and agreed upon
among stakeholders with respect to work involved in VLAP implementation, and in line with arrangements foreseen
during VLAP formulation. ILM Facilitators will coordinate this adaptive management for operations. MoA/DLRC will
ensure that regular follow-up meetings are organized quarterly in order to discuss progress and issues related to
VLAP implementation in their respective Districts of interventions.
55. Activity 1.2.2 VLAP Implementation. EbAM will target a net intervention area of about 83,240 hectares across
communal and agriculture land use, within the total micro-catchment area. This activity will enable the actual delivery of
investments outlined in each of the 111 VLAPs developed under sub-component 1.1. EbA investments financed under this
sub-component will be targeting communal lands (e.g., forests, grasslands/rangelands, floodplains, riparian buffer zones
and wetlands) over an area of approximately 67,040 hectares (while Component 2 will target 16,200 hectares of on-farm
interventions through the Farmers Field Schools - FFS). Detailed calculations are provided in the Feasibility Study. The
estimated sub-cathment planning area and micro-watershed intervention area (i.e. landscapes under EbA) per WRU and
districts are highlighted in table B.3.3. The Activity will consist of the following sub-activities:
- Sub-activity 1.2.2.1: Technical assistance to VLAP implementation (financed by GCF, executed by FAO).
This sub-activity will focus on the mobilization of the required expertise for the implementation of VLAPs. This
expertise will be composed of both (i) the 60 ILM facilitators (30 two-person teams) already engaged through NGOs
under sub-component 1.1., as a way to ensure continuity in the facilitation process, engagement with communities,
and continuity/understanding of the VLAPs; and (ii) technical expertise from qualified and experienced service
providers (international and national NGOs), for example NGOs from the Malawi Climate Smart Agriculture Alliance
(MCSAA171), which have extensive expertise on EbA techniques and climate change adaptation in Malawi, and
have regularly collaborated with MoA/DLRC. Other organisations specialised in agroecology such as Permaculture
Network Malawi will also be consulted for technical advice.
- Sub-activity 1.2.2.2: Access to inputs and equipment ( financed by GCF; executed by NLGFC). This sub-
activity will finance inputs for implementing VLAPs on about 67,040 hectares of communal land. Based on the
district-level potential highlighted in the National Forest Landscape Restoration Assessment, ecosystem-based

=== PAGE 31 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 27
B
adaptation options will include: (i) soil and water conservation (14,352 hectares), (ii) agroforestry, pastureland
regeneration and FMNR (7,308 hectares), (iii) community forests and woodlot restoration (22,416 hectares), (iv)
forest management (22,640 hectares), and (v) river and stream bank restoration (321 hectares). Details per district
are provided in the Feasibility Study, and actual investments will depend on the EbA-based VLAPs. Inputs foreseen
include: native or well adapted/landrace seeds and seedlings to promote high biodiversity, as well as equipment
and material required to perform the works (e.g. boulders, wire, hoes, slashers, wheelbarrows, shovels, rakes,
strings, pruning tools, portable water containers etc.)). This sub-activity will be implemented by the National Local
Government Finance Committee (NLGFC), as Executing Entity (EE, see B.4). As in the case of the GEF-7 funded
Sustainable Forest Management, Dryland Sustainable Landscape Impact Programme, NLGFC will provide
procurement services to the EbAM project at district level. More specifically, NLGFC will receive regular (bi-annual)
updates from the VNRMC (with support of relevant project staff and facilitators) on foreseen needs in terms of
planting material and equipment (see Annex 2 for more detail).
- Sub-activity 1.2.2.3: Monitoring of VLAP implementation (financed by GCF; executed by MoA/DLRC). Under
this sub-activity, and following the leadership of MoA/DLRC, technical facilitators will monitor the implementation
of VLAP priorities with a focus on communal lands, covering a wide range of interventions: (i) soil and water
conservation, for erosion and water runoff control (with green infrastructures such as swales, brush fill, gully plugs
and check dams); (ii) natural forest protection; assisted natural regeneration; (iii) community forest and woodlot
management; (iv) pastureland management; (v) riverbank protection; (vi) and other livelihoods opportunities and
off-farm economic activities (e.g., beekeeping, non-timber forest products – NTFP harvesting – e.g. baobab,
moringa/ medicinal plants, fruit, mushrooms). Based on the agreed upon rules for community works, DLRC will
ensure that community volunteers are present on site, receive the needed tools, inputs and equipment to perform
the works, and will demonstrate and support the implementation of works, while continuing to sensitize about the
relevance and benefits of the applied techniques. ILM Facilitators will also assist in community volunteer’s
mobilization, and ensure that participating women and youth benefit from advice in a meaningful and satisfactory
manner. For works that are particularly labour intensive (specifically those related with soil and water conservation,
with some green infrastructure: swales, gully plugs, check dams, etc.), the mobilized NGOs under Sub-activity
1.2.2.1 will provide direct support with machinery and specialized labour where applicable. In addition to
coordinating this process, MoA/DLRC will support VNRMCs to ensure and monitor that clear rules are established
and followed for the management of achieved interventions.
- Regarding interventions described under (vi) above (livelihoods opportunities and off-farm economic activities -
e.g., beekeeping, harvesting NTFP such as baobab), ILM facilitators and technical facilitators will accompany
groups of local volunteers in setting up specific management plans based on VLAP priorities for the development
and use of local NTFP. These could replicate innovative “Payment for Ecosystem Services” through which
beekeepers rent local woodlots to host their hives (see case study/ box in the Feasibility Study). Such emerging
economic activities can be further supported and structured through subcomponent 2.2. (to develop value-chains
and markets), and 2.3 (to access finance).

component 1 outcomes (ecosystem resilience), and building on the VLAPs developed under component 1.1, this
component – which will directly target at least 16,200 ha of farmlands – will contribute to GCF ARA1 “Most Vulnerable
People and Communities” (with support for livelihood enhancement through increasing resilience), ARA2 “Health, well-
being, food and water security”, and MRA4 "Forestry and land use”. By enhancing extension services through farmers field
schools - FFS (sub-component 2.1), the Project will increase farmers’ understanding of technical responses to adapt to
changing climatic conditions and enhance their capacity to integrate EbA into their farming systems. The component will
support small and medium enterprises (SMEs), producers organisations (POs) and farmer groups within the local food
system to access markets (sub-component 2.2) and finance – such as village savings and loans associations, micro-finance
institutions and banks (sub-component 2.3), which are some of the key barriers to EbA adoption. The component’s
interventions, by boosting nature-positive food production and building resilience to vulnerabilities shocks and stresses, will
contribute to build more resilient food systems at local level.
57. The Component addresses the planning, knowledge, social and financial barriers: the knowledge barrier by
enhancing capacities necessary for adopting ecosystem-based adaptation in the production systems through FFS (sub-
component 2.1), the social barrier by increasing social capital through participatory approaches, and developing capacity
on technical and social issues, including gender and social inclusion (sub-component 2.1) and the financial barrier (sub-
component 2.3) by enhancing access to inclusive finance and markets.
58. Activities under this sub-component are innovative in that they support smallholder’s resilience to climate
change through a food system approach. Project interventions will engage a wide range of stakeholders of the food
system. These include actors involved in the production, processing and marketing of food products that originate from
EbA-based production systems, as well as actors supporting the value-chain functions, such as financial service providers.
Through sub-component 2.1, EbAM will help farmers in selected micro-catchments to adopt and develop integrated, nature
positive production systems, where a variety of climate-resilient, native and well adapted crops are associated. Through
sub-component 2.2, EbAM will also support linkages between selected crops/products from diversified, EbA-based
production systems with public and private market operators engaged in national or international value-chains through a
public-private producers partnerships (4Ps) approach.
59. Activities promoted are sustainable and replicable. The integration of EbA in the extension system will allow
replication of the approach at regional, national and local levels – with a strong scaling-up potential. Activities are
sustainable because EbA integrated in farming systems enhances farmers’ long term capacities to sustain under extreme
weather, enhances biodiversity, reduces maladaptation and strengthens watershed/landscape functions and improves food
security. Furthermore, farmers adopting EbA will positively adapt, safeguard the natural resource base, and provide better
services to ecosystems. Such as reciprocal relationship between farmers and nature will therefore enhance environmental
sustainability – one of the project’s key co-benefits.
60. Sub-Component 2.1: Promotion of EbA-based production systems. (Output 2.1: EbA measures and inputs
are promoted among farmers). EbA is knowledge intensive, so farmers’ learning will be at the core of the investment
strategy, which will build on the Farmer Field Schools (FFS) approach, supported by the use of digital technology and and
targeted technical visits and exchanges. Combined with an enhanced access to varied and adapted genetic material, FFS
will facilitate the full application of EbA – while increasing climate change adaptation, enhancing agrobiodiversity and the
restoration of ecosystem services.
61. Activity 2.1.1 EbA agriculture extension support through FFS. At the level of targeted micro-catchments, EbAM
will support the roll out of Farmers Field Schools (FFS). FFS have proven an effective way for uptake of climate-resilient
and ecosystem based practices through its participatory and context specific methodology (see Box 2 below). The roll out
of the FFS has 3 levels: (i) the Master Trainer's Course (MTC); (ii) the Training of Facilitators (ToF); and (iii) FFS
implementation. The expected output is: 240 MT and 675 facilitators trained and 1,080 FFS implemented, impacting 27,000
farmers over 16,200 ha.
62. The topics covered will incude: (i) Conservation agriculture practices (manure management, zero/reduced tillage
and use of crop residues/cover crops), with emphasis on the importance of soil organic matters and soil structure by using
compost to boost soil fertility and moisture, (ii) Agrobiodiversity and the importance of varied and adapted genetic
resources, such as mixed-cropping of native, non-invasive and locally adapted (landraces) varieties, (iii) Promotion of early
maturing, nutrition sensitive, drought-resistant and climate-resilient crops (based on Malawi-specific climate models
providing some crop suitability analysis at local level174), (iv) Integrated mix-farming systems175 and (v) General principles
and practices of agroecology and permaculture. The trainings will also include climate and weather information analysis
through the Participatory Integrated Climate Services for Agriculture (PICSA)176 promoted under the GCF-funded “Scaling
Up the Use of Modernized Climate Information and Early Warning Systems in Malawi” (GCF FP002). The Project will learn
from and build on the PICSA approach and tools (PICSA field manual), which has promoted a collaboration between

DCCMS and the Department of Agriculture Extension Service (DAES) for the use of historical seasonal climate records,

- Sub-activity 2.1.1.1 Master Trainer's Course (MTC) and Training of Facilitators (ToF) (financed by
GCF, executed by FAO). EbAM will build on the existing capacity of MoA staff on the FFS approach.
During Y1, 4 MTC will be carried out for Agriculture Extension Development Officers (AEDO) and
Agriculture Extension District Coordinators (AEDC) level officers177 from targeted districts178 where no
MTCs have been carried out179. For the remaining targeted districts and sections where MTC were carried
out, 4 refresh courses of 3 weeks will be organized to train extension officials on the EbA approach and
practices, including the importance of agrobiodiversity180. In Y3, after identification of potential commercial
FFS, 2 refresher courses on Farm Business School (FBS) will be carried out for all targeted districts. These
identified FFS group will be linked and supported through subcomponent 2.2. Community Based
Facilitators (CBF) will be identified amongst lead farmers and innovative farmers in targeted villages,
women (at least 50%) and men, prioritizing youth.
- Sub-activity 2.1.1.2 FFS implementation (financed by GCF, executed by FAO). The organization and
setting up of the FFS at village level, will come as a result of the VLAPs, and will therefore be closely linked
with activities from Component 1. FFS groups will be gender-balanced, and women/youth specific FFS
may be organized. Each group will undertake a participatory diagnostic, identify main issues, and define
the objectives of the FFS. The learning subjects will fall under 3 main categories: (i) crop production, (ii)
agroforestry and (iii) agropastoralism, depending on the groups’ interests and agro-ecological areas, and
will include all the EbA practices from the MT and ToF courses. The FFS groups may also evolve into
beekeeping and commercial groups (for example). The FFS will use a participatory action-research
approach181 for the adoption of EbA practices, by working with farmers to redesign: their cropping systems
(or livestock systems, agroforestry systems, etc.), the relations between the various production units, and
even the farming-system as a whole. A total of 1,080 FFS with 27,000 farmers will participate.
- Sub-activity 2.1.1.3 MoA support to FFS roll out (financed by MoA, executed by MoA). The Ministry
of Agriculture will co-finance (in-kind) and support the rolling out of the FFS by availing 153 decentralized
extension staffs’ (AEDOs and AEDCs) time to technically support FFS and monitor their implementation.
The decentralized staff will also support M&E data collection. The MoA will co-finance (in kind) the training
venues for the MTC and ToF courses, which include study plots as well as training centres.
Box 2. Lessons from Farmer Field Schools
Farmer Field Schools (FFS) is one of FAO’s flagship innovation, being implemented in more than 90 countries, and it is
estimated that 20 million farmers globally have participated in FFS since they started. Malawi is not an exception and the
extension methodology is being implemented in many projects sponsored by the World Bank, IFAD and the EU/FAO. FFS
are promoted by the Ministry of Agriculture (MoA) through the National Agriculture Extension Policy as of the main extension
approach to reach out to farmers. Recent FFS initiatives operate within government structures and institutions, and intend
to facilitate mainstreaming of the FFS model. A total of 12,000 FFS have so far been established since 2008. For example,
the FAO-implemented KULIMA Project is currently institutionalizing FFS in the Extension service system and its agency
(DAES) for more sustainability. KULIMA has positively delivered on productivity increase, household dietary diversity and
nutrition, the number of households using improved technology combination and adoption of improved livelihoods options
to cope with climate related hazards.182 Other impact evaluations highlight that FFS allowed to increase food security and
access to climate information183. EbAM will leverage and complement KULIMA on the outreach of the FFS and their focus
on EbA, while KULIMA will ensure long-term sustainability of the process by the institutional work and capacity development
on the National Extension System that KULIMA is developing.
63. Activity 2.1.2 Knowledge and innovation (financed by GCF, executed by FAO). EbA transition and practices
adoption is knowledge intensive. Part of its adoption success and bigger outreach relies on supporting more access to
technical knowledge and as well as climate information complementing the FFS trainings. EbAM will promote exchanges,
visits and trainings to enable different actors to have a first-hand experience and awareness on proposed EbA innovations,
many being found at niche levels in Malawi, and ensure their promotion at scale in the targeted areas184. This will on the
one hand help enhance the technical knowledge promoted through the FFS (Activity 2.1.1), and on the other sensitize
policy makers, supporting component 3. In addition, EbAM will leverage past projects (such as the GCF-funded “Scaling
Up the Use of Modernized Climate Information and Early Warning Systems in Malawi” - GCF FP002), by building on
capacity developed and weather infrastructure established, as well as phones applications created and rolled-out by the

Department of Agriculture Extension Services (DAES).The expected output is 5,000 people participating to visits,
exchanges and short trainings, and 196,000 people accessing climate- and technical-information.
- Sub-activity 2.1.2.1 Knowledge generation and sharing. This sub-activity will support the project in the
generation and sharing of EbA related knowledge. As a starting point, a knowledge management strategy
will be developed aiming at connecting and motivating different project stakeholders to generate, use and
share good practices and help improve the adoption rate and outreach of the EbA approach. The strategy
will be developed during Y1, by a national consultant that will be supporting the process of knowledge
generation on a part-time basis. The national consultant will work closely with the Agroecology-Hub185,
which is spearheding the Agroecology network and generating scientific and applied EbA related-
knowledge in Malawi.
- Sub-activity 2.1.2.2 Visits and exchanges. EbAM will promote visits and exchanges on EbA approaches
and practices for different types of stakeholders, with a twofold purpose: providing real success examples
in addition to the standard demonstration fields, and at the same time offering some extra key technical
training. Targets will include: (i) MoA frontline extension and research staff; (ii) NGOs present in the area
and working with the project; and (iii) facilitators and farmers. These are: (i) exchanges and visits between
FFS (facilitators and farmers) and lead farmers-innovators; (ii) visits and short trainings to Agroecology
Knowledge Hub network institutes186 for farmers and frontline extension staff; (iii) one-day visit for central
MoA staff and some decentralized staff to institutes that are part of the Agroecology Hub network187; (iv)
500 targeted youth from project areas to have a full 3 weeks training on Permaculture and Agroecology in
specialized institutes from the Permaculture/Agroecology Network and support them in the process of
becoming lead farmers.
- Sub-activity 2.1.2.2 Digital extension and climate information. The project will build on the legacy of
the GCF-funded “Scaling Up the Use of Modernized Climate Information and Early Warning Systems in
Malawi” (GCF FP002) as well scaling-up piloting activities financed under the FAO-implemented KULIMA,
and enable farmers and FFS facilitators to benefit from climate information and better develop climate
adaptation strategies, through SMS and/or community radio stations. The Project will partner with DCCMS
for leveraging weather data information for it to be conveyed through SMS and community radios. The
decentralized government staff (AEDOs and AEDCs), the CBFs and other farmers who own cell phones
will receive weather information through SMS. Community radios will be used to broadcast key weather
forecasts and early warning information. Community radio outreach will be enhanced through the
implementation of the Dimitra clubs188.
64. Activity 2.1.3 Agrobiodiversity promotion. Agrobiodiversity – a key feature of EbA - will be firmly integrated in
the VLAPs (sub-component 1.1), and crucial to the sustainability and adaptation of agriculture in the context of climate
change. This activity, which will replicate and scale-up seed production interventions promoted under the FAO/GEF-7
Project, will ensure the sustainable availability of diverse, well-adapted genetic resources for communal lands (to be used
under component 1) and farms in order to enhance EbA and ecosystem services through agrobiodiversity. The expected
output is 30 nurseries, 60 multipliers groups/individuals and 30 community seed banks established.
- Sub-activity 2.1.3.1. Availability of adapted genetic material (financed by GCF, executed by FAO).
In partnership with the different institutes specialized in genetic resources and with the capacity to provide
base seeds, EbAM will ensure multiplication of landraces189, drought resistant crops, native food crops,
including lost crops, native and exotic trees multiplication and dissemination for multiplication (details on
the eligible species and varieties can be found in the Feasibility Study).
- Sub-activity 2.1.3.2 Initial seed and seedling availability (financed by FAO, executed by FAO). As
soon as year 1, EbAM will leverage FAO co-financing through the GEF-7. Sustainable Forest Management,
Dryland Sustainable Landscape Impact Programme - SFM DSL IP (see B.1.) to launch the procurement
of endangered and native seeds and tree seedlings for Mangochi District.
- Sub Activity 2.1.3.3 Capacity development and support to seed multipliers (financed by GCF,
executed by FAO). EbAM will identify existing (or new) seed multipliers producers associations through
self-targeting, who are willing to produce around EbA approaches, to professionalize in seed multiplication.
The multipliers will be accompanied and trained by the MoA and a specialized institution190 and will adapt
official protocols for the improvement of adapted and drought resistant varieties multiplication, storage and
selling. These include locally adapted and native crops, as well as improved and well adapted drought
resistant varieties. The project will support community seed bank groups to evolve into a seed multiplication

businesses. These associations will also be supported in increasing their business capacities (sub-
component 2.2) and in accessing finance (sub-component 2.3).
- Sub-activity 2.1.3.4 Community/individual nurseries and seed banks support (financed by GCF,
executed by FAO). EbAM will support the establishment of at least one nursery and community seed bank
per CMC. Initially, EbAM will provide technical capacity building and initial material for their establishment.
The project will progressively support the professionalization of these nurseries and seed banks, to ensure
their future availability to commercialize their products in all project areas, thus supplying the
implementation of VLAPs land restoration activities (sub-component 1.2), together with the diversification
of farm-level production activities at VLAP level (sub-component 2.1 and 1.2). Technical support will be
provided through MoA decentralized staff (with support from - Genebank and Crop Development),
specialized institutions for tree nurseries (e.g. ICRAF) and from Research department from MoA for the
seed banks. Species and varieties promoted will be those listed as eligible in the Feasibility study. This
activity will target women mainly as they are the normal seed carers, highly involved in seed storage,
selection and multiplication.
65. Sub-component 2.2: Market access and entrepreneurship development (financed by GCF, executed by
FAO). (Output 2.2: Private sector is incentivized to invest in climate-resilient agriculture; and better farmers’ access to
markets). Activities under the sub-component will consist in building business and market relationships between actors of
the food system. It will establish financially sustainable and diverse local EbA-based agri-food business models, such as
public private producer partnerships (4Ps – as already tested by other Projects such as the IFAD-funded TRADE191 or the
World Bank-funded AGCOM – see Annex 2) and micro, small and medium entreprises (MSMEs). Activities will also promote
food-system transformation through the development of an “EbA” brand that creates consumer awareness of the
relationship between food quality, nutritious traditional diets and healthy local food produced in resilient ecosystems under
climate change.
66. A Market Study (annexed to the Feasibility Study) is providing details on marketing opportunities for a set of
selected crops and products. While the EbA approach will result in a multitude of crops being produced by smallholder
farmers in the project areas, the market analysis focused on those (i.e. legumes, oilseeds, perennials/ agroforestry,
horticulture, cereals and non-timber forest products – NTFP) which demonstrate marketing potential for 4P commercial
linkages or local SME development based on the diversity and sustainability of production, as well as suitability in the
context of climate change.
67. Activity 2.2.1 Public-private producer partnerships (4Ps) establishment (financed by GCF; executed by
FAO). The objective of this activity is to facilitate the establishment of EbA-focused 4Ps through a transparent engagement
process, technical and institutional development support, as well as facilitation of linkages with sub-components 1.2 and
2.1 on resilient EbA production, and sub-component 2.3 on access to commercial financing, in order to demonstrate high
sustainability and a robust business model. A 4P is a structured commercial partnership between a public entity, business
agents and small-scale producers, who agree to do a specific, defined, business venture together while jointly assuming
risks and responsibilities, and sharing benefits, resources and competencies. The level of capacity, formality and
management structure they entail, and of support they need, are different from support for the development of agri-MSMEs
owned by small local entrepreneurs that allow them to engage in direct commercialisation (activity 2.2.2). The creation of
EbA farmer organisations will be an outcome of Sub-Component 2.1 that will, where market viable, transition into a group
that is engaged in a formal 4P business arrangement that will be guided by criteria described in sub-activity 2.2.1.1. The
activity targets the creation of around 12 4Ps during the project duration, and the engagement of around 13,000
beneficiaries in the commercial activities, at least 50% of which women and youth. Details of implementation are provided
in Annex 2.
- Sub-Activity 2.2.1.1 Expression of interest. The focus of this Sub-Activity, under the leadership of a
National 4P Expert, is to conduct bi-annual calls for Expression of Interest, followed by selection of 4P
partner applications. This is expected to driven by off-taker interest in partnership development with EbA
farmer organizations.
- Sub-Activity 2.2.1.2 Capacity-building for partners in the process of negotiation of 4P agreement
and operations. This Sub-Activity, under the leadership of an Institutional Development Expert, will focus
on facilitating the engagement of potential supplier and off-taker partners in the 4P negotiation process, by
supporting the following: (i) producers to organise into a commercial entity (See FS Annex: Market Analysis
for detail on types of commercial entities) and (ii) off-takers to establish supplier liaison capacity, which are
a key prerequisite to the sustainability of a potential business relationship.

=== PAGE 37 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 33
B
- Sub-Activity 2.2.1.3 Development of 4P Business plans. The focus of this Sub-Activity, under the
leadership of business development consultants, will be to guide the partners through a participatory
process of business model planning for the entire 4P as an economic entity, that also clearly demonstrates
the cost-benefits for each player and the financial underpinning of the engagement.
- Sub-Activity 2.2.1.4 Support to 4Ps implementation. The focus of this Sub-Activity will be to ensure
continuous advisory support for the 4P arrangements put in place to overcome potential ‘initial hurdles’
related to the novelty of the supply relationship, the required capacity to deliver, communicate and
troubleshoot potential concerns.
68. Activity 2.2.2 Micro, Small and Medium Entreprises (MSMEs) development (financed by GCF, executed by
FAO). The objective of this activity is to stimulate entrepreneurial development, outside of the 4P context through the
creation of local MSMEs that offer new and strengthened opportunities to link farmers adopting EbA to markets, either
through direct market sales or via new supply chain arrangements. Youth and women led entrepreneurial initiatives will be
particularly encouraged and supported by EbAM by focusing on removing technical, capacity and financial access barriers
that impede their involvement in business development (see Annex 8 - Gender Assessment and project level action plan).
The activity will target the creation of around 270 local commercial entities, engaging an estimated 5,400 beneficiaries, at
least 50% of which women and youth. This activity, in contrast to 4Ps, will open the opportunity for smaller scale and less-
structured, independent local business to develop, that can engage groups that may not otherwise have the capacity to be
part of a highly structured and demanding partnership.
- Sub-Activity 2.2.2.1. Identification of common economic/commercial interests of farmers and
establishment of MSMEs – institutional development. Under the leadership of an Institutional
Development Expert, and based on the work done under Sub-Component 2.1 and the FFS and FBS, this
Sub-Activity will focus on the identification and development of farmers and farmer groups, women and
youth groups in particular, who demonstrate an interest and aptitude in developing a joint commercial
activity and establish a commercial entity (for e.g. MSME). This will be based on self-identification and
presentation of business ideas to be supported.
- Sub-Activity 2.2.2.2. Development of commercial business plans. The focus of this activity, under the
leadership of business development consultants, will be to enable the successful business establishment
of the newly formed commercial entities (see Market Analysis for detail on types of commercial entities)
through an inclusive process of business plan preparation that enables all partners/members to gain a clear
vision of the operations; establish a transparent and inclusive management body; and state a clear
business case. An example of such methodology is RuralInvest, a participatory business development tool,
developed by FAO.
- Sub-Activity 2.2.2.3. Support to the establishment and consolidation of business operations. This
Sub-Activity will operate in a similar format as Sub-Activity 2.2.1.4 and will focus on supporting the
consolidation of the MSME operations and business proposition.
69. Activity 2.2.3 Market development through “EbA production system” brand creation (financed by GCF;
executed by FAO). The activity aims to help generate market demand for the EbA products, as such the scope of the
activity is two-fold: (i) to raise the awareness of the consumer about the link between food, tradition and sustainability; and
(ii) to offer EbAM producers a market differentiation tool linked to the production principles they have embraced.
- Sub-Activity 2.2.3.1. Collaboration with government institutions on the creation of a brand to drive
demand for EbA produce. The focus of this Sub-Activity, under leadership from a Brand development
expert, will be the establishment of a product brand under the Ministry of Trade and in coordination with
the existing Let’s Buy Malawi brand192 (See FS Appendix 2: Market Analysis for detail on branding), adding
to the label of national origin a further differentiation based on ecosystem resilience and sustainability of
production.
- Sub-Activity 2.2.3.2. Marketing campaign on the brand and its message. The focus of this Sub-Activity,
led by a local PR/Marketing company will be the creation of an EbAM ‘brand’ and message that clearly
states the value-proposition of the brand, derived from EbA. This will be part of a broader communication
campaign on public awareness of the relationship between food quality, the production ecosystem, human
health and climate change. This will be implemented with the help of national PR company and the national
marketing consultant engaged under sub activity 2.2.3.1.

- Sub-Activity 2.2.3.3 Linking EbA produce to traditional cuisine. The focus of this Sub-Activity will be
the promotion of traditional foods and products, the products for which has been produced under Sub-
Component 2.1. The objective of this Sub-Activity is multi-fold: (i) to stimulate demand for traditional
ingredients and thus create demand for production under EbA; (ii) to provide and promote the social/cultural
component to the EbAM food ‘brand’ that is to be designed; (iii) to link different players of the food-system
from restaurants and retail to producers and consumers and in doing so strengthen knowledge-sharing and
capacity-building related to sustainable food consumption and production, especially in the context of
traditional cuisine; (iv) to highlight seasonality of production and seasonality of recipes, especially in the
context of urban consumer markets, (v) introduce these traditional products to the formal markets, hence
enhance local economy and food diversity.

70. Sub-component 2.3. Access to finance for climate resilient investment solutions. (Output 2.3: Financial
service providers support investment in climate-resilient agriculture). This sub-component aims to remove barriers
identified for access to finance by the project beneficiaries to sustainably invest in the EbA climate resilient solutions
promoted by the project. About 98,500 beneficiary households including 50% women and 25% youth will access adapted
financial services.
71. The sub-component will be implemented by the Ministry of Finance and Economic Affairs, through the FARMSE
Programme, and will address barriers on the supply side by providing technical assistance to financial institutions to develop
and deliver adapted and inclusive services and linking them with financial instruments. In addition, largest, most performing
and impactful SMEs will be linked to impact investment funds. Approaches will be aligned to the specific needs of different
categories of beneficiaries: (i) farmers and MSMEs in the Public-Private Producer Partnerships (4Ps); (ii) producer
organizations and their members; (iii) seeds producers and nurseries business groups; (iv) subsistence farmers trained in
the FFS not involved in any of the two first models; and (v) beneficiaries under Component 1 that will not be enrolled into
the FFS.
72. Activity 2.3.1: Consolidation / expansion of Community Based Financial Organizations (financed by MoF;
executed by MoF). The objective of this activity is to strengthen existing Village Savings and Loans Associations (VSLAs)
or establish new VSLAs in EbAM areas of intervention (i.e. 11 districts and 30 sub-catchments) for access by EbAM
beneficiaries to simple and adapted financial services. VSLAs will also be supported to link with FFIs to access additional
resources to on-lend to their members, or to guarantee the individual loans directly granted by the FFIs to the VSLA
members. These linkages may also allow VSLA members to open formal savings accounts, which contributes to a higher
level of financial inclusion, and open the door to other formal services like loans for financial needs that are not covered by
the VSLAs and insurance, mobile banking and digital services. A total of around 98,500 project beneficiaries households
will benefit from VSLAs improved services.
- Sub-Activity 2.3.1.1 Strengthening of existing VSLAs and establishment of new VSLAs in EbAM
areas. Implementing Partners which are local and international NGOs with experience in supporting
CBFOs contracted by MoF/FARMSE will (i) Conduct a Mapping of VSLAs in EbAM areas and membership
by EbAM beneficiaries, to enable them to determine the number of VSLAs to strengthen and the number
of VSLAs to establish, estimated to be about 5,500 in total; (ii) Promote the services of the VSLAs for the
non-members; and (iii) Provide technical assistance to the VSLAs in various thematic areas based on a
capacity building needs assessment. Studies will be conducted on the sustainability of the VSLA model.
The objective will be to study various sustainability models implemented in neighboring countries and,
based on these experiences, develop and implement adapted models for VSLAs in Malawi. This will
contribute to the viability of the VSLAs and of their services to their members, including EbAM beneficiaries.
MoF FARMSE has supported the Reserve Bank of Malawi (RBM) to improve the financial literacy training
modules . These modules will be disseminated to project beneficiaries by the Implementing Partners, which
will organize financial literacy training sessions for the VSLA members.
- Sub-Activity 2.3.1.2 Technical backstopping and implementation support, knowledge management
and dissemination. MoF/FARMSE PMU rural finance specialists will provide technical advice to its
Implementing Partners based on outcomes of its monitoring and evaluation and supervision missions..
EbAM, through MoF/FARMSE, will generate knowledge management products illustrating how socially-
inclusive VSLAs can contribute to climate adaptation financing. These products will be disseminated
through various channels like EbAM and MoF/FARMSE websites, social networks, TV and radio and
national and international conferences. MoF through FARMSE will also organize at least one knowledge
dissemination workshop per year, each gathering around 50 people from relevant stakeholders like
Reserve Bank of Malawi, Ministry of Finance and Economic Affairs, Ministry of Agriculture and of NGOs
and Projects involved in rural and inclusive finance development, to further share and scale-up lessons

=== PAGE 39 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 35
B
learnt and good practices. EbAM, through MoF/FARMSE, will also contribute to the development of a
financial inclusion portal . This tool will include specific information related to climate adaptation financing
and will be used by rural finance stakeholders to guide policy development and interventions.
73. Activity 2.3.2: Development and delivery of climate adaptation financial services by Formal Financial
Institutions. The objective of this activity is to support FFIs (commercial banks, MFIs, savings and Credit Cooperative
Organisation - SACCOs, insurance companies) to develop adapted financial services for EbA investments by farmers and
SMEs, based on the EbA investments selected and promoted by EbAM. A total of 12,880 farmers and 249 SMEs will
access finance from the supported FFIs. In line with the strategy of MoF/FARMSE to first promote innovations and then to
support the scaling-up of successful innovations, MoF through FARMSE will focus on financing innovations, while GCF will
focus on financing their up-scaling193.
- Sub-Activity 2.3.2.1 Technical support to FFIs to develop and scale up innovative and adapted
financial services (financed by GCF, executed by MoF/FARMSE). Competitive and demand-led calls
for proposals will be issued and managed by MoF through FARMSE as per its current practices. Selection
of the FFIs will be based on a number of appraisal criteria including; (i) commitment to engage with EbAM
beneficiaries, (ii) strategy to develop financial services to support EbA investments, (iii) experience in
agricultural finance for smallholder farmers, (iv) internal capacity to develop and deliver the services, (v)
features of the proposed products (including interest rates and collateral requirements) and delivery
channels (partnerships with other value chain actors, digitization of the products and processes, etc), (vi)
adapted products for the agri SMEs, and (vii) adapted products for women and youths. FFIs proposing to
develop innovative digital services (developing / improving their own platform or partnering with
fintechs/agritechs) will be prioritized. This may include digital tools and process for the loan applications,
digital disbursements and repayments of the loans, digitally enabled credit scoring194 and geodata systems
for climate risk analysis, and digitally-enabled agricultural insurance, including index-based insurance
(weather, area yield or hybrid). It is expected that the delivery of the digital services will involve mostly
youth, more conversant with the digital technologies.
- Sub-Activity 2.3.2.2 Technical backstopping and implementation support, knowledge management
and dissemination (financed by MoF/FARMSE, executed by MoF/FARMSE). EbAM, through
MoF/FARMSE rural finance specialists will provide technical advice to its Partners FFIs based on outcomes
of its monitoring and evaluation and supervision missions. EbAM, through MoF/FARMSE, will produce
knowledge management products on how innovative and inclusive formal financial services promoted by
the project contribute to the promotion of climate adaptation investments, that will be disseminated through
various channels, like for Sub-Activity 2.3.1.3. MoF/FARMSE will also organize at least one stakeholders
engagement workshop per year for knowledge dissemination.
74. Activity 2.3.3: Linkage of partner FFIs to financial instruments providers (financed by MoF/FARMSE;
executed by MoF/FARMSE). MoF through FARMSE will link partner FFIs, on a need and demand basis, to institutions
and initiatives managing financial instruments like concessional credit lines195 and guarantee funds or schemes196 (see
details in Annex 2 - Feasibility Study). This activity aims at incentivizing the FFIs to engage into financing of EbAM targets,
in addition to the technical assistance, and it will contribute to the reduction of the cost of loans for the project beneficiaries.
- Sub-Activity 2.3.3.1 Scoping study of the potential financial instruments. MoF through FARMSE will
mobilize a consultant to carry out a scoping study of the potential financial instruments (concessional credit
lines and guarantee funds or schemes) providers that MoF/FARMSE could partner with for linkages with
its partner FFIs. The study will identify the potential partners, with information on the features of the financial
instruments, eligibility criteria and processes and conditions to access the instruments.
- Sub-Activity 2.3.3.2 Facilitation of linkages by MoF/FARMSE. MoF through FARMSE will facilitate
linkages between the partner FFIs and the identified financial instruments providers. This may involve
technical assistance to support the FFIs to develop their funding application.
75. Activity 2.3.4: Linkage of agri SMEs to impact investment funds (financed by MoF/FARMSE; executed by
MoF/FARMSE). MoF through FARMSE will link on demand basis largest agri-SMEs supported under sub-component 2.2
to impact investment funds for debt and equity financing and technical support.
- Sub-Activity 2.3.4.1 Scoping study of the impact investment funds. MoF/FARMSE will mobilize a
consultant to carry out a scoping study of the potential impact investment funds that MoF/FARMSE could
partner with for linkages with supported agri-SMEs. Examples are provided in the Feasibility Study. The

=== PAGE 40 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 36
B
study will identify the potential partners, with information on the features of their investments and technical
support, eligibility criteria and processes and conditions to access funding. Through these linkages, the
agri SMEs may access alternative or complementary sources of funds to that of the FFIs as well as
technical support, building on the support provided by EbAM. It is anticipated that agri SMEs supported
under the 4Ps model would be eligible for investment, thanks to their linkages with farmers and climate
resilience focus, and target will be to link at least five of them to impact investment funds.
- Sub-Activity 2.3.4.2 Facilitation of linkages by MoF/FARMSE. MoF/FARMSE will facilitate linkages
between the eligible supported agri SMEs and the identified impact investment funds like the Malawi
Agriculture and Industrial Investment Corporation (MAIIC – see details in the Feasibility Study). This may
involve technical assistance to support the agri-SMEs to develop their funding application.

76. Component 3. Enabling Institutional and Financial Environment. The objective (Outcome 3) of this component
is to enhance the enabling environment to sustain, replicate and scale up climate resilient watershed ecosystems and
agriculture practices. This objective will be achieved by leveraging public and private climate finance (sub-component 3.1)
and scaling-up EbA in national policies (sub-component 3.2). It will contribute to GCF results areas ARA1, ARA4 and
MRA4. The component will contribute to the sustainability and scaling-up of EbA activities and well-functioning watershed
ecosystems promoted under Components 1 and 2.
77. This component will address the institutional barriers. As per the theory of change, these include (i) insufficient
institutional capacity to mobilize innovative public and private climate finance and (ii) limited integration of EbA in national
