78. Activities promoted under the component are sustainable and innovative. The Project will support Malawi’s
vision to establish its National Climate Change Fund (NCCF) and will strengthen local trusts (e.g. MEET and Shire BEST).
Together, the activities will facilitate the mobilization of catalytic climate finance, and contribute to sustaining, replicating
and expanding the scale of climate-resilient investments promoted by the Project under components 1 and 2. The Project
is innovative because it will leverage a private sector experience on carbon credits (Climate Asset Management – CAM/
HSBC – which is financing the Restore Africa Programme). Interventions will mainstream and deep-root EbA in national
policies and investment plans, and bring the EbA agenda at sectoral policies level. By integrating EbA in national policies,
the component will contribute to improve the enabling environment, and allow replication and scaling-up of EbA through
other projects and programmes – for massive-scale impact and sustainability.
79. Sub-component 3.1. Leveraging public and private climate finance. (Output 3.1: Sustainable and innovative
public and private climate financing through NCCF and local trusts are in place). At national level, the project will assist the
National Climate Change Fund (NCCF) (activity 3.1.1) and local national conservation trusts funds (Malawi Environment
Endowment Trust - MEET and Shire BEST) to mobilize climate finance for scaling-up climate-change adaptation
interventions, based on EbA (activity 3.1.2). It will also leverage private sector experience on carbon credits in Malawi as
part of the exit strategy (3.2.3). This sub-component will contribute to an improved enabling environment, more particularly
on enhancing access to climate finance and instruments.
80. Activity 3.1.1. Support to Malawi’s National Climate Change Fund (NCCF) (financed by the GCF, executed
by FAO). The Project will provide some capacity development to the NCCF to mobilize resources and build an investment
pipeline focusing on ecosystem restoration, watershed resilience and climate-resilient agriculture, based on EbA. The
objective of this activity is to replicate EbA investments through the NCCF, while sustaining interventions promoted by
EbAM under components 1 and 2. The Project’s proposed technical support to the NCCF, which will start on year 2, will
result in an increased volume of climate finance being available nationally to replicate EbAM activities, in other climate-
vulnerable watersheds, for increased impact. In line with the NCCF’s Standard Operating Procedures (SOP), proposed
technical assistance from EbAM will encompass 4 sub-activities as follows.
- Sub-activity 3.1.1.1: Support to resources mobilization. The objective of this sub-activity is to support the
NCCF to mobilize climate finance. The Project will notably assist the NCCF to meet GCF accreditation
standards, with a view to leverage “direct access” financing towards project end, once the NCCF is sufficiently
well established and experienced. Direct access is a priority identified in the NCCF SOP. Under a longer-term
horizon, the Project will also consider financing some technical assistance to develop a strategy/ feasibility
study for the NCCF to leverage innovative private sector finance instruments - which could include for example
green or climate bonds.
- Sub-activity 3.1.1.2: Support to pipeline building. The NCCF has two priority investment areas for climate-
change adaptation. These include: (i) integrated watershed management, and (ii) climate change community
resilience through climate-smart agriculture production systems. To support investment under these priorities
areas, EbAM will finance investment strategies, with the objective to build a pipeline of quality adaptation
projects, based on EbA. Investment Strategies will build on EbAM’s investment experience/lessons learnt.
These will include: (i) a set of criteria for targeting watersheds (e.g. climate vulnerability, ecosystem/ landscape
degradation, youth/gender inclusion), (ii) a list of technical solutions for climate-change adaptation, including
their effectiveness/efficiency, (iii) a list of potential projects to be funded, including EbAM’s beneficiaries
(communities, farmers, SMEs), (iv) a list of monitoring and evaluation (M&E) indicators for the NCCF’s
monitoring, verification and reporting framework (MRV). EbAM’s “SMART” outcome/outputs indicators and
reporting methodologies will be leveraged.
- Sub-activity 3.1.1.3: Capacity development on EbA. Trainings on the main EbA techniques listed in the
investment strategies will be delivered by FAO. The objective is to fully integrate EbAM’s knowledge into the
NCCF, for better investment/ financing decisions. Trainings will include (i) deep-dive on the EbA techniques
(as described/ listed in Appendix 1 of the Feasibility Study), (ii) costs (equipment/inputs needed for adoption)
and benefits, based on EbAM’s experience. Trainings – conducted by FAO staff and consultants – will also
build on the evidence-based studies prepared under sub-component 3.2 for policy dialogue.
- Sub-activity 3.1.1.4. Capacity development on climate risk analysis. In line with NCCF priority area 4
(Capacity development and knowledge transfer), EbAM will provide targeted capacity development on climate
vulnerability analysis. Trainings (see Feasibility Study for details), conducted by FAO staff and consultants, will

=== PAGE 43 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 39
B
promote FAO-developed tools such as ABC map or the Global Agro-ecological Zoning platform (GAEZ).
Climate vulnerability assessments will allow the NCCF staff to better identify major climate risks for the projects
it will finance, and select suitable adaptation measures.
- Sub-activity 3.1.1.5. Capacity development on carbon balance analysis. In line with NCCF priority area 4
(Capacity development and knowledge transfer), EbAM will deliver trainings to NCCF staff on GHG accounting
with FAO-developed tools/ methodologies such as the FAO Ex-ante Carbon Balance Tool (Ex-ACT) or the
Global Livestock Environmental Assessment Model, interactive (GLEAM-i) tools, which are built on the latest
scientific information. These tools will enable NCCF staff to assess, monitor and evaluate the mitigation
potential of Projects financed by NCCF in the agriculture, forestry and other land use change (AFOLU) sectors.
81. Activity 3.1.2. Support to National Conservation Trust Funds (financed by GCF; Executed by FAO). The
Project will provide capacity development to two (2) local Trusts (the Malawi Environmental Endowment Trust – MEET and
Shire BEST) to scale-up and replicate investments promoted by EbAM. More particularly, the Project will support (starting
year 1) these local funds in broadening their funding base, with the ambition to promote EbA and watershed resilience in
their operations, and implement their mandate to yield positive environment and natural resource conservation, in the
context of climate change.
- Sub-activity 3.1.2.1: Technical assistance for national entities in accessing GCF resources. This
intervention would support MEET in accessing, for example, the GCF Project Specific Assessment Approach
(PSAA) instrument, and be considered as a local Direct Access Entity (DAE) to GCF. MEET direct access to
GCF is a priority for Malawi’s National Designated Authority - NDA (Environmental Affairs Department - EAD).
The Project will support PSAA process for MEET, including a proposed project (including the environmental
and social safeguards), together with the institutional and capacity assessment of MEET. See see Part 2 of the
Feasibility Study for more details.
- Sub activity 3.1.2.2: Feasibility studies to develop innovative finance instruments for ecosystem
restoration. To support implementation of MEET’s Resources Mobilization Strategy (RMS, 2019-2023), the
Project will finance studies to access innovative climate finance instruments for more funding towards EbA.
One instrument identified during design are debt-for-nature swaps (DFES). The Project will support MEET in
financing prefeasibility studies to assess the potential for leveraging DFES in the context of Malawi.
- Sub-activity 3.1.2.3. Capacity development on Monitoring and Evaluation (M&E). The Project will supports
the Conservation Trust Funds to develop indicators for the Fund’s monitoring, verification and reporting
framework. EbAM’s “SMART” outcome/outputs indicators and reporting methodologies will be leveraged to
contribute to the Trusts M&E systems. Synergies with activity 3.1.1 will also be explored, for Trust Funds’ staff
to benefit from other trainings delivered to NCCF.
82. Activity 3.1.3. Leveraging private sector experience on carbon credits in Malawi as part of the exit strategy
(financed by the GCF; executed by FAO). This activity will establish the enabling environment to leverage private sector
finance for ecosystem restoration interventions, and will be carried out in synergy with the Restore Africa Programme,
financed by Climate Asset Management (CAM) – a joint venture between HSBC Asset Management and Pollination. The
Restore Africa Programme is implemented by the Global Evergreening Alliance (GEA) – an alliance of NGOs engaged in
landscape restoration for livelihood improvements (see donor mapping in the feasibility study). GEA, through the leadership
of Catholic Relief Services (CRS) in Malawi, is implementing the Restore Africa Programme in Malawi, which is combining
restoration activities with access to carbon credits. CAM is investing in the Restore Africa Programme against the future
flow of carbon credits generated from restoration activities. The Programme includes a carbon revenue sharing mechanism
with communities allowing them to (i) benefit from restoration activities that improve livelihoods (e.g. better and more diverse
crop yield and market linkages) and (ii) share in the carbon revenue. Carbon credits can be generated from restoration
activities over a period of 30 years – and sometimes even 100 years – allowing for continuous and long term funding
exceeding the GCF funding cycle. Based on the following two sub-activities, the country will be able to further replicate
EbAM types of activities locally, with the sale carbon credits as a mechanism to attract further financing similar to the
Restore Africa Programme.
- Sub-activity 3.1.3.1. Gap analysis and baseline. This sub-activity will aim at performing a gap analysis and
establishing a baseline and additionality assessment during the first months of implementation of EbAM to
assess potential for proposing carbon credit in EbAM’s areas (preferably in one or two districts that Restore
Africa Programme and EbAM have in common, such as Neno and Chitipa) on the mid to long term, as a
possible additional element to the Project’s exit strategy. The gap analysis will allow to assess whether
technical solutions (in terms of potential for promoted trees and shrubs species to sequester carbon, above

=== PAGE 44 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 40
B
and below ground) proposed by EbAM are suitable for generating and claiming carbon credits under
international standards such as VERRA, Gold Standard or Plan Vivo.
- Sub-activity 3.1.3.2. Continuous learning for possible replication. Under this sub-activity, EbAM will
mobilize national and international expertise, in synergy with the Knowledge Platform established under the
Restore Africa Programme, to consolidate the learning process on Restore Africa Programme activities in
Malawi, and propose operational solutions for this approach to be replicated in the country, including through
the involvement of other EbAM partners (NCCF, MEET, Shire BEST, MFIs, etc.), using EbAM intervention
areas as possible entry points.
83. Sub-component 3.2 Scaling-up in national policies. (Output 3.2: EbA integrated in national policies). This sub-
component will improve the enabling environment by promoting EbA as a key instrument for climate change adaptation
within national policies. The ultimate goal of mainstreaming EbA is to enhance the effectiveness, efficiency, longevity of
EbA principles by embedding its practices into policies, sectoral planning and financing – including government budget –
hence contributing to EbAM’s paradigm shift and sustainability. Only the integration of EbA into planning tools and budgets
of sectoral strategies can secure the financial support and human resources needed for it to become viable in the long
term. For this to happen, this sub-component will support: (i) some evidence generation from the Project on the socio-
economic benefits of EbA, drawing on the lessons from VLAP and SCMP implementation (activity 3.2.1), (ii) the preparation
of a policy influencing plan (PIP), based on a policy assessment analyzing challenges and opportunities for mainstreaming
EbA into different sectoral policies (activity 3.2.2), and (iii) implementation of priority actions of the PIP (activity 3.2.3). This
sub-component will be co-financed by, and synergize closely with the GEF-7-funded Sustainable Forest Management,
Dryland Sustainable Landscape Impact Programme.
84. Activity 3.2.1 Preparation of evidence-based studies (financed by the GCF, executed by FAO). The Project
will finance a set of knowledge products, best practices and cases studies based on EbAM experience. These studies will
play a key role in proposing policy changes. Results of the cases will be compiled into recommendations (briefs) with the
objective to stimulate dialogue around EbA-based policies and feed the policy improvement process.
- Sub-activity 3.2.1.1 Policy briefs based cost-benefit analyses (CBA). As part of the M&E system, the
project will conduct CBA – which will be done on farms and communities having benefited from EbAM’s support.
CBA will analyze adoption rates, costs and compute financial indicators such as net margins, net present value
(NPV), internal rate of return and annual cash flows. The project will finance policy briefs to highlight the
efficiency/effectiveness of EbA in the context of EbAM, and provide “business cases”, to inform policy dialogue.
- Sub-activity 3.2.1.2 Policy brief: TAPE197 analysis. Impact of EbA on production systems will carry out
analysis of the socio-economic performance of EbAM, using the FAO Tool for Agroecology Performance
Evaluation (TAPE) methodology. It will evidence the impacts of EbA by carrying out a diagnostic of production
systems with regard to various dimensions of EbA (environmental, social, economic), in the targeted
watersheds ecosystems and communities (watershed ecosystems – component 1, production systems –
component 2.1). This study will evidence the wider benefits of EbA in relation to sustainable development, in
terms of environmental, social, economic and gender-sensitive development co-benefits.
85. Activity 3.2.2. Policy Assessment and preparation of a policy influencing plan (PIP) (financed by FAO;
executed by FAO). For this activity, the Project –through the FAO-managed GEF-7 project - will collaborate with the
Malawi’s National Committee on Climate Change and Disaster Risk Management (NCCC&DRM) who will provide strategic
direction, inter-ministerial coordination (including MoA, MoCCNR, MoF etc.) and policy guidance in relation to Malawi’s
climate policy, including the NDC. NCCC&DRM acts as a forum for cross-sectoral review and evaluation of progress in
NDC implementation.
- Sub-activity 3.2.2.1 Policy Influencing Plan (PIP). Through the FAO/GEF-7 DSLP Project, EbAM will partner
with the Centre for Environmental Policy and Advocacy (CEPA) to carry out a policy review process/
assessment. The result of this policy review process will be a Policy Influencing Plan (PIP) (i.e a policy
advocacy plan) including the in-depth policy analysis and a set of priority recommendations to improve the
mainstreaming of ecosystem restoration, integrated landscape management and biodiversity conservation into
the national policy frameworks.
- Sub-activity 3.2.2.1.2. Dissemination of the PIP. The PIP will be presented at a National Seminar that the
Malawi National Committee on Climate Change and Disaster Risk Management (NCCC&DRM) will call,
involving policy-makers, civil servants, research/academia, extension organizations, farmer organizations,
private sector, development partners and NGOs. PIP will also be disseminated through the production of

=== PAGE 45 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 41
B
leaflets, posters, banners and reports with abundant visual elements, presentations and video presentations
translated in the local languages.
86. Activity 3.2.3 Implementation of the PIP (financed by GCF; executed by FAO). Implementation of the PIP will
be done through policy dialogues, that will aim at promoting a policy shift towards ecosystem-centered measures linked to
sustainable farming, under conservation agriculture, agro-environmental production and climate-resilient crops and native,
well adapted, non-invasive varieties. Objective of this activity is to re-purpose subsidies from inorganic fertilizers and maize
seeds, to incentives linked to sustainable tree-crop-livestock agroforestry farming under conservation agriculture,
biodiversified tree-crop-livestock agroforestry climate-resilient, crops and varieties – as highlighted in the National Forest
Land Restoration Strategy 2017.
- Sub-activity 3.2.3.1. Policy dialogue. Based on the PIP prepared by the FAO/GEF-7 DSLP Project, and using
EbAM’s best practices/ evidence-based studies (prepared under activity 3.2.1), the Project will finance an
iterative series of 5 policy dialogue events led by NCCC&DRM at national level, to provide information about
existing policy rules and regulations, policy constraints and proposed improvements (new or revised policies)
with EbA integrated. Policy dialogue events will target the following stakeholders: (i) policy makers, (ii) civil
servants and public officials, (iii) traditional leaders, and, (iv) district officials. Policy dialogue will involve the
Parliamentary Committee on Agriculture and Natural Resources who can lobby during budget sessions for
more funds allocation into these areas.
- Sub-activity 3.2.3.2 Update of policies and strategic frameworks. These include the Agrobiodiversity
Policy, the National Agriculture Investment Plan (current NAIP covers 2017-2023), National Biodiversity
Strategy and Action Plan (current NBSAP covers 2015-2025) based on the best practices from the
implementation of ILM with EbA integrated. The Project will organize public events to help make an advocacy
case of the revised/new policies, include advocacy-related information in websites, and enroll high-profile
individuals to publicly advocate for the proposed changes.
B.4. Implementation arrangements (max. 1500 words, approximately 3 pages plus diagrams)
Accredited Entity
87. FAO will serve as the Accredited Entity (AE) for this project. As such, FAO will be responsible for the overall
management of the project, including: (i) all aspects of project appraisal; (ii) administrative, financial and technical oversight
and supervision throughout project implementation; (iii) ensuring funds are effectively managed to deliver results and
achieve objectives; (iv) ensuring the quality of project monitoring, as well as the timeliness and quality of reporting to the
GCF; and (v) project closure and evaluation. FAO will ensure these responsibilities in accordance with the detailed
provisions outlined in the Accreditation Master Agreement (AMA) between FAO and GCF.
88. FAO’s role as AE will be attributed to the relevant offices and divisions in FAO Headquarters located in Rome, Italy
(HQ), Sub-Regional Office for Southern Africa located in Harare, Zimbabwe and the Country Representation Office for
Malawi (FAO-Malawi).
89. In order to fulfil the AE functions, FAO will set up a dedicated Project Task Force (PTF) in line with FAO project
cycle guidelines. The PTF will be composed by the Budget Holder (BH), the Lead Technical Officer (LTO), Funding Liaison
Officer (FLO), HQ Technical Officer and other technical officers, as appropriate.
90. The PTF will remain independent from the Executing Entity functions also performed by FAO (see Project execution
section below). In line with the GCF policy on fees adopted through GCF Board Decision B.19/09, the above-mentioned
segregation of responsibilities within FAO will ensure that the Organization can independently and effectively perform the
AE functions listed in the GCF General principles and indicative list of eligible costs covered under GCF fees and project
management costs.

Convention on the Privileges and Immunities of the Specialized Agencies, 2) provisions with respect to the co-financing to
be provided by the Government of Malawi acting through MoA and MoF, and 3) the respective roles and responsibilities of

implementation arrangements outlined above, GCF proceeds received by FAO in its capacity as Accredited Entity will flow

responsibilities, both as EEs and co-financiers, as well as NLGFC responsibilities as EE, together with all financial details,
will be included in the Project Agreement, which will also serve as subsidiary agreement, signed by the Government of
Malawi.

guidance of the PSC and project technical committee (PTC), are to ensure overall efficient management, coordination,
implementation and monitoring of the project through the effective implementation of the annual work plans and budgets
(AWPBs). The PIU will be led and managed by a project-recruited National Project Coordinator (NPC). The NPC will be
appointed by FAO and will be responsible for overall project management and coordination with project stakeholders. The
PIU will also include (part time) a finance officer (50%), operation officer (50%), Human resources & admin officer (50%)
and procurement & contracting officer (50%) as well as a contracts management officer. In addition, the project PIU will
include the following technical specialists: (i) total 6 technical advisors for components 1 and 2: a team of 2 specialists (EbA
& Agroecology specialist, NRM specialist) in each project office (1 central and 2 regional offices); (ii) Agribusiness & Finance
specialist, (iii) Gender and social inclusion specialist, (iv) Environmental and social safeguards international technical
assistance (E&S) – part time 50%, (v) a national safeguards specialist, (vi) M&E / GIS; and (vi) part time Knowledge
Management specialist (50%). All staff will be hired under the project through a competitive process.
96. The CPIU will coordinate closely with the two Regional Project Implementation Units (RPIUs), which will be
established in Blantyre (Southern Region) and Mzuzu (Northern Region). RPIUs will supervise the day-to-day project
operations in each districts, liaising with the Focal Points (appointed by the respective EE) in each district. The regional
PIU will be composed of the two technical specialists (EbA/ Agroecology specialist, NRM specialist) mentioned above,
together with an M&E associate, and an Administrative & Finance associate (part time 30%).
Other Project Partners
97. During implementation, in addition to the above EE, the project will engage relevant government counterparts from
MoA (e.g. Gene Bank within the Research Services), Ministry of Climate Change and Natural Resources – MoCCNR (e.g.
DCCMS) as procured parties. It will also engage knowledge institutions (Agroecology Hub of Lilongwe University of
Agriculture and Natural Resources – LUANAR), training centers (Paradise Permaculture Centre, Kusamala Permaculture
Institute, SFHC Research and Training Centre), local non-profit conservation trusts (MEET, Shire BEST), finance service
providers and the private sector (e.g. Malawi Industrial & Agricultural Investment Corporation – MAIIC).
98. In addition, several partners will be engaged in the project either to ensure complementarity with their activities
and/or delivery of goods works and services. The project will cooperate closely with a consortium of qualified and
experienced service providers (NGOs) from the Malawi Climate Smart Agriculture Alliance (MCSAA), which have extensive
technical expertise relevant for the activities to be implemented by this project, and which have regularly worked with MoA
(DLRC). MCSAA includes CARE, Catholic Relief Services (CRS), Total Land Care (TLC), Development Fund of Norway
(DF Norway), Find Your Feet (FYF). It will also work with NGOs having a proven track-record of implementing EbA/
agroecology activities in the countries or in the region. The partners will be selected as procured parties during project
implementation in accordance with FAO rules and regulations for procuring good and services (e.g. FAO Manual Sections
502 and 507).
Project Governance
99. A Project Steering Committee (PSC) will be established to provide strategic guidance for the project. The PSC
will be co-chaired by the NDA (Environmental Affairs Department, MoCCNR), and co-chaired by the Secretary of the MoA
and FAO Representative to Malawi. It will also include the Secretary of Ministry of Climate Change and Natural Resources
(MoCCNR). The NPC of the PIU will serve as Rapporteur to the PSC. The PSC will include representatives of other key
government departments and agencies, private sector and civil society organizations. These partners will include MoA
Departments for Land Resources Conservation, Crop Development, Agriculture Extension Services, Agriculture Planning
Services, Animal Health and Livestock Development, and respectively. The MoNRCC will also be engaged through the
Departments of Forestry (DoF), Climate Change and Meteorological Services (DCCMS), Fisheries (DoF), respectively. It
will also engage the NLGFC, the Ministry of Finance and Economic Affairs (MoF, Pensions and Financial Sector Division
which is overseeing FARMSE), the Ministry of Community Development and Social Welfare, the Ministry of Lands, the
Ministry of Industry, as well as other key entities such as Lilongwe University of Agriculture and Natural Resources
(LUANAR), the National Smallholder Farmers' Association of Malawi (NASFAM), the National Water Resources Authority
(NWRA), CSOs (Civil Society Network on Climate Change) and NGOs (MCSAA). Representatives of (i) the Development
Cooperation Group on Environment, Resilience and Climate change (DCERCC) of the Environmental Affairs Department
and (ii), the Joint Technical Committee on Climate Change and Disaster Risk Management, the Donor Committee in
Agriculture and Food Security (DCAFS) will also sit in the PSC.
100. The role of the PSC will be to: (i) provide overall guidance and direction to the project, ensuring it remains within
any specified constraints; (ii) address project issues as raised by the national project coordinator; (iii) monitor project risks
and the effectiveness of mitigation measures, and provide guidance on new project risks, and agree on possible
countermeasures and management actions to address specific risks; (iv) review the project progress, and provide direction

=== PAGE 49 ===

and recommendations to ensure that the agreed deliverables are produced satisfactorily according to plans; (v) review and
agree with annual work plan and provide necessary strategic guidance for its implementation; (vi) appraise the annual
project implementation report, including the quality assessment rating report; (vii) make recommendations for subsequent
work plans to build on achievements and address any shortcomings; and (viii) provide ad hoc direction and advice for
exceptional situations when the project coordinator’s tolerances are exceeded.

for the following meeting being agreed under Any Other Business). Extraordinary meetings of the PSC can be requested
by any of its members.
102. The PSC will be supported by the Project Technical Committee (PTC), which will review and, where needed,
advise on the technical delivery of the project. The PTC will be co-chaired by the NDA, the Department of Land Resources
Conservation and FAO Representation in Malawi, which will be the Secretariat for both the PSC and the PTC. Other
members of the PTC will include MoA Departments for Crop Development, Agriculture Extension Services, Agriculture
Planning Services, Animal Health and Livestock Development, and Agriculture Research Services (including the Gene
Bank), MoF/FARMSE and the MoCCNR Departments of Irrigation, Forestry, and Fisheries respectively, and NASFAM,
FUM, NWRA, and relevant CSOs and NGOs. The PTC will: (i) technically oversee activities in their sector; (ii) ensure a
fluid two-way exchange of information and knowledge between their agency and the project; (iii) facilitate coordination and
links between the project activities and the work plan of their agency; and (iv) facilitate the provision of co-financing to the
project.

B.5. Justification for GCF funding request (max. 1000 words, approximately 2 pages)
103. The proposed project is focused on reaching out to the most vulnerable populations in a LDC, with high vulnerability
to climate change. LDCs, and Malawi in particular, are indeed the most vulnerable to the damaging effects of climate
change, since their economic development, growth and food security highly depend on climate-sensitive sectors such as
agriculture.
104. The proposed GCF grant is appropriate to address the needs of the country, since Malawi does not dispose of the
needed public resources to finance the project through public debt. According to the World Bank statistics201, Malawi has
a large stock of public debt (external debt stocks have increased from 28% to 32.5% of gross national income – GNI,
between 2015 and 2019) which has continued to increase in 2020/2021 due to a widening fiscal deficit – mainly due to a
slowdown in revenue collection driven by the COVID-19 pandemic, combined with increasing spending pressures including
from response to the pandemic, debt service costs and unbudgeted arrears. Malawi is at high risk of overall debt distress,

B.5. Justification for GCF funding request (max. 1000 words, approximately 2 pages)
103. The proposed project is focused on reaching out to the most vulnerable populations in a LDC, with high vulnerability
to climate change. LDCs, and Malawi in particular, are indeed the most vulnerable to the damaging effects of climate
change, since their economic development, growth and food security highly depend on climate-sensitive sectors such as
agriculture.
104. The proposed GCF grant is appropriate to address the needs of the country, since Malawi does not dispose of the
needed public resources to finance the project through public debt. According to the World Bank statistics201, Malawi has
a large stock of public debt (external debt stocks have increased from 28% to 32.5% of gross national income – GNI,
between 2015 and 2019) which has continued to increase in 2020/2021 due to a widening fiscal deficit – mainly due to a
slowdown in revenue collection driven by the COVID-19 pandemic, combined with increasing spending pressures including
from response to the pandemic, debt service costs and unbudgeted arrears. Malawi is at high risk of overall debt distress,

=== PAGE 50 ===
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.3.0 | PAGE 46
B
making it difficult for the country to meet its needs (through debt finance) in terms of climate-finance for a paradigm shift
towards climate resilient practices and land restoration.
105. The Government of Malawi requests maximum concessionality to support vulnerable farmers to adapt to increasing
temperatures and rainfall variability attributed to climate change, leading to droughts and floods. The GCF plays a catalytic
and transformative role to: (i) unlock additional investment in climate resilient agriculture, and resilient ecosystems, (ii) cover
the costs of enhancing the capacities of farmers (and their organizations/ communities) to understand and act on climate
change adaptation in their landscapes/watersheds and production systems, (iii) repair ecosystems affected by climate
change, develop resilience-enhancing agricultural production systems, and enhance farm and business planning to
sufficiently stabilize revenues for continued investment in adaptive responses to climate change.
106. The NDC 2021 of Malawi puts the estimated funding requirements for climate change adaptation at USD 1.23
billion, of which 656 million relies on external sources, for the period of 2020-2025 and USD 1.56 billion, of which 818 million
is to be supplied by external sources, for 2025-30. For agriculture, livestock and fisheries, roughly USD 600 million from
external sources is deemed necessary for adaptation in 2020-2040, of which more than half concerns climate resilient
agriculture and soil/water/watershed management. In 2019, it was estimated that USD 55 million would be required per
district for adaptation of climate change resilient agriculture and that access to climate change funds was meagre compared
to the size of the problem. With respect to mitigation, USD 4.21 billion is necessary for 2020-2025, of which 2.55 billion is
to be found, while USD 7.34 billion is needed for 2025-2030, of which 5.39 billion is yet to be secured. Mitigation through
crop management requires some USD 11 billion during 2020-2040, half of which is to depend on the international
community. The situation is similar for forestry and land use, as close to half of more than USD 1.41 billion for the same
period is to come from external sources. References to these data are found in the endnotes.
107. A number of investments (funded for e.g. by the World Bank, the GEF or the EU) have been and are being
implemented to address climate-related risks and threats. Yet, adaptation needs overreach the current scope of
interventions. The NFRLS (2017) reports that (i) up to 3.7 million hectares (39% of Malawi’s total areas) have an opportunity
for conservation agriculture, farmer-managed natural regeneration and agro-forestry and, (ii) about 1 million hectares (11%
of Malawi’s total area) have an opportunity for soil and water conservation. The NDC for Malawi (from June 2021) also
affirms the substantial need for external funding as condition for successfully implementing the adaptation needs. GCF
proceeds will, through the EbAM project, contribute to addressing this financing gap.
108. Co-financing with other initiatives has been thoroughly identified, including with the MoF/FARMSE Programme
(6.44 million USD) and the GEF-7, FAO implemented DSLP (0.52 million USD). The Project also secured national co-
financing from the Ministry of Agriculture (2.95 million) and co-financing from FAO (0.5 million USD). Government co-
financing will ensure ownership, sustainability and replicability. The Project also identified parallel co-financing
opportunities, which include the Restore Africa Programme (under preparation), financed by Climate Asset Management
(CAM) and implemented by the Global Evergreening Alliance (GEA). Leveraged co-financing could also include funding
from the Malawi Agricultural and Industrial Investment Corporation (MAIIC) – as mentioned in sub-component 2.3 (in
section B.3).
B.6. Exit strategy (max. 500 words, approximately 1 page)
109. The project design includes several features to enhance sustainability. By supporting CMC and VNRMC to
systematically mainstream EbA into local development planning (sub-activity 1.1.3.3 and 1.1.4.3), the Project will develop
medium to long-term institutional capacity to mobilize additional climate finance towards climate-resilient investments in
degraded watershed ecosystems, beyond the Project’s investment horizon. The Project support (more particularly under
activity 1.1.3.3) will ensure that operations and maintenance (O&M) needs (e.g. monitoring of land degradation, regular
land maintenance) will be included in VLAPs, and expected to be covered through local governments (districts) funding/
budgets and other sources (see below). This decentralized and participatory planning process will advance the policy and
regulatory frameworks in the field, more particularly the Decentralization Act (which devolves funding from central
Government to districts).
110. The increased financial inclusion of smallholder farmers, FOs and SMEs within local finance institutions, together
with partnerships with financial instrument providers (e.g. MAIIC) developed (and enhanced) by the MoF/FARMSE (co-
financing and co-executing the Project) will contribute to enhance the sustainability of ecosystems-based adaptation
interventions. In addition, (i) support to the Malawi Climate Change Fund (NCCF), (ii) linkages with national conservation
trusts (MEET and Shire BEST) and, (ii) partnerships with the private sector (CAM/ HSBC – which is financing the Restore
Africa Programme) to leverage experience on carbon credits, will facilitate mobilization of climate finance, and contribute
to sustaining, replicating and ensuring the long-term financial sustainability of the landscape restoration interventions, while
expanding the scale of investments promoted by the Project under component 1 and 2. Interventions will mainstream and
deep-root EbA in national policies and investment plans, and bring the EbA agenda at sectoral policies level. By integrating

Table C.3.1. Innovations introduced in EbAM
111. The Project will scale up a number of innovations which are already tried and tested, with a history of delivering
positive adaptation results. The climate-resilient investments promoted by the Project are expected to generate attractive
financial returns for the farmers202 as evidenced in the EFA (see Annex 3). The prospects of stabilized and diversified
incomes and relatively higher returns for the farmers are a key incentive for the long-term adoption and sustainability of
climate-resilient practices and technologies.
112. Through the various capacity development activities, the project will invest in strengthening the capacity of
extension workers and farmers on the topic of climate-resilient agriculture and EbA. The “climate responsive” FFS
programme on climate-change adaptation will build and strengthen a network of FFS master trainers and lead farmers as
FFS facilitators, who will build the needed extension capacity within the farmer communities. These master trainers and
facilitators will be able to support other similar extension interventions inside and outside the targeted districts and
watersheds, beyond the Project lifespan.
113. As mentioned below, the proposed project was designed through the participation of a wide array of public and
private institutions, civil society (including national and international NGOs) to promote ownership of the project; the
project’s Stakeholder Engagement Plan (Annex 7) provides detailed information on how these stakeholders will keep being
engaged during implementation. M&E and KM&L activities will ensure that the lessons learned, documents produced and
the activities implemented during the project are archived (within the Project MIS system), and disseminated to the benefit
of other projects and programmes.

C.3 Capacity building and technology development/transfer (max. 250 words, approximately 0.5 page)
C.3.1 Does GCF funding finance capacity building
Yes ☒ No

C.3.2. Does GCF funding finance technology

114. Communities and farmers’ learning on EbA are at the core of the investment strategy – and will amount
5.53 million of GCF funding. For this reason, capacity development activities will be mainstreamed across the
three components, and will aim at addressing the multifaceted barriers to climate change adaptation in Malawi,
i.e. technical/knowledge, planning, social, financial and institutional capacity. Under component 1, capacity
development focuses on knowledge transfer and capacity building for the implementation of adaptation
measures, gender and social inclusion with a special focus on FPIC and SEAH and GBV, and will target (i)
ILM stakeholders on EbA as well as traditional/community leaders and other key figures, (ii) VNRMCs for the
formulation and implementation of EbA-based VLAPs, and (iii) CMCs for the preparation of EbA-based CMPs.
Under component 2, trainings will include: (i) capacity development on EbA to farmers, through the FFS and
targeted trainings, (ii) capacity development to SMEs for business plan preparation and (iii) capacity
development to financial institutions – including community based financing institutions, such as VSLAs. Under
component 3, capacity development focuses on institutional capacity building for the sustainability of the project
and the enhancement of the enabling environment, and targets: (i) NCCF, and local conservation trusts and
(ii) policy makers. These capacity development activities, combined with an enhanced access to finance to
undertake the recommendations, are a major push factor to achieve the paradigm shift in helping farmers to
positively adapt, safeguard the natural resource base, and provide better services to ecosystems.

D
EXPECTED PERFORMANCE AGAINST INVESTMENT CRITERIA
This section refers to the performance of the project/programme against the investment criteria as set out in the
GCF’s Initial Investment Framework.
D.1. Impact potential (max. 500 words, approximately 1 page)
115. The project objective is to increase the climate-change resilience of the most vulnerable rural communities at
watershed level in Malawi, where climate change accelerates the vicious cycle of low agriculture productivity and
watershed degradation. “Climate-change resilience” will be defined as the enhanced capacity of beneficiaries to
anticipate, absorb, accommodate or recover from extreme weather events and natural disasters resulting from climate
change in a timely, efficient and sustainable manner. This includes protecting, restoring and improving ecosystems and
livelihoods in the face of threats that impact agriculture and hence the economy, food security and nutrition (adapted
from the FAO definition of resilience)204.
116. EbAM will support vulnerable Malawian rural communities to positively adapt to the impacts of climate change
and improve their livelihoods through the adoption of EbA measures, including low-emission climate-resilient
agricultural practices, based on ecosystem restoration and services at landscape (watershed) and farm levels. Well-
functioning ecosystems surrounding ecosystem-like farms bring multiple benefits for producers, including higher yields
through improved soil structure and water retention, and increased resilience to pests. On farm biodiversity enhances
soil organic matter and soil structure, which are continuously deteriorating under conventional agriculture. Improved
soil in turn increase water holding capacity, and hence reduce exposure to climate hazards, such as droughts and
floods. Farms are also resilient when strengthened as ecosystems; diversity means that the farm as a whole is less
vulnerable to specific pests (weeds or insects) and diseases induced by climatic events. In fact, EbA/ agroecology has
been proven to increase productivity in developing countries.205 Further, an ecosystem-based approach to production
also leads to higher producer margins by improving soil fertility and decreasing the need for purchasing chemical
fertilizers. In Malawi, it has been shown that EbA/ agroecology generates higher benefits in agriculture (higher yields,
environment, livelihood, food and nutrition) than conventional agriculture. Due to the context-specific nature of EbA/
agroecology, its precise effects are subject to socioeconomic, cultural and environmental factors of each farm206.
Further, integrated systems facilitate the recycling of nutrients and reduces the need for purchasing chemical fertilizers.
Productive farms support farmers to safeguard the natural resource base and improve their incomes and nutrition, as
well as unlocking their opportunities to expand and diversify their livelihoods – through enhanced access to market and
finance. Through its interventions, EbAM will contribute to GCF ARA1 “Most Vulnerable People and Communities” (with
support for livelihood enhancement through increasing resilience), GCF ARA2 “Health, well-being, food and water
security” and GCF ARA4 “Ecosystems and Ecosystem Services” and GCF MRA4 “Forestry and Land Use”.
117. The proposed project is expected to directly benefit around 270,820 beneficiaries vulnerable to climate-change
(1.42% of Malawian population) in 11 pre-identified districts. Within each of the pre-targeted districts, the project will
invest in 30 sub-catchments (for a total of about 267,500 hectares conserved, restored, and sustainably managed207),
with a total of 1,110 villages. The project investment logic is based on an integrated landscape development approach,
with sub-catchments being entry points. Therefore, the methodology for calculating direct beneficiaries (as one of the
proxy to impact potential) is based on the number of people and households being part of the villages in the targeted
micro-watersheds benefiting from component 1 investments. Detailed on estimated beneficiaries per activity is provided
in the Feasibility Study (section 5.4). Based on use sex-disaggregated data at district level (data from the 2018
household Census), the project expects to reach 52% of women.
118. Villages and people that are not part of the targeted micro-watersheds but belong to the overall selected sub-
catchments were accounted as indirect beneficiaries. These indirect beneficiaries are individuals who do not receive
targeted support from EbAM’s intervention – but will receive a measurable adaptation benefit thanks to well-functioning
SCMCs and EbA-based SCMP developed under component 1. The total number of indirect beneficiaries is then 69,100
households or 304,035 people.
119. FAO’s Ex-Ante Carbon Balance Tool (Ex-ACT) has been used to estimate in detail (in tCO2eq over 20 years)
the mitigation impact of carbon sequestration and avoided degradation. Ex-ACT results (see Annex 22 for details on
results and methodology) suggest a mitigation potential in the range of -2,750,323 tCO2eq over 20 years or -137,516
tCO2eq/year.
D.2. Paradigm shift potential (max. 500 words, approximately 1 page)
120. This project aims to be a catalyst for a broad shift and new sustainable equilibrium for ecosystem, livelihoods
and agriculture across Malawi, from their baseline state of very high vulnerability—in terms of high exposure, sensitivity
and low adaptive capacity to more frequent and intense extreme climate events—to an alternative paradigm in which

watershed ecosystems are conserved, restored, and more sustainably managed, thus granting their adaptation to
climate change, and their supply of services to climate-resilient farming systems, people and communities.
121. To achieve this, the project will promote the locally-led EbA approach combined with integrated landscape
management (ILM) to repair degraded ecosystems, and low-carbon climate resilient agricultural practices to allow
agriculture and other livelihoods to become resilient to climate change.208 The EbA approach – which is the core
transformational driver of the project - is fully aligned with Malawi’s Updated Nationally Determined Contributions
(NDC), 2021209. The latter recommends: development of adaptation planning tools; ecosystem based adaptation;
integrated watershed management; crop diversification; sustainable soil and water management; afforestation;
agroforestry; sustainable forest management; and riparian restoration. Ecosystem-based management of
watersheds/landscapes is also one of the two paradigm-shifting pathways defined by the GCF Sectorial Guide on
Ecosystems and Ecosystem Services. This integrative and game-changing approach brought by the Project
(additionality) will ensure a sustainable transformation not only within, but also across project districts and
watersheds under the projected climate change scenario.
122. The paradigm shift brought forth by the project relies on applying EbA through ILM to sustainably transform
ecosystems (both natural ecosystems and production systems that exist in the same landscape). EbA will help farmers
to positively adapt, safeguard the natural resource base, and provide better services to ecosystems (reciprocal
relationship between farmers and nature). The project will aim at enhancing ecosystem functions at a landscape
(watershed) level large enough to facilitate climate change adaptation at scale. In the context of Malawi’s water
resources governance and decentralization system, EbA-based ILM plans will be at watershed (CMP) and village levels
(VLAP). As a result of the Project, EbA will be firmly integrated in these local plans and processes. ILM allows the
collective identification of climate vulnerabilities and resulting priorities of interventions, to which EbA offers most
relevant solutions. ILM is already implemented at a smaller scale in the FAO/GEF-7 Project in Malawi. It involves long-
term collaboration among different groups of land managers and stakeholders to achieve their multiple objectives and
expectations within the landscape defined by them. As such, ILM is the ideal vehicle to plan and implement EbA. Thus
combined, ILM and EbA yield social sustainability (through the participatory process), together with environmental
sustainability and resilience – hence delivering on GCF ARA1, ARA2, ARA4 and MR4. ILM under the Project will
engage marginalized groups, which will significantly reduce the risk of creating new climate vulnerability210. The
planning and implementation processes will be highly inclusive, with meaningful participation of vulnerable groups (e.g.,
women) to ensure their capacity building, and examination of decision-making power sharing at household and
community levels. Local and traditional knowledge in ecosystem management will be incorporated.
123. Interventions according to EbA are comprised of actions to restore and strengthen ecosystems (see Appendix
1 of the Feasibility Study describing the various EbA solutions applicable to the Malawi context) so that biodiversity
and ecosystem services are maximized, and climate-change adaptation is most effective. EbA all2o1w1s “holistic solutions
for holistic benefits” and is superior to other climate-change adaptation strategies in many aspects. By nature, EbA
boosts ecological resilience212 by strengthening, restoring and sustainably managing ecosystems.213 Resilient
ecosystems are equipped with self-healing and adapting capabilities, which render EbA measures effective in a wider
range of climate situations than other adaptation strategies. EbA, combined with ILM, generates benefits short- and
long-terms benefits214 and is applicable at regional, national and local levels.215 EbA is considered more cost effective
in climate change adaptation than grey infrastructure when economic, social and environmental benefits are
included.216 When local knowledge217 (holistic socio-ecological knowledge, practices and beliefs)218 is integrated, EbA
can avoid maladaptation. Healthy watershed ecosystems better absorb shocks resulting from floods and droughts, thus
reducing their impact, and can limit water pollution exacerbated by extreme events and climate change. In contrast,
improved agricultural productivity through EbA lessens flood damages, makes water available year-round, sustains
itself under extreme weather, enhances biodiversity, strengthens watershed/landscape functions and improves food
security. EbA is often more accessible to the rural poor than other types of adaptation and can bring socio-economic
and environmental benefits beyond adaptation to local communities.
124. The project will boost the efficacy of EbA in food systems through an enhanced and sustainable access to
markets, business opportunities, as well as finance. This shift will support farmers to stabilize and increase their income,
hence making their livelihoods more resilient in the context of climate change. Strong linkages with the FARMSE
Programme under the Ministry of Finance and Economic Affairs (which will co-finance the EbAM Project, and act as an
Executing Entity) will enable farmers’ access to rural finance organizations and institutions. This enhanced access to
finance will allow the adoption of EbA, and shift away from a pure grants-based approach. In addition, the Project will
support Malawi’s vision to establish its NCCF, and strengthen local trusts (e.g. MEET or Shire BEST), which will
ultimately facilitate mobilization, blending, and disbursing of catalytic climate finance, and contribute to sustaining,
replicating and expanding the scale of the Project climate-resilient investments. Similarly, the introduction of PES at the

watershed level will contribute to promoting EbA and putting it on a financially secure footing, thanks to community and
private sector engagement.
The integration of EbA in local plans will contribute to improving the enabling environment, and allow replication
and scale-up of EbA through other projects and programmes. It is expected that projects such as the World Bank-
1fu2n5d.ed “Social Support for Resilient Livelihoods Project”, or interventions under the Restore Africa Programme (see
Part III of the feasibility study with the description of other projects relevant for EbAM) will leverage EbA-based ILM
plans prepared at watershed and village-level under EbAM to implement their activities, hence catalyzing EbA at scale.
In addition, interventions mainstreaming and deep-rooting EbA in national policies and investment plans will bring the
EbA agenda at sectoral policies level – for massive-scale impact and sustainability.
126. Collective learning on EbA will be achieved by training not only the mem bers of watershed management
committees, but with an emphasis on the participation of local inhabitants. The Project employs a landscape approach
to watershed management, whose principal tool is participatory planning based on discussions among stakeholders.
Discussions will be led by Facilitators, who will not impose solutions, but raise awareness during discussions, provide
prompts to deepen the analyses and guide the stakeholders toward sustainable watershed management based on
EbA. The Project also ensures meaningful participation by providing trainings to various stakeholder groups with
priorities given to women and youths. The needs for local inhabitants’ capacity building will also be identified through
the local consultative processes. Gender empowerment is tackled at the root by adopting household methodology,
whose results will be upscaled to community level by tvillage-level organizations, more particularly VNRMCs. These
aspects will create strong ownership of the Project and promote inclusive and meaningful participation of stakeholders
to facilitate awareness improvements and behavioral change. The inhabitants of the area covered by a VLAP will
engage in informal participatory monitoring and evaluation, which will be coordinated by ILM Facilitators. For
establishing a management plan at the sub-catchment level, the experiences at the village level will be shared among
the inhabitants, Traditional Authorities and local government officials. The PIU will integrate the lessons learned from
early phases of the Project to later phases and also share the information at national and international levels. In
particular, the project’s M&E system will generate data, evaluations and studies on the project, some of which will also
be translated into policy briefs, enabling the lessons from the project to be valorized at all levels. The PIU will include a
KM officer who will be tasked with ensuring that relevant lessons are thoroughly documented and disseminated.
D.3. Sustainable development (max. 500 words, approximately 1 page)
127. One key benefit that the Project will generate is enhanced food security (SDG2 – Zero Hunger). EbA practices
will improve soil fertility and boost yields of crops impacted by climate-change (see B.1. climate rationale). For example,
studies in Malawi reported that maize yields could increase by more than 40% under traditional management with
Acacia albida219. Evidence also suggests that yields obtained by smallholder in Malawi could potentially double if
farmers had access to the knowledge, extension services and trainings on sustainable adaptation to climate change220.
Activities will also contribute to poverty alleviation (SDG1 – No Poverty) thanks to their potential to increase household
incomes221.
128. By scaling up EbA practices, the Project will generate environmental benefits in terms of better land and water
use, improved soil quality and water conservation that will lower GHG emissions, hence generating mitigationbenefits
(SDG13 – Climate Action) which are accounted for under MRA4 (Forestry and Land Use – see above). In addition,
erosion control will generate environmental benefits such as sediment retention, hence protecting downstream public
goods (watershed ecosystems including various waterbodies) and private entities222 with valuable fixed assets, hence
contributing to SDG 15 (Life on Land). As highlighted in section B.1, climate change will negatively affect the health of
the population.223 Therefore, as a result of improved climate change adaptation, the Project will also contribute to SDG
3 (Good Health and Well Being).
129. The Project will contribute to gender equality and women empowerment (SDG5), to the National Gender Policy
and address the gender inequalities exacerbated by climate change. It will ensure the full engagement and participation
of women in FFS on climate-resilient agriculture, and mainstream gender in the trainings. The Project will train extension
workers on gender and social inclusion, and create opportunities for dialogues between women and men in the
community. Project will incentivize women’s access to labour saving technologies, nutrition sensitive and early maturing
crop varieties, as well as productivity-enhancing assets. Studies in Malawi224 reported that conservation agriculture
(CA) alone can reduce the labour demand for women farmers by about 34 days.
130. Sustainable adaptation to climate change is unattainable if interventions exclude the vulnerable groups or do
not fully cater to them. The vulnerable groups are characterized by scant access to knowledge, resources and

D.4. Needs of recipient (max. 500 words, approximately 1 page)
131. Current climate change impact pathways put communities under increased pressure to resort to a vicious cycle
of maladaptation, unsustainable ecosystem use and management, and harm to nature. Impacts on people may also
lead to interpersonal conflicts, food insecurity225 and malnutrition as well degraded health conditions. Without a
significant climate-responsive investment project to reverse this cumulative chain of impacts and increase people’s
resilience to climate-change, ecosystems’ ability to supply goods and services to people and local livelihoods will be
constrained, more particularly those underpinning sustainable agricultural production and food security.
132. Shortages of vital ecosystems goods and services will trigger agriculture production shortages. Production of
the main staple crops in Malawi may experience major annual decreases, as much as (i) 770,000 tons for maize
(nationally), (ii) 218,245 tons for root crops (cassava) (Blantyre, Machinga and Shire Valley combined) and, (iii) 160,000
tons for some legumes (pigeon pea), hence creating food security and livelihood challenges for the targeted
communities in the near future226. The economic costs of lost production due to climate change could be as high as
131.2 million USD/ year for maize227, 84.2 million USD/ year for cassava, 86.5 million USD/year for pigeon peas228.
133. The vulnerability to climate change at individual level can be said to originate from social exclusion, which
engenders lack of access to resources and lack of assets and economic opportunities: the very factors that constitute
vulnerability to various shocks and stresses.229 In recent years, economic inequality has significantly worsened.230 In
addition, the youth in Malawi are subject to unemployment and economic exclusion, unwanted pregnancies, high
maternal deaths, sexually transmitted infections and gender-based violence.231 As of 2020, discrimination and violence
toward women and other vulnerable groups remained problematic.232
134. The vulnerable groups – who are rendered particularly susceptible to climate change by social exclusion – are
women (52% of total population), the youth (30% for age 15-35) and 50% for the poor. Eighty-three percent of the
national population lives in the rural areas233 and 80% is engaged in agriculture. 234 Through its investment approach,
the Project will propose meaningful solutions tailored to the vulnerable populations (see more details in the Gender
Action Plan - Annex 8). These approaches include targeting climate vulnerable districts and water resources units,
combined with increased stakeholders’ engagement, including women, youth and other vulnerable groups to plan and
benefit from landscape restoration and on-farm climate-change adaptation interventions based on EbA, with an
improved access to markets and finance.
135. The proposed GCF grant, combined with identified co-financing and parallel finance, is therefore appropriate
to address the needs of the stakeholders, since the Country does not dispose of the needed public resources to
implement the planned project and investments. According to the World Bank235, Malawi has a large stock of public
debt which has continued to increase due to a widening fiscal deficit combined with increasing spending pressures
including from response to the COVID-19 pandemic, debt service costs and unbudgeted arrears. Malawi is overall at
high risk of overall debt distress.
D.5. Country ownership (max. 500 words, approximately 1 page)
136. As described above in section B.1, the Project is aligned to the MGDS III (2017-2020), the NDC, the NAP, the
NAIP 2017-2023, the NFLRS (2017) and the National Resilience Strategy 2018-2030. The NDC puts emphasis on EbA,
integrated catchment conservation and management, capacity development in resilient agronomic practices and water
conservation technologies for smallholder farmers in the agriculture sector. These interventions are in line with Malawi’s
NAP236 (currently under preparation) to reduce vulnerabilities to the adverse effects of climate change.
137. By including implementation of climate change adaptation into SCMPs and VLAPs, the Project will support
implementation of the Decentralization Act (1998), which devolves powers and funding from the central government to
districts. It is also consistent with the Environmental Management Act (2017), which aims to ensure sustainable use of
natural resources, facilitate restoration of ecological systems and preservation of biodiversity; and promote community-
based natural resource management. It will support the National Water Resources Act (2013), which provides a
mechanism for coordination, allocation and delegation of responsibilities among stakeholders (CMCs) for the protection
and integrated management of water resources. The Project will also support the new National Disaster Risk

138. Broad stakeholders consultation processes were conducted during preparation to guarantee country
ownshersip, and ensure that the needs of the recipient were taken into account into the Proposal (see Annex 7). The
NDA (Environmental Affairs Department) has been directly involved at all stages of project preparation, in close
collaboration with the FAO Country Office. Through national workshops, community engagement meetings at district
level and field visits over 2021 and 2022, the preparation of the Funding Proposal (CN process included) involved a
large range of stakeholders, which included: (i) the Director of the NDA, (ii) Government Ministries, such as MoA
(Director of the Department of Land Resources Conservation, Department of Planning Services, Department of Crop
Development, Department of Animal Health and Livestock Development, Department of Research and Technical
Services, Department of Water Resources, Department of Irrigation, Department of Climate Change and Meteorological
Services – DCCMS, Department of Fisheries and Department of Forestry, Gene Bank), MoCCNR (Environmental
Affairs and NCCF Team), MoF (Pension and Financial Inclusion Division, Directorate of Debt and Aid) and NLGFC
(Executive and Deputy Executive Directors); (iii) NGOs (CARE, CRS, TLC, DF Norway, FYF, SFHC237, CADECOM,
SCOPE), (iv) CSO (CISONEC), (v) international research Institutions (International Centre for Research in Agroforestry
– ICRAF, International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics – ICRISAT), (vi) academia (LUANAR) and
knowledge centre (Paradise Permaculture Institute); (vii) the private sector (NASFAM, Ilovo Sugar Company, Climate
Asset Management – CAM/ HSBC), (vii) trusts (Malawi Environment Endowment Trust – MEET, Shire BEST), (viii)
SACCOs, MFIs, commercial Banks and national Development Finance Institution (Malawi Agricultural and Industrial
Investment Corporation plc. – MAIIC) and, (ix) parastatal (National Water Resources Authority), (x) other Projects
(MoF/FARMSE, FAO/GEF-7, Restore Africa, World Bank MWASIP) and (xi) agribusinesses and retail/ distribution
businesses. The Funding Proposal (CN process included) was discussed with the Development Cooperation Group on
Environment, Resilience and Climate change (DCERCC) of the Environmental Affairs Department, the Joint Technical
Committee on Climate Change and Disaster Risk Management, the Donor Committee in Agriculture and Food Security
(DCAFS) and other UN systems entities (including UNDP, in particular for the NCCF). All stakeholders engagement
processes are documented in Annex 7 of the Funding Proposal, which also highlights how stakeholders will be engaged
during implementation.
D.6. Efficiency and effectiveness (max. 500 words, approximately 1 page)
139. EbAM is expected to have multiple benefits for project participants and society as a whole. Broadly, these
benefits can be classified as i) increased productivity on farmland, resulting from EbAM activities in Component 1 and
support to producers in Component 2 (e.g. FFS and improved access to finance); ii) additional post-production value
and improved access to markets through the activites in Component 2 (e.g. the 4Ps and improved access to finance)
iii) a significant reduction in greenhouse gas emissions from EbAM and improved agricultural practices and iv) additional
benefits of EbAM such as an increased production of Non-Timber Forest Products and other, less easily quantifiable,
ecosystems benefits.
140. The ex-ante financial and economic viability of EbAM is demonstrated through an economic and financial
analysis, a cost-benefit analysis of the project. The analysis is based on farm and enterprise models assessing the
costs and benefits of proposed project interventions. The financial analysis considers the profitability of these
investments from the point of view of project participants, while the economic analysis considers the profitability of
invesments for the entire project from the perspective of society.
141. At the economic level, one important project benefit will be the project mitigation impact. As mentioned above,
the project is expected to lead to a reduction in emissions of 137,516 t CO2e per year on average over a 20-year period.
This reduction in GHG emissions was converted into an economic value using two price ranges (low and high ranges
of social carbon prices as adopted by the World Bank) and considered in the Economic Analysis.
142. The results of the financial analysis shows that the proposed investments are financially viable for project
beneficiaries, as all financial models have positive Net Present Values (NPV) and Internal Rate of Returns (IRRs) above
the financial discount rate of 14.2%. These results mean that EbA solutions have proven to be cost-efficient, which is
a key incentive for the long-term adoption and sustainability of these climate-resilient practices and technologies by the
farmers.
143. The Economic Analysis further shows that the project as a whole also has a positive return on investment, with
an NPV of 68.5 MUSD and an Economic Internal Rate of Return (EIRR) of 32.8%, above the economic discount rate
of 10%. These results are those of the baseline scenario, defined as the scenario that includes the value of avoided

GHG emissions using the low social carbon price. Using the high social price of carbon, the project EIRR increases to
54.6%. Without the value of avoided GHG emissions, the project has a much lower, albeit still positive, EIRR of 12.7%.
144. The sensitivity analysis further shows that the project remains economically viable in different scenarios,
including a decrease in benefits of 20% and an increase in costs of 20%. The cost per beneficiary (197 USD/person)
is comparable to/consistent with recent GCF funding proposals.
145. These ex-ante results are confirmed by other analysis in the country. For example, landscape restoration
investments under the World Bank-funded MWASIP project show an EIRR of 15.6%238 (without of the value of avoided
GHG emissions). Enhanced watershed management through improved crop management, tree planting and soil and
water conservation measures in the upper catchments foreseen by the GEF-funded ERAS Project are estimated (at
design) to have an EIRR of 27.5%239. Similarly, catchment management interventions conducted within the SRBMP
project are found (at completion) to generate an EIRR of 25.9%240 (without of the value of avoided GHG emissions).
The cost-benefit analysis conducted within the Malawi NFLRA shows that agriculture-based restoration interventions
(e.g., conservation agriculture, agroforestry, farmer managed natural regeneration), and forestry-based activities such
as community plantations and private woodlots generate positive NPVs 241. Ignaciuk et al. (2021) find that the IRR of
adopting maize-legume intercropping in the southern Malawian districts of Blantyre, Neno, Phalombe, and Zomba is
about 19% as opposed to 15% of maize monocropping (which is the traditional way of growing maize in Malawi)242.
Mutenje et al. (2019), using a sample of 1,440 households in both mid-altitude plateau and lakeshore plains AEZs show
that growing maize adopting conservation agriculture, drought tolerant varieties, intercropping/rotating with legumes
generate positive economic benefits in terms of NPV and IRR243.
The economic and financial analysis (EFA) is presented in more detail in Annex 3.

E.7. Monitoring, reporting and evaluation arrangements (max. 500 words, approximately 1 page)
146. In its role as Accredited Entity (AE), FAO will oversee project implementation according to the Accreditation Master Agreement (AMA) signed between FAO
and GCF and will bear overall responsibility for ensuring that reporting is provided to the GCF in a timely manner and in accordance with the required standards.
The M&E unit will use the data from the MIS to prepare the draft performance reports, which will in turn be sent to the PSC/PTC. As per the GCF Monitoring and
Accountability Framework, FAO will provide the GCF with: Inception Report, Annual Performance Reports, independent Mid-term Evaluation report, Project Closure
Report, and an independent Final Evaluation report. FAO will also provide semi-annual and annual Financial Reports throughout project implementation. The
monitoring team will also share its findings with the CPIU so that they may discuss implementation issues as they arise.
147. Project monitoring will be conducted by the M&E unit composed by: a National M&E specialist with GIS skills, and two M&E Associates (in the regional
hubs). The unit will be complemented by the M&E unit of the MoF/FARMSE Programme. FAO will ensure the existence of a well-designed, operational, and effective
impact monitoring and measurement system (MIS). Project oversight will be carried out by the Project Technical and Steering Committees (PTC and PSC), the
Central Project Implementation Unit (CPIU) and relevant Technical Units in FAO HQ. The project will be implemented based on the annual workplan and budget
(AWPB) which will be adjusted as envisaged by the CPIU, subject to the Budget Holder (BH) approval (FAO AE). Project components will be monitored separately
as well as in relation to the achievement of higher level project results and overall GCF goals. Monitoring data will be stored, compiled and displayed in a dedicated
module of the Monitoring Information System (MIS) to be developed by the CPIU. The MIS will serve to track on the project implementation, including the outputs,
outcomes and targets in the results framework. It will also track implementation of the project’s Gender Action Plan and Environmental and Social Management
Plans.

RISK ASSESSMENT AND MANAGEMENT
F.1. Risk factors and mitigations measures (max. 3 pages)
Selected Risk Factor 1: Political (collaboration between Government stakeholders)
Category Probability Impact
Technical and operational Medium Medium
Description
Limited collaboration between stakeholders from different ministries (e.g. Ministry of Agriculture - MoA, Ministry of
Climate Change and Natural Resources – MoCCNR) and departments (Department of Land Resources Conservation
in MoA, Department of Forestry in MoCCNR) on land restoration activities. This low collaboration may negatively affect
project implementation, resulting in limited information and knowledge-sharing on climate-resilience practices and
technologies, and ultimately impair the overall long-term project impact.
Mitigation Measure(s)
All actors (MoA, MoCCNR) will be engaged in the Project Steering Committee (PSC) and Project Technical Committee
(PTC) to ensure that government organisations work hand-in hand. At local (district) level, all activities will be
coordinated under the District Executive Committees (DEC), District Environment Sub-Committee (DESC) to ensure
collaboration between all government stakeholders. These actions will lower the probability of risk to low.
Selected Risk Factor 2: Political (changes in the development priorities of the Government of Malawi)
Category Probability Impact
Governance Medium MediumSelect
Description
Low enforcement of development priorities, strategies and international commitments preventing from fully engaging in
ecosystem based adaptation – EbA. Turnover and changes in decision makers and institutional arrangements beyond
the control of the project lead to a volatile environment that hampers the long-term success of the work.
Mitigation Measure(s)
Project priorities are well aligned with the international commitment of the GoM and with the most recent national
strategies, policies and legislation. As mentioned in section B.1, the Government of Malawi has enabling/ favorable
policy instruments (such as the Nationally Determined Contribution – NDC 2021, the National Forest Landscape
Restoration Strategy – NFLRS 2017) that promote ecosystem-based adaptation. The project’s implementation
arrangements have foreseen that the highest level of project governance – the Project Steering Committee (PSC) –
will include multi-sectorial high-level representatives (at least at Permanent Secretary level) and will debate together
with the NDA about any changes in government policy and any changes in the project governance that might have an
impact on the project, its activities and its implementation modalities. The FAO Representative in Malawi, which has
been operating in Malawi since 1986 without discontinuity under any changes in the government, will remain in constant
dialogue with the Government counterparts to anticipate potential changes in policies and strategic directions and to
propose the necessary measures. AE will inform the GCF in case of any major changes in the government policies and
strategic directions that may have adverse impacts to the project. In addition, the project will invest in evidenced-based
policy dialogue (sub-component 3.2) which will sensitizing the importance of ecosystem-based adaptation not only for
the direct project counterparts but also at the national level. The Project will make strong business case for EbA-
investment for climate change resilience and demonstrate how this supports national policies and GoM’s international
commitments. These actions will lower the probability of risk to low.

Other Medium Medium

Exogenous risks include: (i) climate risks: more extreme weather events impacting negatively all landscape
restoration efforts; (ii) COVID-19 and other sanitary crisis disturb implementation. These risks would translate into
