operational disruptions and discontinuation of activities’ implementation (if COVID related), and would threaten EbA
investments, livelihoods and producers’ resilience (if climate related).
Mitigation Measure(s)
The project seeks to restore and enhance the services provided by watershed ecosystem that support sustainable and
resilient livelihoods. EbAM will support investments in ecosystem restoration, ecosystem-based adaptation that include
diversified, locally adapted, non-invasive, and drought-resistant crop species and varieties that climate change
scenarios consider the best climate-adapted to Malawi. Additional tree enhancement in farmland through agroforestry
and farmer-managed natural regeneration, combined with production diversification will strengthen producers’
resilience. During the course of the formulation of EbA-based Village Level Action Plans (VLAPs) under output 1.1,
areas that are high risk (such as inundation zones) will be identified and VLAPs may also identify areas where physical
interventions, e.g. terraces or bunds are required to reduce erosion / water flows. Activity 2.3.2 will support the
development and delivery of innovative climate adaptation financial services (which may include agriculture insurance
to communities).
Risks mitigation strategies against the COVID-19 pandemic will include (i) adjusting stakeholders’ engagement plans,
adopt higher flexibility and adaptive management and use remote communication whenever possible, (ii) maintaining
social distancing, (iii) reviewing and adjusting implementation and stakeholder engagement arrangements to
compensate staff shortages.
These actions will lower the impact of risk to medium.
Selected Risk Factor 4 : other (Maladaptation behaviours)
Category Probability Impact
Other Low High
Description
Communities resort to short term and maladaptive practices and discontinue adopting EbA.
Mitigation Measure(s)
Communities’ buy-in will be maximized by (i) the participatory nature (including women and youth) of the development
of VLAPs and SCMPs, (ii) the participatory selection of EbA priority interventions, (iii) accompanying capacity
development actions, (iv) access to inputs (seeds, seedlings, equipment) and (v) access to finance. In addition, the
project design recognizes at the outset that capacity development is a long-term endeavour requiring continuous
support. Therefore, the project will place a strong focus on community learning and participatory planning (sub-
component 1.1), gender-inclusive extension, coaching and practical trainings (sub-component 2.1) to promote and
adopt EbA. It will ensure capacity development, knowledge generation and learning at local level through FFS and
innovation & learning centres (e.g. LUANAR AgroEcology Hub, Kusumala Institute). FFS will be conducted through
well qualified master trainers and facilitators, with the support of experts from public and private organizations. It will
use media and community mobilization tools (Dimitra Clubs, radios), as well as digital apps for extension, to disseminate
information on the benefits of EbA. This will help consolidate the long term adoption of practices. These actions will
lower the final level of risk to low.

persons living with HIV/AIDS. The project will rely on participative community approach, the Dimitra Clubs; and on
gender-transformative approach, the Household Methodology that promote the participation of all community and

Selected Risk Factor 6: Money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism (ML/TF)
Category Probability Impact
Governance Low Low
Description
Risks of money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism.
Mitigation Measure(s)
FAO includes in the project agreement signed between FAO and the Government of Malawi clauses related to
AML/CFT, as follows:
a) The Government shall comply, and shall require all persons and entities engaged in its activities under the Project
to comply, with all internal anti-money laundering, counter-terrorism financing laws, rules, and regulations;
b) The Government confirms it has obtained sufficient undertakings from all persons and entities involved in its activities
under the Project that they shall not engage in any prohibited practices; the Government undertakes and confirm that
it shall comply with the substantive objectives of the GCF’s Policy on Prohibited Practices;
c) Consistent with numerous United Nations Security Council resolutions adopted under Chapter VII of the UN Charter,
the Government and FAO are firmly committed to the international fight against terrorism and, in particular, against the
financing of terrorism. It is the policy of the Government and FAO to seek to ensure that none of their funds are used,
directly or indirectly, to provide support to individuals or entities: i) associated with terrorism, as included in the list
maintained by the Security Council Committee established pursuant to its Resolutions 1267 (1999) and 1989 (2011);
or ii) that are the subject of sanctions or other enforcement measures promulgated by the United Nations Security
Council. This provision must be included in all agreements that may be concluded with third parties for the
implementation of activities under the Project.
During project implementation FAO, as AE, will ensure close monitoring and supervision through its offices in the
regional office and HQ in order to ensure that the activities are implemented in full compliance with the signed project
agreement.

GCF POLICIES AND STANDARDS
G.1. Environmental and social risk assessment (max. 750 words, approximately 1.5 pages)
150. During project formulation, an environmental and social management framework was developed – see the
Environmental and Social Management Framework (ESMF) in Annex 6. An initial risk assessment was carried out
against FAO’s Environmental and Social Safeguards (http://www.fao.org/3/a-i4413e.pdf). All project activities considered
gender, social, and environmental aspects, and identified priority design elements to proactively address these. A
stakeholder engagement process was carried out to identify and engage with all stakeholders of the project, from national
to local authorities, relevant technical institutions, to NGOs and CSOs, among others, as outlined in Annex 7. As per the
Environmental and Social Management Guidelines of FAO, EbAM has been screened to establish its overall
environmental and social risk categorization. The ESMF (Annex 6) identifies the project as Category B (Moderate Risk),
based on the fact the project contains activities with potentially limited adverse environmental and/or social risks and
impacts that individually or cumulatively, are few, generally site-specific, largely reversible, and readily addressed
through mitigation measures.
151. Overall, the project is expected to bring about major positive impacts, thanks to the socially inclusive participatory
process, with a strong focus on women, youth and vulnerable groups; and the major environmental co-benefits resulting
from Ecosystem-based Adaptation (enhanced biodiversity, soil and water conservation, land restoration, etc.), which will
be promoted at farm and watershed level. Even with these expected positive impacts, the project has been classified as
Moderate Risk, due to the fact that: (i) farm-level activities may access genetic resources, and/or access traditional
knowledge associated with genetic resources that is held by local communities and/or farmers; (ii) crops may be
introduced that were not previously grown; (iii) seeds will be provided for cultivation; (iv) there may be establishment or
management of forests; (v) the project will operate in sectors or value chains that are dominated by subsistence
producers and other vulnerable informal agricultural workers, and are more generally characterized by high levels
“working poverty”; (vi) the project will operate in situations where youth work mostly as unpaid contributing family workers;
and, (vii) the project will operate in situations where major gender inequality in the labour market prevails (e.g. where
women tend to work predominantly as unpaid contributing family members or subsistence farmers, have lower skills and
qualifications, lower productivity and wages, less representation and voice in producers’ and workers’ organizations,
more precarious contracts and higher informality rates). These elements correspond to FAO Environmental and Social
Standard (ESS) 2 Biodiversity, Ecosystems, and Natural Habitats, ESS3 Plant Genetic Resources for Food and
Agriculture, ESS7 Decent Work, and ESS9 – Indigenous Peoples and Cultural Heritage (see screening Table G.1.1
below).

G.1. Environmental and social risk assessment (max. 750 words, approximately 1.5 pages)
150. During project formulation, an environmental and social management framework was developed – see the
Environmental and Social Management Framework (ESMF) in Annex 6. An initial risk assessment was carried out
against FAO’s Environmental and Social Safeguards (http://www.fao.org/3/a-i4413e.pdf). All project activities considered
gender, social, and environmental aspects, and identified priority design elements to proactively address these. A
stakeholder engagement process was carried out to identify and engage with all stakeholders of the project, from national
to local authorities, relevant technical institutions, to NGOs and CSOs, among others, as outlined in Annex 7. As per the
Environmental and Social Management Guidelines of FAO, EbAM has been screened to establish its overall
environmental and social risk categorization. The ESMF (Annex 6) identifies the project as Category B (Moderate Risk),
based on the fact the project contains activities with potentially limited adverse environmental and/or social risks and
impacts that individually or cumulatively, are few, generally site-specific, largely reversible, and readily addressed
through mitigation measures.

To manage adverse risk associated with the handling and supply of seeds for
cultivation, the project will: (i) Avoid undermining local seed & planting material
production and supply systems; (ii) Ensure that the seeds and planting materials are
from locally/regionally adapted crops and varieties that are accepted by farmers and

(PGFRA), and over associated traditional knowledge are respected, along with the

ESS8 – Gender Equality YES Standard 8 is triggered by the EbAM project since the project may face either
passive or active opposition to women's involvement and efforts to enhance women's
empowerment within the communities.

approaches.

groups such as female-headed households, female youth, girls, and persons living

as the Household Methodology will promote gender equality through open discussions
on gender and social inclusion related issues, including gender-based violence (GBV)
and Sexual exploitation, abuse and harassment (SEAH). Training for religious,
traditional, and community leaders, project team and facilitators will enhance their
capacity to mobilize communities and promote gender equality. The project will
promote Gender equality and women empowerment (GEWE) and will monitor the
progress using the Gender Action Plan (GAP) to ensure alignment with project
objectives.

156. In addition, there will be zero tolerance of sexual exploitation, abuse, and harassment (SEAH), and the
project’s ESMF, consequent ESMP as well as implementation safeguards documents will mainstream SEAH risk
mitigation, in accordance with the FAO ESMG. The project will support gender sensitization and trainings for project staff

linkages to related services and redress for anyone affected by SEAH.
Grievance and Redress Mechanism (GRM):The grievance redress mechanism (GRM) is an integral project
management element that intends to seek feedback from beneficiaries and resolve complaints on project activities and
1p5e7rf.ormance. The mechanism is based on FAO require ments and most importantly, it is based on existing, community-
specific grievance redress mechanisms preferred by the local beneficiaries. FAO and EEs will inform communities about
the GRM through culturally appropriate mechanisms, ensuring information on mechanisms at all four levels is
communicated (i.e. community-based, project-level GRM, FAO-level GRM, and GCF’s Independent Redress
Mechanism). The CPIU and Regional Project Offices will be responsible for managing the grievance and redress
mechanism. The GRM has a strong link with FAO Malawi’s competent officers to ensure the right application of GRM
principles. Project-related SEAH and GBV grievances will be managed through the existing FAO GRM system, which
will also be strengthened to include a procedure for handling SEAH that is inclusive, survivor-centred and gender-
responsive, complemented by GBV referral pathways. The pathways will be established and operationalized under the
project in collaboration with UNFPA, including medical care, psychosocial support, legal and social/reintegration support
(see Section 9 of the ESMF in Annex 6 for more detailed information).
G.2. Gender assessment and action plan (max. 500 words, approximately 1 page) – See Annex 8 for details
158. Gender Analysis. An analysis of the gender-related aspects of the project was also undertaken during the
development of the ESMF and Gender Action Plan (GAP) (Annex 8). Although the Government of Malawi ratified most
of International and regional instruments and developed several national laws that promotes human and women’s rights,
gender inequalities persist. These inequalities are due to entrenched social norms including the co-existing of patriarchal
and matriarchal structures, that allocate to women and men specific roles, expectations and property rights. Women are
assigned the heavy burden of domestic tasks, remain disadvantaged regarding productive and paid work and are
sidelined in decision-making process. They must also bear the consequences of HIV/AIDS’ high prevalence as well as
harmful social practices such as gender-based violence and child marriage. Regarding income generating activities and
economic opportunities, men dominate activities and sectors of high productivity and profit margin; and even if women
comprise about 70 percent of the agricultural labor force, they face unequal use of land inputs, lower access to farm
labor, inferior access to improved agricultural inputs and technology, manifest difficulties to access markets and finance
their activities. As for climate change adaptation capacity, women, men and youth have limited knowledge and weak
capacity to consider catchment and landscape management into integrated planning process.
159. The EbAM gender strategy and action plan aims at reducing inequalities and removing the above-identified
barriers; mainstreaming social inclusion and sensitivity toward vulnerable groups; ensuring effective participation of
women, men, youth in the development process; in order to promote gender and youth transformation in the longer term.
The project’s interventions will focus on (i) instilling mindset change by enhancing the social acceptance of gender and
youth empowerment, (ii) promoting equitable and inclusive sharing of decision-making power at household and
community levels, (iii) building the capacity of women and youth for their meaningful participation in domestic and public
life, and (iv) economically empowering the vulnerable particularly women and youth.
160. For these purposes, EbAM will rely on the use of the Dimitra Clubs and Household methodology (also refered
as “household approach” - HHA), two methodologies that have a strong replication potential in terms of community
engagement, social inclusion, collective action, gender equality and equitable sharing of decision-making power both at
household and community levels. Under component 1, the Dimitra Clubs will be used as entry points for community
mobilization and engagement in the planning and implementation of ILM. Women and youth’s capacity will be
strengthened to increase their technical and social participation in ILM. The HHA will promote participatory dialogues
that will allow women, men and youth household members understand and challenge gender norms, while at the same
time developing a common vision and planning for household activities. Dialogues at community and household levels
will put a particular focus on GBV and SEAH. Under component 2, the project will strengthen women, men and youth’s
capacity in the adoption of EbA-solutions. Those showing the potential to move towards commercial group activities
(MSMEs) will be supported to strengthen their marketing skills and access markets. EbAM will also support women and
youth’s access to finance through CBFOs/VSLAs and the development and delivery of adapted financial services by
FFIs. Under component 3, NCCF and national conservation trust funds will be supported in developing their gender
strategy and action plan, the project will support them to consider gender principles in their interventions and to promote

specific grievance redress mechanisms preferred by the local beneficiaries. FAO and EEs will inform communities about
the GRM through culturally appropriate mechanisms, ensuring information on mechanisms at all four levels is
communicated (i.e. community-based, project-level GRM, FAO-level GRM, and GCF’s Independent Redress
Mechanism). The CPIU and Regional Project Offices will be responsible for managing the grievance and redress
mechanism. The GRM has a strong link with FAO Malawi’s competent officers to ensure the right application of GRM
principles. Project-related SEAH and GBV grievances will be managed through the existing FAO GRM system, which
will also be strengthened to include a procedure for handling SEAH that is inclusive, survivor-centred and gender-
responsive, complemented by GBV referral pathways. The pathways will be established and operationalized under the
project in collaboration with UNFPA, including medical care, psychosocial support, legal and social/reintegration support
(see Section 9 of the ESMF in Annex 6 for more detailed information).
G.2. Gender assessment and action plan (max. 500 words, approximately 1 page) – See Annex 8 for details
158. Gender Analysis. An analysis of the gender-related aspects of the project was also undertaken during the
development of the ESMF and Gender Action Plan (GAP) (Annex 8). Although the Government of Malawi ratified most
of International and regional instruments and developed several national laws that promotes human and women’s rights,
gender inequalities persist. These inequalities are due to entrenched social norms including the co-existing of patriarchal
and matriarchal structures, that allocate to women and men specific roles, expectations and property rights. Women are
assigned the heavy burden of domestic tasks, remain disadvantaged regarding productive and paid work and are
sidelined in decision-making process. They must also bear the consequences of HIV/AIDS’ high prevalence as well as
harmful social practices such as gender-based violence and child marriage. Regarding income generating activities and
economic opportunities, men dominate activities and sectors of high productivity and profit margin; and even if women
comprise about 70 percent of the agricultural labor force, they face unequal use of land inputs, lower access to farm
labor, inferior access to improved agricultural inputs and technology, manifest difficulties to access markets and finance
their activities. As for climate change adaptation capacity, women, men and youth have limited knowledge and weak
capacity to consider catchment and landscape management into integrated planning process.
159. The EbAM gender strategy and action plan aims at reducing inequalities and removing the above-identified
barriers; mainstreaming social inclusion and sensitivity toward vulnerable groups; ensuring effective participation of
women, men, youth in the development process; in order to promote gender and youth transformation in the longer term.
The project’s interventions will focus on (i) instilling mindset change by enhancing the social acceptance of gender and
youth empowerment, (ii) promoting equitable and inclusive sharing of decision-making power at household and
community levels, (iii) building the capacity of women and youth for their meaningful participation in domestic and public
life, and (iv) economically empowering the vulnerable particularly women and youth.
160. For these purposes, EbAM will rely on the use of the Dimitra Clubs and Household methodology (also refered
as “household approach” - HHA), two methodologies that have a strong replication potential in terms of community
engagement, social inclusion, collective action, gender equality and equitable sharing of decision-making power both at
household and community levels. Under component 1, the Dimitra Clubs will be used as entry points for community
mobilization and engagement in the planning and implementation of ILM. Women and youth’s capacity will be
strengthened to increase their technical and social participation in ILM. The HHA will promote participatory dialogues
that will allow women, men and youth household members understand and challenge gender norms, while at the same
time developing a common vision and planning for household activities. Dialogues at community and household levels
will put a particular focus on GBV and SEAH. Under component 2, the project will strengthen women, men and youth’s
capacity in the adoption of EbA-solutions. Those showing the potential to move towards commercial group activities
(MSMEs) will be supported to strengthen their marketing skills and access markets. EbAM will also support women and
youth’s access to finance through CBFOs/VSLAs and the development and delivery of adapted financial services by
FFIs. Under component 3, NCCF and national conservation trust funds will be supported in developing their gender
strategy and action plan, the project will support them to consider gender principles in their interventions and to promote

women’s participation in various capacity strengthening. Women’s and youth’s participation in policy dialogue will also
be promoted.
161. Coordination of the implementation of the Gender Action Plan will be the responsibility of the PIU Gender and
Social Inclusion Specialist. The Specialist must ensure that project planning, implementation, monitoring and evaluation
and reporting are gender sensitive and socially inclusive. The project logical framework and monitoring and evaluation
system should include measurable indicators related to women and youth that allow assessing the sensitivity of project’s
component and sub-component to these groups. Data collection during project implementation will be gender and age
disaggregated. The various technical and progress reports should also consider gender-disaggregated information and
analysis.
G.3. Financial management and procurement (max. 500 words, approximately 1 page)
162. Financial management and control and procurement processes will be implemented as per FAO rules and
regulations, which were certified as acceptable to the GCF in the FAO accreditation process. FAO has an Administrative
Manual organized across various Chapters covering Finance, Human Resources, Travel and Procurement. The FAO
Intranet provides access to this Manual and to other procedures, information and guidance via the “FAO Handbook”.
163. FAO has deployed an Oracle based ERP system the Global Resources Management System" (GRMS) to its
world-wide offices, which provides all FAO employees, in all locations globally, with travel, human resource, procurement
and finance functionalities. Using GRMS improves the flow of financial information, supports financial monitoring and
reporting, increases transparency and visibility, and strengthens internal control. FAO maintains a chart of accounts
which is used by the whole organization and that allows for a separation of income and expenditure by donor and project
and supports and provides a standardized coding structure that enables data to be recorded, classified and summarized
to facilitate internal management and external reporting requirements.Procurement and Letters of Agreement Services
are managed by a dedicated FAO unit, which provides policy and operational support to ensure that the Organization
procures goods, works and services based on "Best Value for Money" principles as embodied in the Manual Section 502
and for Letters of Agreement under Manual Section 507.
164. As mentioned in Section C.4. FAO as the Accredited Entity of the GCF will have overall responsibility for quality
assurance and oversight of co-executing entities, and shall assume fiduciary responsibility in accordance with FAO
standards and procedures. In addition to this, FAO will be responsible for the financial execution of GCF funds according
to FAO rules and regulations mainly contained and detailed in the FAO Handbook (including those referred to financial
monitoring, audit and procurement).
165. During implementation, FAO will provide oversight and quality assurance in accordance with its policies and
procedures. This may include monitoring missions, spot checks and participation at project governance meetings. The
project will be audited internally and externally following FAO’s Financial Regulations.
166. FAO Country Representative in Malawi (FAOR) is responsible for financial monitoring and is supported by a
management team comprised of a Program Assistant, Management Assistant, and a Strategic Operations Officer. Such
team will interact and support the work of the PIU.

198 MoA – more particularly the Department of Land Resources Conservation (DLCRC) - originated the Project idea. MoA is strongly engaged

technical activities at local level with the districts and with all the actors of the decentralized local government system i.e. District Executive

199 NLGFC is constitutional body with the mandate to facilitate fiscal decentralization, financial management and local development in local
governments. Similar to the GEF-7 funded Sustainable Forest Management, Dryland Sustainable Landscape Impact Programme - SFM DSL
IP, NLGFC will provide the procurement services to the EbAM project (based on the AWPB prepared by MoA), being in charge of investigating
sources of supply, obtaining price quotations, negotiating with suppliers on price and delivery and monitoring the transfer of procured inputs
to the project beneficiaries (VLAPs). This will facilitate accessibility for innovative technologies for the restoration, sustainable management,
production and manufacturing of agriculture and forest products. Through this partnership, the Project will support implementation of the
Decentralization Act (1998), which devolves powers and funding from the central government to districts, hence ensure project sustainability,
and support a paradigm shift towards an increased ownership by districts.
200 MoF/FARMSE’s development objective is to increase access to, and use of, a range of sustainable financial services by rural households
and micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) (see Feasibility Study, section 4 for more details). It has a national coverage and has a
strong comparative advantage to support EbAM in enhancing the financial inclusion of smallholder farmers.

2.

II. Summary of the Secretariat’s assessment
2 .1 Project background
3.
The objective of “Ecosystems-based Adaptation for resilient Watersheds and
Communities in Malawi (EbAM)” is to enhance the climate-change resilience of rural
communities in Malawi through a comprehensive approach that integrates EbA with ILM.
1
Targeting 11 vulnerable districts across Malawi, the project aims to mitigate the negative
impacts of climate change, including increased temperatures, erratic rainfall, and the frequency
of climate-induced disasters such as droughts and floods. The EbAM project is strategically
designed to restore and sustainably manage watershed ecosystems to support agriculture and
improve livelihoods, with a significant emphasis on involving vulnerable groups such as women
and youth in the process and using local knowledge for forest management. These districts have
been selected due to their significant exposure to climate change impacts, including extreme soil
loss and degradation, erratic rainfall, increased temperatures, and frequent climate-induced
d isasters like droughts and floods.
4.
The EbAM project is structured around three interconnected components. The first
component focuses on reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and enhancing the climate
resilience of watershed ecosystems by restoring ecosystem functions at a large enough scale to
facilitate broad adaptation and mitigation efforts. This involves the application of the EbA
approach, which uses biodiversity and ecosystem services to help communities adapt to climate
change. The second component aims to stabilize productivity and farmers’ incomes by making
livelihoods and food systems more resilient to climate variability. This will be achieved through
promoting climate-resilient agricultural practices, improving access to markets, and facilitating
financial inclusion for farmers. The third component seeks to strengthen the enabling
environment for climate resilience by enhancing policy frameworks and mobilizing innovative
fi nance solutions to support the sustainable scaling up of the project’s interventions.
5.
Overall, the EbAM project embodies a paradigm shift towards sustainable ecosystem
management and climate-resilient agricultural practices in Malawi. By integrating EbA within
local planning processes, fostering public–private–producer partnerships (4P), and leveraging
innovative financing mechanisms, the project aspires to contribute to a more sustainable
pathway for resilient ecosystems, livelihoods, and agriculture across the country. This shift is
expected to reduce Malawi’s high vulnerability to climate change, improve food security, and
contribute to sustainable development goals, ensuring a lasting impact on the country’s rural
co mmunities.
6.
The project’s exit strategy is crucial for sustaining the project’s impacts beyond its
lifetime. It emphasizes local planning (e.g. EbA-based Catchment Management Plans (CMPs) and
Village Level Action Plans (VLAPs)), institutional strengthening, community engagement (i.e.
with the Catchment Management Committees (CMCs) and Village Natural Resources
Management Committees (VNRMCs)), policy advocacy, financial sustainability, knowledge-
sharing (including digital services), and robust monitoring.
1
The 11 vulnerable districts targeted by the EbAM project were chosen due to their high climate vulnerability. These
districts are Dedza (located in the Central region of Malawi); Zomba, Mangochi, Thyolo, Neno, Mwanza, Nsanje (all
located in the Southern region of Malawi); and Nkhata Bay, Rumphi, Karonga, and Chitipa (all located in the
Northern region of Malawi).

=== PAGE 110 ===
GCF/B.39/02/Add.13
Page 110
7.
This strategy ensures that project initiatives are deeply integrated into local and
national frameworks, empowering communities and institutions to continue practices and
support essential services and extension support that bolster climate resilience. Through
innovative financing mechanisms and private-sector engagement, the strategy aims to mobilize
additional resources for expanding these practices to other regions, embedding ecosystem-
ba sed adaptation into the fabric of Malawi’s development and climate-resilience efforts.
8.
The proposal outlines a total budget of USD 53.22 million, including a USD 42.81 million
grant requested from GCF. Co-financing totalling USD 10.42 million will be provided by the
country’s Ministry of Finance and Economic Affairs (MoF) and the Ministry of Agriculture
(M oA), and the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO).
9.
The budget allocation across the project components is detailed as follows:
(a)
USD 24.60 million is dedicated to component 1, aimed at integrated landscape
management to increase the climate resilience of watershed ecosystems and reduce
greenhouse gas emissions.
(b)
USD 22.50 million is allocated to component 2, focusing on stabilizing productivity and
farmers’ incomes through more resilient livelihoods and food systems.
(c)
USD 1.18 million is designated for component 3, which seeks to enhance the enabling
environment for sustaining, replicating, and scaling up climate-resilient watershed
ecosystems and agricultural practices.
(d)
Additional allocations include USD 2.32 million for monitoring and evaluation (M&E)
activities and USD 2.62 million for project management.
10.
The project’s risk assessment identifies political factors such as collaboration challenges
between government stakeholders and changes in the government’s development priorities as
significant risks, categorized as having medium probability and impact. Specific concerns
include limited cooperation between partners i.e. different ministries and departments, which
could hinder effective implementation and knowledge-sharing about climate-resilient practices.
To mitigate these, the project involves key governmental actors in committees to ensure
cohesive work across agencies. Another political risk arises from potential shifts in government
focus, which may affect commitment to ecosystem-based adaptation strategies. This is mitigated
by the strong alignment with Malawi’s current complementary policies. High-level government
officials are also included in decision-making processes to address policy changes proactively.
Additional exogenous risks like extreme weather events and health crises like the coronavirus
disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic are also noted, with plans to enhance ecosystem services
that support resilient livelihoods and adjust project management practices to ensure continuity
despite these challenges.

engagement. The project prioritizes the development of technical capacities in watershed
management committees and local communities, emphasizing the inclusion of women, youth,
and vulnerable groups. Through active and inclusive stakeholder engagement at various levels,

15.
Moreover, component 2 emphasizes sustainability by promoting practices such as EbA
via the Farmer’s Field Schools. By integrating diverse and locally adapted crops into farming

viability of agricultural production with a wide view lens of the Food system approach. The
component also focuses on facilitating market access and entrepreneurship development for
farmers through a public-private producers partnerships (4Ps) approach. By establishing
partnerships and creating market branding initiatives, it opens opportunities and best practices

also contributes to the overall resilience of local food systems and the development of micro,

based financial organizations and providing tailored financial services to farmers. Farmers are
enabled to invest in climate-resilient agricultural practices and improve their overall economic
stability. The replicability of the approach is a significant strength. By designing interventions
that can be scaled up and adapted to different contexts, component 2 offers potential for
widespread impact beyond its immediate target areas especially with the investment pipeline
for National Climate Change Fund. This scalability enhances the sustainability and long-term
eff ectiveness of the component’s initiatives.
17.

livelihoods and food systems, leveraging innovation, sustainability, market access, and financial

III. Assessment against investment criteria
Scale: High
3. 1 Impact potential
24.
The project is considered to have significant impact potential, aiming to transform the
vulnerability landscape of Malawi’s rural communities through comprehensive environmental
and social interventions. Through the application of ecosystem-based adaptation strategies, the
project aims to enhance agricultural yields, improve soil quality, and increase water retention,
the reby strengthening the region’s ability to withstand climatic challenges.
25.
Primarily an adaptation project, it aims to empower project beneficiaries to effectively
prepare for, respond to, and recover from climate-related extremes and disasters – focusing on
mitigating the cycle of low agricultural productivity and watershed degradation exacerbated by
cli mate change.
26.
With a strategic focus on ecosystem-based adaptation and integrated landscape
management, the project is poised to directly benefit 270,820 people, target approximately 30
sub-catchments (for a total of about 267,500 hectares) over six years, and generate mitigation
benefits of –2,750,323 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent.

=== PAGE 113 ===
GCF/B.39/02/Add.13
Page 113
Scale: High
3. 2 Paradigm shift potential
27.
The project aims to catalyse a significant shift towards sustainability in ecosystems,
livelihoods, and agriculture across Malawi, which currently face high vulnerability to climate
change impacts. It seeks to transition from the current state of vulnerability to one where
ecosystems are conserved, restored, and managed sustainably, providing adaptation to climate
ch ange, and supporting resilient farming systems and communities.
28.
As noted above in the project’s description, to achieve this, the project will promote a
locally led approach called ecosystem-based adaptation (EbA) combined with integrated
landscape management (ILM). EbA focuses on restoring and strengthening ecosystems to
maximize biodiversity and ecosystem services, making them more resilient to climate change.
ILM involves collaborative planning and management of landscapes to achieve multiple
objectives. These approaches will be integrated into watershed and village-level plans, engaging
ma rginalized groups, and incorporating local and traditional knowledge.
29.
The project will implement various EbA interventions such as ecosystem restoration
and sustainable agricultural practices, aiming to enhance ecological resilience and improve food
security. It will also enhance access to markets, business opportunities, and finance for farmers,
making their livelihoods more resilient. Additionally, the project aims to strengthen the
enabling environment for EbA, facilitating replication and scaling-up through other projects and
programmes. It will promote collective learning on EbA through training and participatory
pla nning processes involving stakeholders at various levels.
30.
Overall, the project seeks to create a sustainable and resilient future for Malawi by
integrating EbA into local plans, policies, and investment strategies, while ensuring meaningful
participation of stakeholders and knowledge-sharing at various levels.
Scale: High
3. 3 Sustainable development potential
31.
The project is strategically poised to contribute significantly to sustainable development
in Malawi, particularly aligning with Sustainable Development Goals 2 (Zero hunger), 6 (Clean
wa ter and sanitation), 13 (Climate action), and 15 (Life on land).
32.
By promoting ecosystem-based adaptation and integrated landscape management,
EbAM aims to enhance agricultural resilience, ensure water security, combat climate change
impacts, and preserve biodiversity. This comprehensive approach supports the creation of
resilient food systems, the restoration and sustainable use of terrestrial ecosystems, and the
strengthening of adaptive capacities to climate-related hazards. Through its commitment to
restoring degraded landscapes, improving agricultural productivity, and promoting sustainable
land management practices, the project’s approach is expected to lead to improved food
security, income stability, and enhanced adaptive capacity to climate change, contributing
significantly to the Sustainable Development Goals in Malawi.
Scale: High
3. 4 Needs of the recipient
33.
The project targets the acute needs of Malawi’s rural population and agrarian economy,
challenged by climate change, poverty, and food insecurity. Focusing on vulnerable
communities, the project aims to improve resilience through sustainable watershed
ma nagement, agricultural practices, and ecosystem restoration.
34.
It addresses soil erosion, erratic rainfall, and the increased frequency of floods and
droughts, which impact agricultural productivity. By empowering communities with sustainable
resource management skills, enhancing food and water security, and building institutional

=== PAGE 114 ===
GCF/B.39/02/Add.13
Page 114
capacities, EbAM seeks to foster long-term sustainability and resilience against climate change,
setting a replicable model for development in Malawi.
Scale: High
3. 5 Country ownership
35.
The project exemplifies strong country ownership, aligning closely with Malawi's
national strategies and policies on climate change, environmental conservation, and sustainable
development. This initiative is deeply integrated into the country’s broader efforts to combat
climate change impacts, as outlined in its nationally determined contributions and the Malawi
Growth and Development Strategy. By working in concert with local ministries, governmental
agencies, and community organizations, the project ensures that its objectives are in harmony
with national priorities and leverages local expertise and resources for implementation. This
approach not only enhances the project’s effectiveness and sustainability but also fosters a
sen se of national commitment and responsibility towards achieving its goals.
36.
Country ownership is further strengthened by actively involving local communities in
the planning and execution phases, ensuring that interventions are tailored to meet their
specific needs and conditions, thereby maximizing the project’s impact on enhancing resilience
and sustainable development in Malawi.
Scale: Medium to high
3. 6 Efficiency and effectiveness
37.
The project expects enhanced productivity on farms, value addition post-production,
market access improvements, significant greenhouse gas emission reductions, and the
bolstering of non-timber forest products, among other ecosystem benefits. Financial analyses
reveal positive net present values and internal rates of return for beneficiaries, highlighting the
cost-efficiency of EbA solutions. Economically, the project demonstrates a high return on
investment with a net present value of USD 68.5 million and an economic internal rate of return
of 32.8 per cent, significantly above the economic discount rate, indicating substantial societal
be nefits.
38.
The inclusion of avoided GHG emissions further enhances the project’s economic appeal,
with economic internal rate of return potentially increasing under higher social carbon pricing
scenarios. Sensitivity analyses confirm the project’s resilience to cost and benefit fluctuations,
underscoring its economic viability and alignment with global climate financing goals. This
comprehensive approach, underscored by supportive financial metrics and broader societal
benefits, illustrates the project’s potential to deliver sustainable, climate-resilient development
in Malawi.

S

u al exploitation, abuse and harassment (SEAH).
60.
The revised GCF Environmental
and Social Policy adopted by decision B.BM-2021/18 requires safeguarding from SEAH in GCF-
financed activities. The accredited entity (AE) provided SEAH safeguarding in its submission for
this funding proposal. The project identifies SEAH as a significant risk. As a mitigative measure,
the AE outlines programme interventions to reduce SEAH-related risks, including the Dimitra
Clubs and the Household Methodology. The proposed interventions will facilitate open
discussions on gender-based violence (GBV) and SEAH in more particular within households
and in the community. Other steps include interventions to improve environmental and social
outcomes by reducing inequalities and eliminating gender-related barriers within the project
through mainstreaming social inclusion and sensitivity towards vulnerable groups. With regard
to a grievance redress mechanism (GRM) for SEAH, the AE will prioritize the needs of survivors
and incorporate a gender-responsive perspective, and facilitate access to relevant services and
redress mechanisms for those affected by SEAH. The AE will also implement a comprehensive
GRM that comprises four parallel systems: (i) a community-based system; (ii) a project-specific
formal system (project-level GRM); (iii) the approach of FAO to the GRM (FAO-level GRM); and
(iv) the GCF Independent Redress Mechanism. Project-related SEAH and GBV grievances will be
managed through the existing FAO GRM system, which will also be strengthened to include an
inclusive, survivor-centred, and gender-responsive procedure for handling SEAH. This will be
complemented by GBV referral pathways, established and operationalized under the project in
collaboration with the United Nations Population Fund. These pathways will provide medical
care, psychosocial support, legal assistance, and social/reintegration support. Risks and
effectiveness of mitigation measures will be reviewed and monitored by tracking activities,
assessing the project’s progress, and providing guidance and recommendations.
4. 2 Gender policy
61.
The AE provided a gender assessment and action plan with the funding proposal and
therefore, complies with the requirements of the updated GCF Gender Policy. The gender action
plan has been integrated in the project’s overall work plan to ensure that the gender
mainstreaming approach is effective and to reduce the risk of treating gender equality and
women’s empowerment as an add-on. The gender assessment and its accompanying gender
action plan build on primary data collected through community consultations. The main sectors
of the project – agriculture, food security/nutrition, Water, Sanitation and Hygiene for All and
policy are analysed through a gender lens. The project will take a more in-depth approach to the
gendered dimensions of food insecurity and nutrition and includes actions to address the root
causes of gender inequalities by engaging traditional and religious leaders. The risk of possible
resistance to addressing sensitive topics such as hegemonic masculinity and patriarchy is
recognized as a separate risk factor, and there is a clearer needs analysis which takes
intersectionality and differences into consideration. Lastly, the results framework is revised to
include indicators to measure qualitative changes related to gender equality and women’s role
in society.

4. 5 Results monitoring and reporting
75.
The funding proposal is based on a clear theory of change and logical framework, that
together could facilitate effective results monitoring and reporting. These tools, along with the
M&E plan that sets out the budget and data sources and data collection methods, are consistent
with the requirements of the Integrated Results Management Framework and the GCF
Ev aluation Policy.
76.
The theory of change illustrates how the combination of sustainable management of
landscapes and watershed ecosystems improved the capacity of farmers to implement climate-
resilient agriculture alongside improved access to markets, and policies that are conducive to
climate change adaptation and climate finance could lead to improved climate resilience for
rural communities and reduced GHG emissions. Critical assumptions that underlie this
relationship have been identified and include the uptake of integrated landscape management
by farmers, engagement of the financial and private sectors, enabling sociocultural factors for
women and youth, and recovery of the country from the COVID-19 pandemic. Hence, the
assumptions captured the broader economic and political environment and cultural dynamics.

=== PAGE 121 ===
GCF/B.39/02/Add.13
Page 121
In the Malawian context where markets are thin and in places even non-existent, the role of the
fin ancial and private sectors to achieve the desired climate outcomes would be important.
77.
The logical framework contains the main outcomes of interest such as GHG emissions
reduced (core indicator 1), direct and indirect beneficiaries reached (core indicator 2),
beneficiaries who adopted more climate-resilient livelihoods (supplementary indicator 2.1), and
natural resources restored and brought under improved management (core indicator 4 and
supplementary indicator 4.1). The means of verification have been improved to systematically
include both primary and secondary data collection as well as qualitative and quantitative data
sources. Some output-level indicators have been strengthened to demonstrate better the logical
progression between results levels. However, some indicators (e.g. training delivered), which
the AE decided to retain, are arguably activity-level indicators.
78.
The M&E budget includes provision for important roles such as specialist skills on the
Geographic Information System and additional M&E resources at the regional and national
levels. The budget allocated for the interim and final evaluations as well as the collection of
evaluative data complies with the requirements of the GCF Evaluation Policy and can
realistically support evaluative activities in Malawi.
4. 6 Legal assessment
79.
The Accreditation Master Agreement was signed with the Accredited Entity on 8 June
2018 (the “AMA”), and it became effective on 4 October 2018. The Accredited Entity’s five-year
accreditation term lapsed on 3 October 2023 but was extended by Decision B.37/18, paragraph
(q), until the earlier of three years from the date of lapse of the five-year accreditation term or
the date on which a revised accreditation framework is adopted by the Board. The Board
approved the re-accreditation of the Accredited Entity pursuant to Decision B.37/18, and
ne gotiation of the Amended and Restated Accreditation Master Agreement is ongoing.
80.
The Accredited Entity has provided a legal opinion/certificate confirming that it has
obtained all internal approvals, and that it has the capacity and authority to implement the
pr oject.
81.
The proposed project will be implemented in the Republic of Malawi in which GCF is not
provided with privileges and immunities. This means that, among other things, GCF is not
protected against litigation or expropriation in this country, the risks of which need to be
further assessed. The Secretariat submitted the first draft of the privileges and immunities
agreement to Malawi in 2015. In 2023 Malawi expressed an interest in restarting the
discussions on the Privileges and Immunities Agreement. The latest discussion in that regard
wa s held in February 2023.
82.
The Heads of the Independent Redress Mechanism and Independent Integrity Unit have
both expressed that it would not be legally feasible to undertake their redress activities and/or
investigations, as appropriate, in countries where GCF is not provided with relevant privileges
and immunities. Therefore, it is recommended that disbursements by GCF are made only after
GCF has obtained satisfactory protection against litigation and expropriation in the country, or
ha s been provided with appropriate privileges and immunities.
83.
In order to mitigate risk, it is recommended that any approval by the Board is made
su bject to the following conditions:
(a)
Signature of the Funded Activity Agreement in a form and substance satisfactory to the
Secretariat within 180 days of the date of Board approval; and
(b)
Completion of the legal due diligence to the satisfaction of the Secretariat.

Independent Technical Advisory Panel’s assessment of
FP238
Proposal name: Ecosystems-based Adaptation for Resilient Watersheds and
Communities in Malawi (EbAM)
Accredited entity: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)
Country: Republic of Malawi
Project/programme size: Medium
I. Assessment of the independent Technical Advisory Panel
1
1.
This funding proposal for a medium-sized cross-cutting project in environmental and
social safeguards Category B is submitted by the Government of Malawi through the Food and
Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) which will be the accredited entity (AE).
The two executing entities (EEs) are FAO and the Government of Malawi acting through three
state entities: the Ministry of Agriculture, the Ministry of Finance and Economic Affairs, and the
N ational Local Government Finance Committee.
2.
The total cost of the proposed project is USD 53.22 million, of which USD 42.81 million is
proposed as GCF finance and USD 10.41 million is co-finance from FAO and the Government of
M alawi (see section 1.6 below).
3.
The project objective is to increase the climate-change resilience of the most vulnerable
rural communities at watershed level in Malawi, in 11 districts (out of 28 districts in the
country) that have a combination of high exposure and/or sensitivity to climate change, with
low capacity to adapt positively to climate change impacts. These districts are: Dedza in the
centre; Zomba, Mangochi, Thyolo, Neno, Mwanza, Nsanje in the south; and Nkhata Bay, Rumphi,
K aronga and Chitipa in the north.
4.
In these districts, increases in temperature, rainfall variability and intense precipitation
events are leading to increased frequency and intensity of disasters such as floods, droughts and
landslides, which are interacting with directly human-caused soil erosion and land degradation
reducing agricultural productivity and causing human suffering. The project aims to be a
catalyst for a shift for ecosystems, livelihoods and agriculture in the country, from their baseline
states of high vulnerability to an alternative paradigm in which watershed ecosystems are
conserved, restored and sustainably managed, enabling these systems to adapt to climate
ch ange and continue supplying services to rural communities as the climate evolves.
5.
To achieve this, the project will promote an ecosystems-based adaptation (EbA)
approach – within the framework of participatory planning for integrated landscape
management – to repair degraded ecosystems, and promote low-carbon climate resilient
agricultural practices. This involves working through existing local governance structures to
develop integrated landscape/watershed management plans, already provided for in the
legislation of Malawi, applying an ecosystems-based approach. The sub-catchment and village
plans will then be implemented through a range of interventions on communal land, including:
soil and water conservation for erosion and run-off control (with contour bunds, swales, brush
fill, gully plugs and check dams); natural forest protection; assisted natural regeneration;
community forest and woodlot management; pastureland management; riverbank protection;

At farm level, technical assistance will promote agroecological approaches that can also
be regarded as EbA, including: use of climate-resilient crop species/varieties which are local,
native and/or well-adapted; crop diversification for better nutrition; agroforestry; integrated
pest management; and agronomic techniques for soil and water conservation. The project will
support producers in accessing markets and finance for further resilience investments, and will
enhance the enabling institutional and financial environment for scaling up of EbA approaches
na tionally.

1 .1 Impact potential
8.
The project is cross-cutting, with 95 per cent of GCF resources considered as
contributing to adaptation to climate change, and 5 per cent towards climate change mitigation.
The three targeted adaptation results areas are: enhancing the resilience of (i) most vulnerable
people and communities; (ii) health and well-being, and food and water security; and (iii)
ec osyste

9.
The funding proposal highlights the vulnerability of Malawi to
climate change, with drought caused by rising temperatures and more erratic rainfall; and
floods, wind damage and landslides caused by the increasing frequency and intensity of tropical
storms and cyclones. In all targeted districts, climate change effects will alter the onset of the
rainy season, translating into limited water availability at key growing times, and increased
water stress, with negative impacts on both cash and subsistence crops, and the overall rural
eco nomy and society.
10.
The project is expected to directly benefit around 270,820 members of smallholder farm
households in the 11 districts pre-identified for their high vulnerability to climate change
(methodology detailed in feasibility study, annex 2 to the funding proposal). These will be
residents of the 111 micro-catchments to be selected according to hydrological, ecological and
socioeconomic factors, from the 30 target Water Resource Unit sub-catchments within the
prioritized districts. An average micro-catchment will contain 10 villages in a cluster (see Figure
8.3.4 from the funding proposal, reproduced below), so that they are ecologically linked and can
be nefit from interventions at the landscape scale.
11.
Annex 2 to the funding proposal provides detail on how the projected number of
beneficiaries for each of the various capacity-building and extension activities was calculated,
and the assumptions made in these calculations. The vulnerability of these communities to
drought and flood damage will be reduced through collective investments in the landscape, and

12.
More than 300,000 people in villages that are not part of the targeted micro-catchments,
but are included in the selected sub-catchments, are considered to be indirect beneficiaries of
the project. Almost 70,000 households will not receive targeted support, but “will receive a
measurable adaptation benefit thanks to well-functioning Sub-Catchment Management
Committees and EbA Sub-Catchment Management Plans developed under Component 1”. Based
on this, the total number of project beneficiaries is estimated at nearly 575,000 people, of which
just over half are women. Neither the funding proposal nor annex 2 explain specifically what
indirect benefits are expected to flow from this improved planning environment, but these
could be assumed to include downstream benefits from catchment restoration, including
reduced flood damage and siltation from erosion, and increased availability of groundwater

13.
The project’s adaptation impact has the potential to be significant, but the extent to
which this can be quantified, measured and reported remains unclear, since the detailed
monitoring and evaluation (M&E) framework will be developed only during project
implementation, which poses some risks for fulfilling this potential. The indicators in the logical
framework (funding proposal section E.6) are incomplete. In relation to resilient livelihoods and
food systems, for example, no baseline information is yet in place for the indicators of stability
of household income, stability of crop yields, or volume of crop sales, nor any clear methodology
for assessing change, other than mentions of records, surveys and evaluations. For the number

14.
. Climate change mitigation through anticipated avoided and reduced
greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions as a result of project interventions, is expected to total
2
2,750,323 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (t CO eq) over 20 years, or an average of
2
137,516 t CO eq per year, contributing to the GCF forestry and land-use results area. This will
be achieved through communal landscape interventions and household on-farm interventions,
both of which involve changes in how forest, cropland and grassland are managed, to capture
an d store more carbon above and below ground.
15.
FAO’s own Ex-Ante Carbon Balance Tool (Ex-ACT) has been used to estimate in detail
the anticipated impact over 20 years of the resultant carbon sequestration and avoided
degradation, with results and methodology detailed in annex 22 to the funding proposal. In
response to a written question from the iTAP about why there is only one sentence about
monitoring, reporting and verification in annex 22, the AE elaborated on the planned process.
The M&E Geographical Information Systems specialist in the central Project Implementation
Unit will be trained on Ex-ACT, and will run the tool based on activity data collected through the
M&E system, with an M&E manual detailing the system to be developed and disseminated at
2
inc eption stage, describing the data sampling and analysis methodology.
16.
In response to a question from the iTAP about how precisely the list of landscape and
on-farm interventions to be tracked by the M&E specialist and technical experts from non-
governmental organizations will be related to the complex set of management changes
quantified in the ex-ante estimates, the AE developed a more detailed table that is useful in
clarifying these relationships as the basis for the detailed M&E plan (including mitigation
monitoring, reporting and verification) that is still to be developed. The table shows, for
example, that the Ex-ACT change in management from cropland under full tillage and low
carbon input (business as usual) to cropland under improved management with reduced tillage
and higher input of organic material (with project) is derived from Component 1 activities on
soil and water conservation and agroforestry, as well as Component 2.1’s Farmer Field School
support to conservation agriculture, manure management, reduced or zero tillage and the use of
cover crops and residues. The iTAP trusts that, in developing the M&E plan, the AE will spell out
these linkages in a clear system for tracking and reporting on parcels of land successfully
brought under new management practices, such that the area under changed management
practice can be taken as a proxy indicator of enhanced carbon sequestration/reduced
emissions, as per the Ex-ACT calculator methdology.
17.
The iTAP assesses the impact potential of the project as medium to high.
Scale: Medium
1. 2 Paradigm shift potential
18.
The proposed project aims to be a catalyst for a broad shift for ecosystem, livelihoods
and agriculture in the country, from their baseline state of very high vulnerability to an
alternative paradigm in which watershed ecosystems are conserved, restored, and sustainably
managed, thus granting their adaptation to climate change and their supply of services to
communities, people and their farming systems.

Additional written responses from FAO to the iTAP on 24 May 2024.

Upscaling and replication.
19.
The project design includes several features to enhance
sustainability, including using existing local governance structures and plans as the basis for
planning village and catchment-level EbA interventions in Component 1, and integrating village
plans into district plans. In response to a question from the iTAP on how replication will occur
beyond the sites, the AE highlighted that each Sub-Catchment Management Plan (SCMP) under
the project will cover beneficiary as well as non-beneficiary villages. Non-beneficiary villages
will thus be exposed to and can learn from their neighbours’ activities on village planning and
3
natural resource management. This kind of learning – simply through proximity – seems
optimistic, particularly given the scattering of the 111 micro-catchments across the country in
11 non-contiguous districts. This does not contribute to a clear pathway to scale, that is
necessary for the country to eventually achieve wall-to-wall coverage of catchment and village
pla ns and governance structures.
20.
Component 2 supports upscaling through incentives to the private sector to partner
with EbA producers, and uses government extension staff to support and learn from the
implementation of agro-ecological approaches and Farmer Field Schools. Component 3 directly
tackles the enabling institutional and financial environment, aiming to leverage climate finance
and to mainstream EbA approaches and practices into policies, sectoral planning and financing,
including government budgets, based on evidence generation on the benefits of EbA, best
practices and cases studies, and the preparation and implementation of a policy-influencing
plan. On the finance side there will be support to local financing institutions to develop new
products for financing EbA, with assistance from the Ministry of Finance and Economic Affairs
by integrating climate change responses into the existing “Financial Access for Rural Markets,
Smallholders and Enterprise” (FARMSE) project. These local financial institutions will be linked
to sources of capital, helping to trigger investment into them, so that they can step up their EbA
len ding

21.
Overall, the project relies heavily on temporarily funding a
large number of facilitators and consultants to provide capacity development, input delivery
and extension support. Although it is positive that these project-funded personnel will
cooperate and share learning with Ministry of Agriculture extension staff and other officials, it
may be difficult to sustain this level of support once the project implementation period ends. It
seems likely that similar fiscal constraints to those highlighted in relation to the needs of the
recipient country will still be in place after six years, making it difficult for government to
absorb these posts into the public sector wage budget, and impossible to create these kinds of
positions across the country. This means that sustaining results in the target districts and the
scaling up of SCMPs and Village Level Action Plans (VLAPs) to other sub-catchments in the
target districts, and to other districts in the country, may remain dependent on future donor
inv estments.
22.
Preparing to access voluntary carbon markets in future is presented as a part of the
project’s exit strategy, and this is welcomed by the iTAP, although the degree of success will
depend on many factors beyond the project’s control. The project itself will take only a limited
step in this direction, developing a baseline by taking an inventory of carbon stocks in the
project districts and catchments (including biomass measurements, forestry inventory, and soil
testing), using an existing methodology developed through the Restore Africa Programme, and
sh aring lessons through a knowledge platform.
23.
Also relevant are the project’s efforts to leverage climate finance through support to the
National Climate Change Fund (NCCF) and two conservation trust funds, but the strategy relies
heavily on supporting NCCF to become accredited to GCF, and supporting the Malawi
Environmental Endowment Trust to utilize the GCF Project Specific Accreditation Approach
modality and/or become accre dited. While the inclusion of feasibility studies on innovative
financing instruments is welcomed, including debt for nature swaps for th e Malawi

Microorganisms in soil regulate the flow of nutrients to plants, decompose organic matter, play a key role in

mycorrhizae, microbial fungi can massively extend the roots’ reach – critical in conditions of water scarcity.

1. 4 Needs of the recipient
31.
As highlighted in the funding proposal, Malawi is a least developed country, ranks low in
the United Nations Development Programme Human Development Index, and is among the 20
most vulnerable countries according to the Notre Dame Global Adaptation Initiative Index 2021.
The high exposure of Malawi to climate change can be characterized by the rise of temperatures,
rainfalls becoming more erratic, and increased frequency of climate-change induced disasters,
including droughts and floods. Moreover, the country is very sensitive to climate change
because of its high population density and growth, seriously degraded landscapes and
ecosystems, and large rural population in deepening poverty with high food insecurity. Adaptive
capacity is constrained by the limited literacy rate and low level of human development,
including for youth and women who are subject to unemployment and economic exclusion, with
women further subject to unwanted pregnancies, high maternal deaths, sexually transmitted
inf ections and gender-based violence.
32.
The project targets particularly vulnerable communities with severe adaptation needs in
the 11 targeted districts, where climate change effects will alter the onset of the rainy season,
resulting in limited and modified water availability and increased water stress. This will have
negative impacts on both cash and subsistence crops, resulting in adverse effects on the overall
rural economy and society. Production of the main staple crops in Malawi, including maize,
cassava and pigeon pea, are expected to experience major annual decreases in yield, with
8
corresponding loss of household nutrition. Communities under increased pressure from
declining crop yields may resort to a vicious cycle of maladaptation, unsustainable land use, and
harm to natural ecosystems. Shortages of vital ecosystem goods and services will, in turn,
wo rsen agricultural production shortages.
33.
The funding proposal states that the proposed 100 per cent concessionality of GCF
funding for the project is motivated by the high risk of overall debt distress in Malawi. It is
difficult for the country to meet its needs through debt finance for a paradigm shift towards
climate-resilient agricultural practices and land restoration. Although the figures on the
country’s indebtedness in the funding proposal are three years out of date, the iTAP notes that
the country had a debt-to-gross domestic product ratio of 74.5 per cent in 2023, while sovereign
9
de bt had increased to USD 10 billion.
34.
Overall, based on the above, the iTAP rates the needs of recipients as high.
Scale: High

36.
The proposed project is well aligned with the country’s
policies and strategies – including the Malawi Growth and Development Strategy III (2017–
2022), the nationally determined contribution (NDC), the National Agricultural Investment Plan
2017–2023, the National Forest and Landscape Restoration Strategy (2017) and the National
Resilience Strategy 2018–2030. By integrating climate change adaptation into SCMPs and
VLAPs, the project will support implementation of the Decentralization Act (1998), which
devolves powers and funding from the central government to districts. It is also consistent with
the Environmental Management Act (2017), the National Water Resources Act (2013), the new
National Disaster Risk Management Act of 2023 (the bill is referenced in the funding proposal)
an d implementation of the National Resilience Strategy (2018–2030).
37.
For adaptation, the NDC of Malawi (as updated in July 2021) puts emphasis on EbA,
integrated catchment conservation and management, and capacity development in resilient
agronomic practices and water conservation technologies for smallholder farmers. These
interventions are also in line with the country’s national adaptation plan, currently under
development with financial support from GCF. For mitigation, the updated NDC includes an
indicative emissions reduction contribution from the forestry and land use sector, through
implementation measures including afforestation, riparian restoration, agroforestry and
sustainable forest and landscape management, with adaptation and resilience co-benefits
highlighted. In the agriculture sector, dealt with separately, relevant practices are proposed
under crop management, including efficient use of fertilizer (including crop residue and

1. 6 Efficiency and effectiveness
44.
Of the project’s total proposed budget of USD 53.22 million, 80 per cent (USD 42.81
million) is proposed to be a GCF grant, and 20 per cent (USD 10.41 million) is made up of co-
fin ancing to the project, closely woven into the project logic. The co-financing is as follows:
45.
The Ministry of Finance and Economic Affairs will provide USD 6.44 million in grant co-
financing through the IFAD-funded FARMSE programme – supporting village savings and loans
associations; linking commercial banks, microfinance institutions, savings and credit
cooperative organizations, and insurance companies to climate financiers; and linking small and
me dium-sized enterprises to impac t investors.
46.
The Ministry of Agriculturewill provide in-kind co-financing for a total amount of USD
2.95 million in the form of the time of district heads of agriculture, agriculture extension
development officers and coordinators, and provision of venues for training of master trainers
an d facilitators.
47.
FAO will provide USD 523,000 of grant co-financing through the Global Environment
Facility -funded “Sustainable Forest Management, Dryland Sustainable Landscape Impact
Programme” and USD 500,000 through FAO’s Technical Cooperation Programme, covering
elements serving both projects: a policy assessment and the preparation of a policy influencing
plan; production of seeds and seedlings of native plant species; free, prior and informed consent
consultations; and an environmental and social assessment. Through this co-financing, the
project will form part of FAO’s contribution to the long-term vision for complementarity

The financial analysis considers the project investments in
farmland (landscape restoration, promotion of climate-adaptive crop-farming, agroforestry and
forest-based honey production) from the perspective of a beneficiary household. Costs and

labour), with models created for each of the two main activity types in the two landscape types,
as well as for honey production from beekeeping. Each of the five models compares the costs
and benefits of the beneficiaries’ activity with project and without project, and results are
discounted using a discount rate of 14.2 per cent, based on the real interest rate paid by
co mmercial or similar banks.
52.
The analysis presents the internal rate of return (IRR) only for honey production,
providing a high rate of return of 62 per cent, “because the investment in year 1 only amounts to
producers’ own capital contribution, since the rest is financed by a loan that is repaid in year 3”.
This loan is not mentioned in the funding proposal, or the feasibility study, though a proposed
“payment for ecosystems services” approach to honey production is outlined, building on an
interesting scheme piloted in Mitundu, Malawi, in which beekeepers lease trees from other
farmers with forested land, with local chiefs as intermediaries, creating an incentive for these
10
far mers to maintain the forest.

No IRR is shown for the other four production models, with the funding proposal
arguing that they represent shifts in agricultural practices based on annual crops with recurrent
and variable costs, rather than a large upfront investment cost, without which “the return on
investment is not a meaningful indicator”. The results in annex 3 simply show that the other
interventions would result in positive returns for beneficiaries, with net present values above
zero. It is then somewhat confusing that the funding proposal states in paragraph 142 that “all
financial models have… IRRs above the financial discount rate of 14.2 per cent”. If this is in fact
the case, then the provision of concessional loans rather than grants might have been more
appropriate for some of the production activities, bearing in mind that FAO is not accredited
wi th GCF for on-lending and/or blending (loans, equity and/or guarantees).

avoided and reduced GHG emissions as a result of the project interventions. This is
approximately USD 19 per tonne when considering the project as a whole, or USD 15 per tonne
when considering only the GCF investment, which seems high for the type of interventions
pr oposed.
